#### The Organizing Society: 

##### GDMB Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology 

The GDMB is a non-profit organization. Its activities focus on combining science with practical experience in the fields of mining, engineering, tunnelling, mineral processing, extraction, recycling and refining of metals, as well as on the manufacturing of semi and finished products. There is an increasing emphasis on associated environmental issues. The GDMB is internationally active with a European basis and covers a wide variety of topics from applied geology via processing to recycling. These include many important areas of chemistry, especially the complex metallurgical chemistry and, last not least, also analytical chemistry. As a consequence of their increasing importance, aspects of industrial minerals are addressed in addition to the traditional fields of metals and alloys. In order to remain a vibrant and attractive professional society, the GDMB draws on the experience and interests of its worldwide members.

#### Preface 

###### Copper – Indicator of the progress of civilization 

This is the motto for the 7<sup>th</sup> international copper conference, the most important copper seminar in the world, which has been organized by the GDMB, the German based Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology, together with IIMCh from Chile, MetSoc from Canada, TMS, SME from USA and MMIJ from Japan. 

The copper conferences bring together the highest level of science and technology: universities, metal producers, manufacturing companies, suppliers and finally the people who work with copper: scientists, technicians, engineers, traders and many more. 

An extensive programme has been arranged for this conference and an abundance of contributions from all over the world dealing with the different aspects of copper making and its use are registered already, for which we gratefully thank the authors. Apart from plenary addresses, separate sessions will be held for economics, mineral processing, pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, electrowinning and -refining, downstream fabrication and application, process control and automation, recycling and sustainable development, environmental control, health and safety. Copper, one of the oldest metals used by mankind, is still today one of the most important industrial metals and indispensable for modern life. It is the indicator of industrialization and progress in every country. It is used everywhere, where electricity flows and thus is still valued so highly today. The increased economic potential of newly industrialized countries, above all East Asia and China, has increased the significance of the red metal once again. More recent technologies in production, processing and application often provide new answers to old questions. From the middle of the last century there was another innovation surge resulting in totally new technologies, a trend still going on. This has made each copper conference into an exciting adventure. It is positive and reassuring that particularly the high industrialized countries have become the vanguard, not just in technical innovation, but also protection of environment and nature and preserving resources. They repeatedly prove that ecology and economy may go hand in hand. 

Many sponsors have contributed to the conference’s success, for which I would like to express my sincere thanks! 

Hamburg is expecting its guests! Hamburg, the old Hanseatic city with a 1200 year long tradition, one of the biggest and most beautiful cities in Germany, combines a wonderful mixture of industry, commerce, nature and culture. Not only the “Copper 2

010” in the Congress Centre awaits you, but rich offerings of sightseeing and shopping in a cosmopolitan city, one of the largest harbours in Europe, the Alster lake in the city centre, green parks and plenty of cultural events, some of which we hope to show you in the companions programme. 

We are delighted that you will join us and look forward to a highly interesting conference! 

_Michael Kopke_ Chairman Copper 2010

###### Is the Copper Industry Fit for the Future? 

Dr.-Ing. Bernd Drouven, CEO, Aurubis AG, Hamburg, Germany 

The copper world has already changed a great deal during recent years. But what still lies ahead of us? What are the changes in conditions that we have to cope with and how will our solutions look? 

The rise in the demand for raw materials is unrelenting. At the same time, both the primary and secondary feed materials have a specific complexity, the customers’ needs are becoming increasingly differentiated and their orders are placed at increasingly short notice. Production times for metals have to be faster and inventories minimised. 

The volatility of the metal prices has increased significantly in recent years and we will probably have to live with that in the future as well. The LME functioned well in the crisis, but the copper price is being influenced more and more by funds. 

How can the value added chain change to adapt to this? Which consequences will that have for process technology, production planning and logistics? How will the consolidation of our industry continue? 

This keynote will go into the various effects and challenges – in particular from the perspective of a European custom smelter and fabricator – and present possible approaches for solutions. 

###### Sustainable Growth Strategy for Japanese Copper Business 

Toshinori Kato, Managing Director, Mitsubishi Materials Corporation, Tokyo, Japan 

Business environment, for any industry, has changed dramatically over the last decade. Copper industry is no exception and those involved are experiencing an unprecedented period of upheaval. The landscape of the market has completely altered, with large-scale M&As taking place among miners - creating an oligopoly situatio

n - and a rapid expansion of smelting capacity within developing countries, driven by strong economic growth. Traditional copper smelters and fabricators have been facing challenges, but a long-term sustainability of Japanese copper business is achievable. 

Firstly, an immense amount of effort has been made over the years to develop the clean and one of the most environmentally-friendly processes in the industry. Mitsubishi Materials (MMC) particularly plays a great role in establishing Japanese smelters’ reputation as the most energy-efficient operations in the world. It is our strong commitment to be a leader in this expertise by sharing our technologies with the industry.

Secondly, infrastructures for copper smelting have been utilized in developing the recycling business. Exemplified by the operations at Onahama smelter, which has the world’s largest furnace for treatment of shredder residue, the industry has worked closely with other sectors and municipalities. Building an effective structure to make the best use of our facilities is a key for success in this field. It is fair to say that Japanese copper smelters, including MMC, are now regarded as an indispensable part of national environmental policy. 

Finally, progression of integration in the copper fabrication sector has strengthened the industry’s capability of providing a variety of high-value-added products to end-users. Tight relationships with the consumers have been beneficial in developing new use of copper. Evidence of a promising future can be seen in increasing use of copper in the growing sectors such as hybrid automobiles and renewable energy. 

###### Copper Sulphide Smelting: Past Achievements and Current Challenges 

Dr. Carlos M. Dнaz, Adjunct Professor, University of Toronto, Private Consultant, Toronto, Canada 

In the last three decades, increased oxygen consumption in copper sulphide smelting and converting and the implementation of computerized process control, among other factors, have led to higher process intensity and smelter concentrate processing capacity, decreased smelting energy consumption and improved SO2 capture from process gas streams. An annual primary smelting furnace throughput of one million tonnes of concentrate is the new industry standard. Top submerged lance smelting has become an important processing route in recent years. Two new continuous converting routes were commercialized in the 1990s. However, due to substantially improved converting practice and larger converters, Peirce-Smith converting still maintains its position as the dominant technology. 

A major realignment of world copper smelting has taken place in the last 30 years. Spurred by rapid economic expansion and the resulting huge increase in demand for basic materials, a number of modern, large capacity copper smelters have been built in China, India and other Asian countries. Only moderate growth in smelting and electrorefining capacity

has taken place elsewhere. Moreover, ER cathode output in the USA has substantially decreased. 

In this paper, the author examines recent technological advances and industry changes and highlights issues, such as energy consumption and the corresponding greenhouse gas emissions that will become the focus of future discussion. 

###### Energy as a Key Factor of Sustainability 

Javier Targhetta, Vice President, Freeport McMoRan, Phoenix, Arizona, USA 

Energy must be seen as the prime mover for development and is therefore vital for economic equilibrium and social welfare. Energy will continue to play a key role in the coming decades being not only an environmental challenge but also a fundamental issue in terms of the progress of humanity. Nevertheless, harmonizing several aspects related to energy management will be of essence for the

near future and will make energy one of the greatest challenges of the 21<sup>st</sup> century. It is becoming increasingly important to maintain the appropriate equilibrium between environmental issues (global warming, the future of nuclear waste, the integration of renewable energies…), coordinated governments policies to ensure that global energy costs are kept competitive and companies finding a balanced, rational and fair model of energy utilization based on the review of ethical business aspects and the establishment of social responsibility principles. 

This paper develops the idea that the rules and procedures for future energy use must be based on a reasonable equilibrium between technical aspects mainly associated to environmental issues, political decisions made by governments and public administrations and social responsibility programmes that companies themselves must assume and implement.

David Coombs 

Brook Hunt (a Wood Mackenzie Company) 45 High Street Addlestone, England 

**Keywords:** Costs, prices, capital, operating, cost escalation 

#### Abstract 

Over the last three decades of the twentieth century, and into the start of the first decade of the twenty-first century, cash operating costs for the production of copper witnessed a structural decline. This reflected the development of new technology including the widespread adoption of leach technology, and also reflected the economies of scale to be seen in the move towards larger scale open pit mining, again made possible due to advances in technology. Costs were also positively influenced by geo-political changes, with for example the opening up of Chile to foreign investment in the early 1980s with its abundant copper resources. 

Over the past five years however the industry has noted an acceleration in both capital and operating costs which has reversed this thirty year or so trend. The paper comments upon this cost escalation and opines that most of these costs are permanently embedded. 

The paper describes the factors that go to make up operating costs, describes changes over the period 2002 to the present and provides Brook Hunt’s view as to how they may evolve over the next decade. 

The paper reveals how capital costs have escalated over the last five years and the impact this had had on capital intensity and the prices required to achieve a viable rate of return on investment. The capital intensity of projects in construction at end-2009 is almost 50 % higher in real terms than those mines developed over 1985 to 2005, and unfunded projects have capital intensities typically 70 % higher. This provides justification for significantly higher long-term cycle average prices. 

By reference to the demand for additional mine capacity it is concluded that the price expectations potential investors must hold if adequate capacity is to be developed to keep the market in balance is around $1.80/lb on a five year view and in excess of a $2.00/lb view looking out a decade.

#### 1 Introduction 

Over the last three decades of the twentieth century, and into the start of the first decade of the twenty-first century, cash operating costs for the production of copper witnessed a structural decline. This reflected the development of new technology – the focus of this conference, including the widespread adoption of leach

technology, and also reflected the economies of scale to be seen in the move towards larger scale open pit mining, again made possible due to advances in technology. Costs were also positively influenced by geo-political changes, with for example the opening up of Chile with its abundant copper resources to foreign investment in the early 1980s. Over the past five years however the industry has noted an acceleration in both capital and operating costs which has reversed this thirty year trend. The paper will comment upon this cost escalation and provide opinion as to whether these costs are permanently embedded or are cyclical and may reverse. The presentation will conclude by offering our thoughts as to what the implications these factors will have on copper prices over the next decade. #### 2 Long Term Copper Prices Figure 1 illustrates the copper price in real 2009$ terms over the past century with a schematic as to how we look out into the future – which will be returned to. It shows that the copper price is cyclical and over the period from the 1970s to mid-2000s appeared in structural decline. This paper will outline our view as to why we believe this downtrend has reversed and provide some pointers as to likely future prices. The Brook Hunt approach to forecasting copper prices over the longer-term – which in this context will be defined as over the next price cycle, or approximately ten years, is driven by our estimates for the demand for refined copper. These refined demand estimates are based on the intensity of use of copper in various sectors and regions and end-use demand growth in these segments. In practice growth is assumed to remain cyclical with global industrial production the key economic driver. This itself is impacted by advances in technology, changes in environmental legislation and the economics of scrap processing. In 2009 scraps processed at smelters and refineries accounted for 16 % of refined production at 2.9 Mt. Further to this scrap supply, the direct use of scrap (3.8 Mt) accounted for the equivalent of 22 % of refined demand (17.1 Mt) in 2009. We forecast that scraps will contribute around 32 % of total copper demand over the next price cycle, and note that the availability of scrap is cyclical influenced by price, with scrap likely

to contribute between 28-36 % of total use. These price levels relate directly to the forecast cost structure of the industry. As the correlation between industry costs and the copper price are less strong over the entire cycle than at periods of excess supply, we believe that the best indicator as to future cycle average prices (indicated by the bold line on Figure 1) reflects the costs of investing in new capacity and the financial returns that these investments can potentially generate. We form our view as to cycle average price by examining the incentive price to achieve a given rate of return from each project. #### 15 Conclusions 

Over this decade commencing 2010 we anticipate operating costs at mine-site to remain at 2009 levels with much of the cost increases witnessed over the latter half of the last decade structurally embedded. Unless excess smelting and refining capacity is closed, commercial terms are likely to remain favourable to miners and largely offset the small reductions in by-product credits anticipated. Based on December 2009 exchange rates, cycle trough prices of around $1.40/lb are anticipated. 

Over the next five years, the capital and operating costs of projects suggests that companies need to believe in a long-term cycle average copper price in excess of $1.80/lb if new supply is to meet demand. Going out further into the future copper prices in excess of $2.00/lb will be demanded. 

Potential changes in water rights in the Atacama could increase operating costs in this region of the order of 20 c/lb and tip the balance against development for certain projects. This said other projects may benefit from more global competition in the construction sector. 

Capital and operating costs have been particularly volatile over the last five years and given the dynamics driving these, this volatility is unlikely to dissipate. The individual assets vulnerable to closure and those viable to develop will therefore continue to evolve over time.

### Impact of the CO2 Emission Trading Scheme on the Copper Industry 

Ulf Gehrckens 

Aurubis AG Corporate Energy Affairs HovestraЯe 50 20539 Hamburg, Germany 

**Keywords:** CO2 emissions, energy efficiency, direct emissions, indirect emissions, recycling 

#### Abstract 

Europe is the global leader in its endeavours to prevent the climate change caused by CO2 emissions. The target of a 20 % reduction in CO2 emissions could have been increased to 30 % on account of the Copenhagen agreement. 

EU ETS phase III refers to the period from 2013 to 2020. As a rule, all CO2 emission rights will be auctioned. Electricity generators will participate in auctions to purchase CO2 emiss

ion rights, but they will be able to pass on the cost of CO2 in their electricity prices. 

The copper industry is one of the sectors exposed to the risk of carbon leakage and therefore generally receives free emission rights for direct emissions, but the recycling sector is facing difficulties in receiving free certificates. However, the final compensation method is the most important issue (grandfathering, benchmarking, fallback option). 

But the impact on the copper industry is three-fold: the impact due to its own emissions, as mentioned above, called direct emissions and the impact due to purchased electricity, which includes the costs for CO2 emissions during the generation of electricity, called indirect emissions. Moreover additional indirect costs are expected as a result of increased operating supplies and transport costs. 

At the moment the biggest threat is the sharpening of the compensation criteria for indirect emission costs by EC DG Competition, because indirect costs are more than two times as important as direct emissions. 

Furthermore, these measures do not reflect the international character of the copper industry where the prices are quoted on the LME and it is not possible for the European industry to pass the CO2 costs on to their customers. Compensation equal to the financial burden is therefore needed for the

copper industry and the compensation method has to include future additional capacity to ensure further growth in Europe. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Scientists are largely in agreement that the unlimited discharge of CO2 worldwide represents one of the main reasons for the greenhouse effect and if the annual rate of increase continues, the result will be an imminent climate catastrophe. The international community is therefore striving to reduce CO2 and to manifest this in a global agreement. Thus, following Rio and Kyoto, politicians from all over the world met in Copenhagen in December 2009 to define the basic conditions. The Western European industrial nations, as the driving force, are prepared to make firm agreements on concrete reduction targets until 2020 and then until 2050 for their countries, but at the same time demand firm undertakings in this respect from other countries. 

On the European side, it is surely possible to argue convincingly against the USA, since the latter emits disproportionately more CO2 than Europe and in a direct comparison, i.e. per capita, discharges about twice as much. The discussion with the Chinese is however more difficult, because although they are the world champions in CO2 emissions and have a huge annual rate of increase, emissions per capita are only one tonne per annum, i.e. only a tenth of the European and consequently a twentieth of the USA’s emissions. As an illustration of the magnitude: running a small car (Fiat Panda) with an average way of driving is sufficient to cause about one tonne of CO2 emissions, but th

ere we do not have an cooker, heating, dishwasher, washing machine, holiday trips, air conditioning, toaster, computer, lighting, etc. not to mention a medium-size vehicle or even luxury car. Inasmuch the vision that we Europeans would reach Chinese per capita levels by sinking our living standards is rather an illusion. On the other hand, it is very thinkable that the Chinese, of whom only every twentieth is a car owner today, have set their sights on reaching our or even the American living standards, and thus their current emissions will rise significantly; not to mention those of the Africans, Indians and South Americans. Since it is human nature to have an urge for more comfort, we can only stabilise global CO2 emissions or even reduce them if technically mature products achieve the same benefit with considerably less energy consumption, and the needed basic materials for their fabrication – such as copper and other nonferrous metals - are produced in the most environmentally compatible manner. That the „climate protectors’“ need to impose levies on energy-intensive industry for their CO2 emissions seems to be sensible at first glance, since this motivates ideas to make production processes with even less emissions, wherever possible. However, if this does not happen worldwide at the same time, and local industry already uses the best available technology (BAT), since energy prices already offered massive incentives for reducing consumption in the past, an additional levy for CO2 represents a simple tax and no longer an incentive for improvement. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2118 _Impact of the CO2 Emission Trading Scheme on the Copper Industry_ Since the copper market is a global market, it is not possible for a copper smelter to pass on this additional tax to its customers and as a consequence its competitiveness could be weakened compared with other copper smelters which happen to be located in a country without such levies. Since European copper smelters have on an international average the lowest energy input per tonne of produced copper, the CO2 emissions would tend to increase by relocating production facilities to non-European countries. We call this effect „carbon leakage“, and it must be urgently avoided in order that the CO2 exposure is not increased artificially. Aurubis Hamburg

#### 4 Direct Emissions 

To receive licences for its own CO2 emissions free-of-charge, it is imperative that the company is on the list of the „exposed sectors“. It is however not guaranteed that the quantity of certificates allocated free-of-charge will be sufficient to ensure that there is no competitive disadvantage compared with copper smelters in countries operating without ETS. 

The EU Commission has requested several institutes to propose a benchmark system, which identifies the 10 % best production plants per sector, which should receive the highest possible allocation.

All other production plants receive only as many licences as the benchmark and must buy additionally required certificates. 

The institutes were informed as a general condition that the feed material was not of importance. It was only significant how much CO2 discharge was produced per tonne of finished product. The Fraunhoferinstitut was used for copper, which divided production into primary copper production and copper recycling. The latter is being treated separately as a consequence. Several discussions between Fraunhoferinstitut, the European Copper Institute (ECI), Eurometaux (EM) and the main European copper producers reached the conclusion that a uniform benchmark system cannot be sensible in view of the very heterogeneous production processes, although they were certainly a good idea for their respective regions, and the low number of copper smelters (7). In order to filter off the 10 % best smelters, a basic number of 30-40 is generally required. The Fraunhoferinstitut also realised that the starting material could not be ignored, not only due to the varying complexity, but also owing to the different C values already at the concentrate stage. Further questions quickly arose: 

- How should smelters be treated which are installed in a region without gas grids and thus use oil with comparably high CO2 emissions? 

- What action should be taken if a metallurgical process requires a specific fuel with higher CO2 load? Etc. 

The interim result is now a so called „fallback option“: fuel mix benchmark with natural gas as reference. Exemption is justified when a process is tied to another specific fuel (e.g. oil or coke) or if no gas

grid is available. Or grandfathering whereby on the one hand attention must be paid that carbon in the concentrate receives full free-of-charge licenses and no further reduction factor is demanded if this does not apply as well for other main industrial sectors with benchmarks. On the other hand production expansions must receive free licences – as mentioned above – with the aim of reducing total global emissions. 

Since as of 2013 part of 20 % of the required certificates, in 2020 then 70 % and in 2027 finally 100 % have to be purchased by the producers in auctions, it is still unclear whether these factors will be applied as well to the certificates from the exposed sectors that are to be auctioned. 

#### 5 Indirect Emissions 

Indirect CO2 emission costs basically mean costs that the energy supplier passes on to its customers, since as of 2013 they must pay 100 % (i.e. without payment stages as for the direct CO2 emission costs) for their largely – up to now – free-of-charge licences. For the copper industry, in this case particularly for Aurubis, the indirect CO2 costs represent a disproportionately higher financial burden than for the direct CO2 emissions. One reason is that more than 30 % of our electricity consumption is used for environmental abatement measures. Thus we are adversely affected twice over

2122 

_Impact of the CO2 Emission Trading Scheme on the Copper Industry_ 



and quasi punished, for example, for operating each electrical filter which is used to clean a blower, despite its environmentally exemplary operation as regards SO2 or other emissions. 

The EU Commission basically left it to the member states in December 2008 whether and to what extent they wanted to give companies in the exposed sectors compensation for indirect CO2 costs so as to avoid carbon leakage. The idea was that the member state should give back part of the money to the energy-intensive industry which was received by the energy suppliers in the auctions to compensate for the additional CO2 costs in electricity as of 2013. In the second half of 2009 this resulted in irritation since DG Competition pleaded that there should be new more stringent criteria for possible compensation for indirect CO2 costs, which varied from those defined by the EU Commission in December 2008. This would mean that the copper sector is no longer exposed as regards indirect CO2 costs and thus, for instance, Germany no longer authorised to pay Aurubis compensation, unless this was regarded as state aid. Much more serious was however the resultant loss of confidence in the European policy, particularly as such an authorisation would be illegal in accordance with a legal opinion we have received. A final result cannot probably be expected before 2011, but there is no doubt that the uncertainty governing until then will have a dampening impact on capital investment. 

But even if these irritations could be removed, it is still completely unclear

how high a possible compensatory payment might be. The average CO2 discharge from all power plants in Europe amounts to about 0.4 tonnes of CO2 per Megawatt hour (MWh) produced. The average is considerably less in France on account of the high portion of nuclear energy and in Sweden due to the high water power portion, but in Germany it is much higher at 0.6 tonnes of CO2 per MWh due to the significant coal-fired portion. A modern coal-fired power plant produces about 0.75 tonnes of CO2/MWh, a brown coal power plant about 1 tonne of CO2/MWh, a gas power plant 0.35 tonnes of CO2/MWh. However, some 0.8 tonnes of CO2/MWh are calculated definitely in Germany, since the electricity price in Germany is formed on the European Energy Exchange (EEX) in accordance with the Merit Order Principle and therefore is based on the last bad power plant with high CO2 values in the price and not the average value. From the energy supplier’s perspective, this is understandable since it wants to have costs covered with the input of its last power plant – including the CO2 costs that must then be paid. 

Industry’s simple demand is that the compensation must correspond with the real actual burden! In other words no windfall profits but also no additional financial burdens. 

Unfortunately it will not be easy to determine the correct pricing factor per region at all and this in addition will constantly change depending on the mode of operation of the various power plants. This also poses a problem in the view of the member states, since the finance ministers receive on average licence fees for 0.6 tonnes of CO2/MWh and should pay out 0.8 tonnes of CO2/MWh to the industry. The windfall profits are achieved by the energy suppliers, which operate power plants and water power plants, and cash in licence fees for these of 0.8 tonnes of CO2/MWh from the average customer without having any financial burden for these power plants at all.

The basic problem was recognised by the Commission as far back as December 2008 and as a result the word „average” CO2 factor was replaced by the word „relevant” CO2 factor in the directive. This point will also cause considerable discussion. 

Only to give the whole picture there will be additionally indirect CO2-costs besides the ones paid in the electricity price: All the deliveries from local producers needed for the treatment and refining process will be more expansive. 

#### 6 Recycling 

According to ECI, 40 % of the entire copper demand in Europe is covered by recycling. Copper can be recycled as often as required without loss of quality. Copper recycling stands for sustainability, the conservation of resources and provides the only valid local raw material source in Germany. Recycling of pure copper scrap emits 4 times less CO2 and uses 3 times less energy than primary production. 

It was also not possible to find a uniform Europe-wide benchmark for recycling because the complex

ity of the feed materials alone make a simple comparison of „CO2 discharge per tonne of cathode copper produced “ impossible. Particularly the recycling of complex feed materials was always the aim of the EU Commission so that the metals could be recovered and the landfills relieved. The production of cathode copper from such starting materials with possibly only 3 % Cu is however not comparable with copper production from pure copper scrap (99 % Cu) since a much greater total mass must be melted down for complex materials and they must go through numerous additional processing stages. The CO2 discharge can be 20 times higher with the result that when the benchmark is calculated for pure copper scrap, a recycler of complex scrap must purchase quasi 95 % of its required CO2 licenses. If the additional costs were included in the price, this would have the unavoidable consequence that the company could not obtain the respective scrap quantities on the global market but would lose out to a competitor in a country outside the EU27 with no such requirements. The result is refuse tourism and a processing method, which in no way meets our environmental or occupational safety needs.

#### 1 Rise of the Phoenix 

##### 1.1 History of the Phoenix Mine Site 

The Phoenix mine is located approximately 13 miles southwest of Battle Mountain, Nevada, USA toward the southern end of the Battle Mountain range. The site lies geographically between San Francisco, California and Salt Lake City, Utah. Figure 1 below shows the relative location of the site. 



Figure 1: Location of Newmont Mining Corporation’s Phoenix Mine (MapQuest, 2009).

The Phoenix mine site is no stranger to mining activity. Initial mining can be traced back to as early as the 1860’s. Modern mining at the site began in 1964 by the Duval Corporation with a copper (Cu) flotation facility at what is known as Copper Canyon. 

It was not until an exploration program in the early 1970’s that Duval realized they were literally sitting on a gold mine. Millions of tons of low grade gold-silver ore were deposited near the existing site. In 1977, mining and milling of the copper ores ceased and the turn toward gold (Au) production began. In 1979, the Fortitude gold mill was started. Duval utilized the existing mill facilities and added a cyanide (CN) leach carbon in pulp (CIP) circuit. 

In 1977, Duval constructed one of the first copper leach – solvent extraction – electrowinning (L-SX-EW) facilities in the country at the nearby Copper Basin mine. Utilizing dump leaching with three extraction and two strip stages, the facility had a production capacity of 7665 short tons per annum. This innovative new technology was utilized at the site from 1979-1984. 

In 1984, Battle Mountain Gold Corporation was spun off from Duval. Battle Mountain Gold operated the gold mill through 1993. The Reona heap leach was operated from 1994 through 1998, when ore placements on the pad stopped. 

Newmont merged with Battle Mountain Gold in 2001. The Phoenix Project feasibility study began almost immediately. The feasibility study was completed in 2003. The leach pad and carbon in columns (CIC’s) operated with no mining activity occurring until Newmont began placing ore back on the Reona leach pad in early 2004. 

Construction on the Phoenix mill began in November 2004. Mill start-up took place in March of

2006, signifying that the _Phoenix_ had indeed risen from the ashes. The 33,600 short ton per day (30,481 tonnes per day) Phoenix mill consists of a gravity gold recovery and treatment circuit, a flotation circuit which produces a copper/gold/silver concentrate, and a leach-CIP circuit to recover any residual gold from the tails. 

In 2005, recognizing the potential to further exploit the mineral deposit at Phoenix, a scoping study was initiated around options for recovering copper from the oxide portion of the ore body. A run-ofmine (ROM) heap leach and SX/EW plant were selected as the best options to pursue. A prefeasibility study followed in 2006, further affirming the chosen technology and some of the basic plant design concepts. In 2007 work began on the feasibility study which continued to the end of 2008 when the project was temporarily put on hold due to the economic downturn and the drastic reduction in copper prices. The L-SX-EW project will be the focus this paper.

#### 2 Project Design<sup>1</sup> 

##### 2.1 ROM Leach Pad 

The Phoenix copper leach project will utilize a conventional leach pad design to facilitate the stacking of ROM copper oxide and transition ores as well as the subsequent leaching and solution collection and pumping. 

The leach pad is designed in three phases. Phases I – III have capacities of 54 million tons, 52 million tons, and 44 million tons respectively. The pad will be constructed in 20 foot (6.1 meter) lifts to a maximum height of 300 feet (91.4 m). The total leach pad area encompasses nearly 400 acres (161.8 hectares). 

The leach pad is a double lined pad, utilizing a compacted clay liner (prepared subgrade) with a permeability of less than 1x10<sup>-6</sup> cm/s at 92 % of the maximum dry density [20]. This layer is overlain with a double textured 80-mil high density polyethylene (HDPE) geomembrane. A protective layer of sand and gravel or silt and a maximum size of 1” (25.4 mm) will be placed on top of the liner, followed by the coarse aggregate drainage layer and solution collection piping. 

A process component monitoring system (PCMS) was incorporated into the pad design to allow for operational monitoring of each cell independently of the others. The leach pad has a total of ten cells. The PCMS is also incorporated into the leak monitoring system design. 

In addition to the pad, the leach circuit also consists of four ponds: the raffinate (raff) pond, the pregnant leach solution (PLS) pond, the Phase I events pond, and the Phase II events pond. The ponds are double lined with a smooth 80-mil HDPE geomembrane and an 80-mill textured primary liner. Each pond has a sloped bottom and a leak collection and recovery system (LCRS). The pad phases, cells, and ponds of the leach pad are shown in Figure 2 below.

The raff pond, the PLS pond, and the Phase I events pond are required for the construction of the Phase I leach pad. The Phase II events pond is adequate for both Phases II and III of the leach pad. Operating ponds are designed to handle the operating volume as well as having freeboard for unplanned power losses. The events ponds are designed to accommodate pad drain down as well as a 100 year storm event. The ponds have a total volume of nearly 85 million gallons (322 million liters). 

The raff pond is located approximately two miles northeast of the leach pad near the SX/EW facility. The raff pond has a capacity of approximately four million gallons (15,141,647 liters). The pond location is also approximately 200 feet (61 m) higher in elevation than the leach pad. To capitalize on the elevation difference, the raff feed to the leach pad will be achieved utilizing five selfpriming pumps to feed a constant head tank which will then gravity flow down to the leach pad. Recognizing that as the pad gets higher, gravity flow will no longer be feasible, booster pumps were also incorporated into the design for future integration. 

Organic entrainment in the raffinate is inevitable. As such, an organic recovery system will be implemented on the raff pond. The pond layout is such that the prevailing winds are expected to assist

in collecting any organic in the northeast corner of the pond where the skimmers will be located. The skimmers will pump the material to a separation tank to remove the raffinate. The organic will be run through the crud treatment system prior to being reintroduced into the organic stream. 

The raffinate is distributed to the leach pad via drip emitters at a design rate of 12,500 gallons per minute (gpm) (47,318 lpm) [21]. The Phoenix ores vary in acid consumption by ore type. The average acid consumption is anticipated to be 30 pounds per ton (lb/ton) (12.4 kg/tonne). The pH in the raffinate will be maintained between 1.5 and 3. 

Because the Phoenix site is in a high desert climate, temperature had to be considered in the design. Although the summers can be very warm, several months in the year see average temperatures at or below freezing (32 °F or 0 °C), while every month of the year has below freezing temperatures recorded. In fact, it is not uncommon to see the temperature fall below 0 °F (-18 °C) in the winter months. As a result, the drip emitters will be lain in shallow ripped trenches on the pad and pushed over to help insulate the lines from freezing during these months. 

The leach pad will be on a 90 day leach cycle before the pad is allowed to dry and new ore is placed. Unlike many copper heap leach operations, Phoenix saw no benefit to an acid cure. However, ut

ilizing a high flow, low flow application does have a positive effect on leaching. The design application rate is 0.01 gpm/ft<sup>2</sup> (0.41 lpm/m<sup>2</sup> ) for the first two weeks of operation. For the remaining period of the leach cycle, a rate of 0.005 gpm/ft<sup>2</sup> (0.20 lpm/m<sup>2</sup> ) will be utilized. 

The PLS will be collected and monitored with the PCMS. Ultimately all PLS will report to the PLS pond. In order to reduce the introduction of fine particulates into the SX plant, the inflow to the PLS pond initially reports to a segregated sediment storage compartment. This will allow these fine solids to settle out before the PLS overflows an internal berm into the operating portion of the pond. Five 500 horsepower (hp) vertical turbine pumps will be utilized to pump the PLS from the pond to the SX plant. These are the same pumps already utilized in the mill reclaim circuit with the exception that the PLS pumps will be CD4MCu stainless steel for corrosion resistance. 

Both the PLS and raffinate solution conveyance pipelines will be constructed of varying sizes and densities of HDPE pipe. The pipelines will run in a 12 ft wide by 3 ft (3.66 m x 0.91 m) deep lined channel. As with the leach pad and ponds, 80 mil double textured liner will be utilized over a layer of prepared subgrade. This will prevent solution loss and environmental release in the event of a line failure. 

Due to the environmental permitting sequencing in Nevada, the leach pad can be constructed with one lift of ore placed upon receipt of a Water Pollution Control Permit (WPCP). However, leaching and plant construction cannot begin until a Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement (SEIS) is approved, which will be the lagging permit. With the anticipated approval dates and construction durations, the leach pad will have ample ore placed to begin leaching approximately three months prior to plant startup. This will allow time to build solution inventories and for a higher grade PLS to be generated. This will provide for a reduced duration between startup and cathode production.

##### 2.2 Solvent Extraction 

As mentioned, the solvent extraction plant is located approximately two miles northeast of the leach pad, and due west of the existing mill facility. Solution will enter the plant via an HDPE pipe as described above. The Phoenix SX plant has a design PLS grade of 0.66 grams per liter (g/L). Recognizing that the PLS grade will vary over time, such as with the initial flows, as well as depending on ore type being leached, the plant was designed for flexibility. 

The plant design will utilize two extraction mixer-settlers to selectively remove the copper from the PLS solution by loading it onto the organic extractant. A single stage strip mixer-settler will be employed to strip the copper from the loaded organic into the electrolyte. To allow for the potential variances in the PLS grades, th

e extraction mixer-settlers are designed to be operated in either series, counter current flow or in parallel flow. 

The intent is to start the plant in series flow (2 + 1) and change to parallel flow (1 + 1 + 1) as operating conditions level out and the PLS grade stabilizes. The circuit will begin with E1 and S1 operating as organic continuous with E2 aqueous continuous. Once the circuit is changed to parallel flow, the entire circuit will be organic continuous to help minimize organic loss to raffinate. 

The mixer-settlers will be arranged in a four square versus the more traditional linear arrangement. The fourth “square” of the circuit is the loaded organic tank which will serve as the storage tank for the bulk loaded organic for feeding the strip mixer-settler. Each settler tank is 102 ft (31 m) long by 94 ft (28.7 m) wide and 51 in (1.3 m) deep. The material of construction was chosen to be 316 stainless steel for the corrosion resistance to acidic solutions. The piping in the SX area is also 316 stainless steel. The mixer-settlers will be covered to reduce the introduction of outside particulates, and protect he process from wind, sunlight, and evaporative losses. 

A 40-hp pump mixer is designed to provide the initial contact between the PLS and the barren organic in the extractors. Secondary and tertiary turbine mixers will be installed in individual mix boxes to maintain the contact PLS and organic mixing. Each pump will utilize a 7.5-hp motor. The strip mixer-settler will be equipped with one 40-hp pump mixer and one 7.5-hp turbine mixer. Figure 3 below shows the general profile of a mixer-settler.

Each of the extraction settlers will utilize two rows of picket fences for dispersion to ensure parallel flow down the length of the settler. The first fence is in a reverse V-shape while the second row fence runs horizontal across the settler. The organic overflows a weir into a trough while the aqueous passes under the trough to then overflow a separate, adjustable aqueous weir. 

Rather than pump mixers, the loaded organic surge tank will have two 50-hp vertical-centrifugal pumps in an enclosed pump box. One pump will be an operating pump with the other pump as a standby. The loaded organic tank is designed with an aqueous decant pump to remove any aqueous that settles out. This allows the aqueous to be returned to the extraction circuit. The exact extractant has not been chosen to date, though metallurgical test work with both Cognis and Cytec products showed favorable results at 10 volume percent in a kerosene diluent. 

With a one stage strip, the lean electrolyte will be used to strip the loaded organic. The lean electrolyte flow will be a bleed stream from the tankhouse recirculation stream. The lean electrolyte will have an average copper grade of 35

g/L. Discharging the strip settler, the rich electrolyte will report to the electrolyte filter system in the tank farm. The rich electrolyte will have an average grade of 47 g/L copper. The combined grade of the advance electrolyte feeding the EW plant is expected to be 37 g/L copper. 

The tank farm is located south of the SX plant. The tank farm will house the electrolyte filter system and the crud treatment system. There are three electrolyte filters, designed to have two active and one backwash filters. The filters are common across the industry and will utilize anthracite over garnet. 

Sulfuric acid storage is located to the east of the SX plant and consists of three tanks. Two of the tanks will be utilized for bulk acid storage, which will be supplied from a variety of sources, including from a Newmont roaster in Carlin, Nevada, USA. However, since the acid may not always be 93 %,

The SX plant will utilize a simple air diaphragm pump to remove crud from the circuit. The pump is portable so that it may be utilized at any of the mixer-settlers. The crud collected will report to the crud treatment tanks. The crud treatment and organic recovery system consists of a backwash tank, crud treatment tank, a pressure clay filter a three-phase decanting centrifuge, and a recovery system for organic from the sump area. ##### 2.3 Electrowinning 

The EW plant is located due west of the SX plant. The plant is designed to contain 42 polymerconcrete electrowinning cells as opposed to concrete with paraliners as was previously common in the industry. Each cell will contain 60 permanent cathodes and 61 anodes. The plant is designed for expansion to 52 cells if production in future years warrants it. 

The cathodes will be 316 stainless steel with a solid copper hangar bar and will have an active plating area of 3.28 ft x 3.28 ft (1 m x 1 m). Edge strips will be utilized to define the plating area on the cathode. The cathode design chosen utilizes an inverted “V” shaped bottom which provides adequate space to prevent the two sheets from growing together on the bottom of the blank. The anodes are designed as lead-calcium-tin with solid copper hangar bars. Any lead sludge collected will be sent back to the manufacturer for recycling. 

Each cell will have a pipe manifold system to ensure uniform electrolyte distribution within the cell. The anodes will utilize the “steer horn” design so the hangar bar is positioned lower than that of the cathodes. The anodes and cathode

s will be supported and insulated from each other with common cell-top furniture. Triangular bus bars on each will be utilized to make the connections from cell to cell. 

A new substation will be installed to reduce the overhead 120 kV line down to 13.8 kV. This is then stepped to 480 VAC to feed the six motor control centers (MCC’s). For electrowinning, two 4.7 MVA rectifiers will be installed with a harmonic filter. The rectifiers are fed with the incoming AC power, which is then converted into DC current for electrowinning. A diesel driven generator, rectifier will be used as a backup in the event of a power failure. 

The cathodes will be on a five to seven day harvest cycle and will take place on day shift only. The harvest will be performed utilizing an overhead crane and will pull 1/3 of the cathodes (20 cathodes) at a time for stripping. The cathodes will be washed before being run through a semiautomatic stripping machine. Clean cathodes will be put back into the cell while those that were removed are being stripped. Cathodes will be bundled and banded manually, targeting 4950 lbs (2250 kg) per bundle.

##### 2.4 Plant Innovations and Considerations 

###### 2.4.1 Fire Prevention and Protection 

There were a number of areas where this project is considering innovative design concepts. While Phoenix is certainly not the SX/EW plant to utilize the technology under consideration, it may be the first to utilize all of the individual components in the same plant. 

One of the first considerations was the SX plant layout. Square layouts are not necessarily a new concept, as a number of recent plants utilize this design. With Phoenix, however, it is the reason for the layout that sets it apart. The SX plant was designed with fire protection and suppression in mind 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

2145 

_House, Orr, Nees_ 



The choice for designing the loaded organic surge tank similar to the mixer-settlers, and even the decision to place it in the SX area rather than in the tank farm whe

re organic tanks have historically gone was based on fire protection. Placing the tank in the tank farm separates the organic inventory creating two areas with highly flammable reagents are being used. The Phoenix design keeps the flammable liquids in one place. 

Many traditional SX plants were designed in true train fashion, often having multiple SX trains. The spacing between mixer settlers was often less than 4 ft (1.2 m). In the United States, the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) [22] is drafting a new set of rules specifically targeting solvent extraction plants (NFPA 122). The proposed distance between “large flammable liquid storage areas” is 100 ft (30.5 m). Since mixer-settlers and organic tanks would be considered “large”, this would be the required spacing. For Phoenix, in order to be proactive in the design, it was agreed upon that a spacing of 30 feet be utilized between mixer-settlers and 75 feet between the nearest mixer-settler and building. The four square arrangement also limits the length of the organic pipe runs. 

Materials of construction for piping were also a consideration. In addition to the corrosion resistance of the 316 stainless steel pipes, this was also chosen for fire protection. It has been suggested that the use of HDPE pipe for conveyance of solutions containing organic are at risk for fire. It is cited that the accumulation of static as these solutions flow through the lines is great enough that a spark could discharge with enough energy to ignite any organic mist or vapor present [23]. Therefore, to reduce this risk, all piping within the SX plant is stainless steel. 

Traditional clothing for operations and maintenance personnel in an SX/EW plant has long been a 65 % or higher polyester blend for the acid resistance. However, it is believed that synthetic fibers may be sources of static buildup that could result in discharge, and natural fibers are suggested [24]. At the present time, operator safety from acid exposure due to degradation of the clothing was deemed to be a more probable scenario that a fire from clothing. Therefore, all personnel are still anticipated to utilize blended polyester work wear. 

Fire traps and system dumps were also discussed and considered as part of the feasibility study. It was quickly determined that the requirements for either of these is neither economically or technically feasible and neither option will be pursued further. 

In order to reduce the amount of organic mist generated, the plant design is such that all pipes should run full. A minimal flow cascade will take place at the weir of 1 to 3 inches (2.54 cm to 7.62 cm) on the settler side. This is opposite of the discharge pipe, so mist generation should be limited. 

In an effort to have early fire detection in the plant, Protectowire fire wire detectors are intended to be installed in pipe racks and cable trays throughout the SX plant. This will also be inside the loaded organic tank, settlers, mixers,

and the loaded organic pump box. If activated, the wire will alarm and report to the central fire control panel, which will relay the information to the plant control room.

Fencing around the perimeter of the SX plant with a secure gated entry is also being considered. The idea is to reduce the inadvertent entry of someone not trained in the area that could potentially create a fire hazard. This is only one of a number of procedural items that will also be addressed. 

All of the above areas were intended to address fire prevention. The Phoenix design also wanted to be well prepared in the unlikely event that a fire does break out. Some older or more traditionally designed plants with multiple trains may consider the entire train to be “sacrificial” in the event of a fire with protection aimed at protecting the remaining trains and structures. Phoenix does not have that option. A fire in any mixer-settler or tank would be catastrophic. 

For a number of years, aqueous film forming foams (AFFF) and other foam systems have been utilized as the primary fire suppression media. There were a number of issues uncovered with regard to the foam interaction with the process. While effective at putting out fires, foam systems had a negative impact on the SX operations. From impacting kinetics to affecting disengagement times as well as degrading the organic, these systems were installed with reservations. Many plants, knowing the potential effects of an accidental discharge, choose to leave their fire system in manual rather than automatic. This delays the deployment of the system in the event of a live fire. 

In addition to the operational issues, AFFF systems are also known to have health and environmental risks associated with them. Employees are at risk if they are inside an enclosure when an AFFF system deploys. And cleanup of AFFF, should it leave a primary containment area, will be treated as a hazardous waste with regard to disposal of the material. 

As an alternative to AFFF, Newmont brought together an extractant supplier and a firefighting chemical manufacturer to test another possible solution. The fire company offers an alternative product to AFFF. It is a water-based gel that has profound firefighting capabilities, as well as offering excellent structure protection. Because it is water-based, it is also environmentally friendly and far less of a risk to employee health. Initial test work indicates that it may be better suited for use in operation with less impact on recovery and organic quality than an AFFF system; however, this still has yet to be determined. 

Rather than relying on systems that could potentially ruin an entire inventory of organic if accidentally discharged or have yet to be proven out, Newmont chose to utilize a new type of technology for the primary fire suppression system. HI-FOG utilizes a high-pressure water mist that rapi

dly cools any burning gases and fills the remaining effected volume with an atmosphere of water vapor. This starves the fire and helps to absorb the radiant heat. 

These systems have proven effectiveness in a number of industries, including marine vessels as well as numerous land-based applications. Historically, mist systems have not proven themselves in oilbased fire applications. But HI-FOG has not only proven their technology works in these applications in controlled test environments, they have had numerous installations around the world that have been noted for safe, efficient fire suppression in live emergencies. 

The HI-FOG systems will be installed in the mixer-settlers and in the organic surge tank. The system will be linked to the Protectowire monitors which will tell the HI-FOG system where to con-

Because the HI-FOG system is a simple water mist, the risks to the environment and employee health do not exist. In addition, the risk to the organic quality and circuit recovery is also eliminated. The risk to the plant is reduced as well, as the system can remain in auto. Not only is there no concern for accidental discharge, the system may actually be live tested at regular intervals to ensure proper operation in the event of a fire. 

To ensure adequate secondary fire suppression capabilities exist, fire hydrants will be located around the plant perimeter. At least two portable systems of either foam or gel based fire fighting agent will be positioned around exterior of the SX plant. They will be able to tie directly to the hydrants in the event that the primary system fails or is not sufficient to contain a fire. 

In addition to the HI-FOG system and the secondary cart systems, Newmont is considering employing one additional firefighting tool. It runs on tracks and is capable of dragging up to 1000 ft (305 m) of charged 2 inch (5.1 cm) hose. The Monitor can be utilized with foams or gels, but it allows the operator to fight the fire without putting him or herself in unnecessary danger. 

###### 2.4.2 Acid Mist Control 

Acid mist generation is a common problem in electrowinning plants. From tarps to hollow plastic balls to chemical agents or even nothing at all, a number of attempts to control acid mist have been made. Cross flow ventilation and roof top ventilation were utilized. The success of each varied, with a number of operations opting for combinations of the above to control the mist. Many of these options, including combinations were insufficient. In order to protect employees, some operations sugges

ted or required using respirators if the conditions warranted it. 

Phoenix will implement a mixed approach as well. A combination of hollow plastic balls and a chemical additive, FC-1100 will be employed. However, because history suggests that even when used together, these systems are not entirely effective. As a result, it was decided to install a much more efficient system for acid mist control. 

A number of years ago, SAME, Limitada, a Chilean company, entered the picture. SAME provides a hood and manifold collection system that is positioned over each of the cells. The air draw through the hood captures the acid mist significantly reducing the exposure to employees, not to mention the savings on corrosion to the EW plant. In order to keep the mist from being released to the environment, the air stream is run through a high-efficiency wet scrubber. The scrubber wash water can then be recycled back to the SX plant for makeup water, as well as to recover any residual copper that it may contain.

###### 2.4.3 Cathode Stripping Machine 

The cathode stripping machine is another area where Phoenix is looking to take advantage of technology. There are numerous varieties of stripping machines commercially available ranging from manual machines to semiautomatic to essentially fully automatic units. Because of the weight of each cathode, any manual manipulation becomes very labor intensive. 

At present, Phoenix has designed for a fully automatic robotic stripping machine by EPCM Services, Ltd. This machine was quoted against stripping machines from a number of vendors and was found to be very competitive. In addition to an attractive price, the EPCM machine utilizes a seemingly reliable process. 

The cathodes will still be harvested manually and placed into the wash rack by an operator. However, as the cathodes exit the wash station, a robotic arm will pick up a single cathode and place it in the strip rack. A hydraulic ram will flex the cathode from each side breaking the top of the copper cathode free from the stainless blank. As each edge comes free, a retaining arm will lower to pull the two sections of the cathode apart. With the halves spread, two hydraulic “axes” are deployed to break the cathode free from the bottom of the blank. 

The robot can then remove the bland, placing it on a rack to either be returned to

a cell or repaired if necessary. As the cathodes come off the blank, they are transferred to a stacking and corrugating machine. The machine can be set to corrugate every second or third pair of cathodes. Once the bundle is full (weight based), the process will be temporarily halted while the bundle is banded and removed via a forklift. 

Despite the confidence in the machine’s capabilities, a strip operator will be present at all times during operation. This is primarily to ensure that there are no issues that occur while stripping is occurring, such as a sticking cathode, or a cathode getting hung up when it drops from the rack. Overall, the machine is expected to reduce manual handling of cathodes, and provide consistent and efficient cathode stripping.

The Phoenix Copper Leach Project experienced a number of challenges related to engineering. The feasibility study was conducted during the economic peak. However, it was not just this project that experienced engineering issues over the last few years. With the booming economy and surge in metal prices, engineering companies in the United States became inundated with work. 

As a result of the above conditions, projects of varying size and complexity were all competing for the same resources. Some firms were unable to bid on jobs due to resource constraints, while others took on work that was more than they were capable of handling at the time. 

Many firms also lacked the adequate experience. It has been recognized for some time that there is an age gap in the engineering world. There was a period where few engineers were being produced, and as more and more experienced engineers began to retire, the gap widened. Today, there are still a large number of veteran engineers, but the work coming in could not all be handled by these personnel. 

In order to fill some of the gap, many companies turned to new or recent graduate engineers with little or no experience. Because workloads were so great, a number of engineering companies were assigning work to these new engineers that were outside their capability. While the opportunity to learn, grow, and gain experience is invaluable, it was often at the client’s expense. Numerous revisions and major oversights were rampant in areas that were historically not a problem. However, as the situation sat, there was either a lack of experience in the office, or a lack of oversight by the experienced engineers. In either case, it proved quite challenging with projects. 

Traditionally, project managers tended to follow the engineering talent when it came to bidding work. They knew that firms A, B, C, and D were very strong with one type of project, while W, X, Y, and Z may be better for another type of project. ##### 4.1 Yerington, Nevada 

###### 4.1.1 History 

The Yerington Mining site is located in Western Nevada, U.S.A. and covers approximately 3400 acres (1376 hectares) [11]. Approximately 51 percent of the land is private with the other 49 percent on land administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) [15]. The Empire Mine operated at Yerington between 1918 and 1920. There were no mining operations at the site between 1920 and 1952. The Anaconda Mining Company (Anaconda) began mining operations in 1952. Copper oxide ore was crushed and vat leached and recovered as cement concentrate (83 percent copper), which was shipped off-site for smelting at the Washoe Smelter in Anaconda, Montana. Sulfuric acid used for vat leaching was created from an on-site roaster and produced approximately 450 tons of 93 percent sulfuric acid per day [2]. Anaconda constructed a mill and concentrator in 1965 to allow the processing of sulfide ores, which was done via an iron launder with the precipitates also being shipped off-site for smelting at the Washoe Smelter. In 1977 Anaconda sold the property to the Atlantic Richfi

eld Company (ARCO), which operated at the site until June 1978. In 1978 the site was sold to a private land owner and several different mining companies operated on the site until the site was sold to Arimetco in 1989, which operated at the site until 2000. 

Arimetco operated five lined heap leach pads covering approximately 250 acres [18] and solution extraction/electro-winning (SX/EW) facility. The leach pads and SX/EW facility were designed as zero discharge facilities. A one percent dilute (20-30 g/L) sulfuric acid solution as applied to ore on the pads [2]. In November 1996 Arimetco filed for bankruptcy. In November 1998 the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP) ordered Arimetco to cease operations at the Yerington site, which included active mining and solution application. Arimetco continued to recover copper from the leach solution until November 1999 before abandoning the site in January 2000. In January 2000 there was approximately 92 million gallons (348,200,000 L) of pregnant leach solution (PLS) remaining in the five heap leach pads and processing system. 

###### 4.1.2 Site and Fluid Management 

NDEP took over management of the site in January 2000 with BLM and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) support. NDEP’s primary goal was fluid management at the site. Management of the site was contracted out by NDEP. Initial draindown flows from the leach pads was approximately 1300 gallons per minute (gpm) (4900 Liters per minute) and the ponds would overflow and result in upset condition within eight hours. Draindown flows have since decreased to less than 5 gpm. Power costs have decreased from $25,000 per month. EPA took over site management in December 2004. 

###### 4.1.3 Groundwater Contamination 

Unlined evaporation ponds were constructed at the site between 1953 and 1978 and covered approximately 104 acres (42 hectares). These ponds served to store and evaporate process solution

##### 5.2 Phoenix Copper Leach Project Permitting 

###### 5.2.1 Timeline 

Initial meetings were held with State and Federal agencies to discuss the proposed Phoenix Copper Leach Project (Project) in June and August of 2006. The initial Water Pollution Control Permit (WPCP) application, a State permit, was submitted on December 12, 2006, but was withdrawn in February 2007 for revisions. An amended Plan of Operations (PoO), a Federal permit, was submitted to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) on May 30, 2007. A revised WPCP was submitted in August and December 2007 and a revised PoO amendment was submitted in January 2008. Several revisions have been made to the Tentative Permanent Closure Plan (TPCP), which is part of the WPCP application. The TPCP describes how closure and reclamation of the Project will be done after operations have ceased. As of September 2009 the TPCP has been revised and submitted for review on five separate occasions. 

###### 5.2.2 Challenges and Issues 

The two biggest challenges facing the Project is that no zero-discharge copper heap leach pads have been successfully closed in Nevada and historical issues at the Yerington and Tonopah mine sites, which are both copper leach facilities. The Project has been designed as a zero-discharge facility, which means no solution may be released into the surrounding environment. All process components have been designed with double containment (i.e. pipe-in-pipe and double lined ponds). Addressing these challenges have resulted in a substantial amount of time, effort, and money being put into developing a closure strategy for the Project. 

Newmont worked with both State and Federal agencies to develop a closure strategy for the Project. The proposed closure strategy is broken down into three phases. Phase 1 consists of active evaporation on top of pad and recirculating solution back to the top of the pad. Evaporation and recirculation will continue until all draindown from the pad can be handled via active evaporation (i.e. atomizers), which will begin Phase 2. The existing process ponds, excluding the Raffinate Pond, will be converted to backfilled evaporation cells (E-cells) and Phase 3 will begin when solution draindown can be handled in the E-cells with no active evaporation. When draindown has ceased the E- cells will be completely backfilled, covered, and reseeded.

The agencies major concern is precipitate accumulation within the pad and E-cells. A Geochemistry analysis was completed to determine if the proposed heap leach would drain completely, what would precipitate in the pad and E-cells, would the facilities bind off, how long before the precipitates fill the pore space in the E-cells, and will the draindown solution ultimately evaporate. The Geochemistry study looked at the mineralogy of both Yerington and Tonopah and compared that to the copper mineralogy of the Project. The Yerington mineralogy

is mostly copper oxides (i.e. chrysocolla) and the Tonopah mineralogy is composed of copper sulfides (i.e. chalcocite and chalcopyrite). Phoenix copper mineralogy is composed of copper oxides and looking at the mineralogy and the geochemical reactions that would occur in the pad it was determined that less than 2 % of the pore space within the pad would be filled with precipitates and that the pad would not bind off due to precipitates or degradation and would drain completely. Although the Tonopah pad had high concentrations of fluorite, which broke down into clays, the pad is still draining down and has not binded off. 

The second concern the geochemistry study looked at was what precipitates would form in the pad and E-cells. Goethite and Gibbsite would be the major precipitates in the pad and Gypsum and Epsomite in the E-cells. Although there will be a large quantity of salts contained in the solution draindown the study determined that the solution would ultimately evaporate with in the E-cells. The next addressed in the study was to look at the amount of time it would take for the E-cells to fill up with precipitates. Based on a steady drain down rate of 15 gpm, which is not anticipated, the four E-cells would fill up in approximately 4.5 years. In order to address agency concerns solution will be alternated between E-cells, four in total, and precipitates that accumulate will be removed from the E-cells and disposed of onsite. 

The Agencies have agreed that the proposed closure strategy is a sound approach and data will be collect during active operations to develop a Final Permanent Closure Plan.

Engineering challenges have eased with the slowing economy. ### Outsourcing of By-Products: An Opportunity for Process Improvement 

Christina E. M. Meskers, Guy Daelman, Sybolt Brouwer

**Keywords:** Recycling, anode slimes, slag, impurity management, by-product treatment 

#### Abstract 

The generation of by-products or sidestreams is a fact of life in the non-ferrous industry. These streams can contain impurity elements like As, Sb, Sn, Bi, Se, Te combined with valuable elements like Ag, Au. Adequate treatment is therefore crucial from a cost and residue management perspective, as well as from a material resource (sustainability) point of view. 

Many smelters and refiners process these by-products themselves via internal recycling and/or additional (side) processes. The cost nor disadvantages of these are rarely fully recognized. Furthermore the capital hold up in the metals contained can be significant. 

In case of internal recycling the impurities go through a recycling loop several times before they leave the flow sheet. Also they carry a subs

tantial amount of recoverable elements into this recycling loop, creating a build-up of elements. Since internal recycling takes up capacity as such it can limit the freedom on composition and amount of fresh feed material. 

Sidestream operations bring a different set of disadvantages. As the operations are often of limited size the benefits of economies of scale or scope are missing, while extra efforts in operation, maintenance, Environment Health & Safety (EHS), logistics, expertise and management have to be made. Lastly, by-product treatment is seldom a core activity for non-ferrous producers. 

Outsourcing of by-product treatment to specialized companies should be evaluated as an alternative. Umicore operates highly efficient processes for dedicated by-product treatment as their core business, making it complimentary to its clients operations. Clients benefit from the economies of scale, the high recovery of valuable metals, the flexible processing capacity to deal with fluctuations in byproduct quantity and quality, and the knowledge on impurity management. Solutions are tailor-made for each by-product to achieve win-win situations.

#### 1 Introduction 

The generation of by-products or sidestreams is a fact of life in the non-ferrous industry. Mined ores and other materials contain besides non-ferrous or precious metals a wide range of other metals. In the case of copper these can be precious metals, special metals (In, Se, Te, Sb, Bi) or base metals such as Pb, Sn or Ni. In ores they are often closely interlinked with the copper bearing minerals, either chemically – via substitution or solid solution – or physically –as intergrown minerals – and end up in the copper or precious metals concentrate. During metallurgical processing the target elements are separated from the other metals, which accumulate in by-products or sidestreams generated during the different processing steps. These streams can contain impurity elements such as As, Sb, Sn, Bi, Se, Te combined with valuable elements like Ag, Au. Often also the target element is included in the sidestreams, the amount depending on the type of sidestream. 

Typical examples from the copper industry are: 

- Anode slimes from electrorefining of copper 

- Dorй slags and flue dusts generated during slimes smelting 

- Residues of hydrometallurgical treatment of anode slimes 

- Precious metals containing residues and cements from hydrometallurgical processes 

- Refractory bricks from precious metals smelting 

In Table 1 the valuable and impurity elements present in some of these streams are indicated, together with by-products from the lead industry, as the considerations discussed in this paper are also applicable to the by-products, such as matte, speiss and dross, generated during the production and recycling of lead. Even for other non-ferrous industries the issues/considerations discussed in this paper are to a l

arge extend valid. 

From Table 1 it can be concluded that sidestreams are highly complex materials, and even within one category considerable differences exist. Anode slimes from primary copper production are rich in gold (up to ~ 4 %), silver (up to ~ 25 %) and selenium (> 10 %) [1, 2], while most of them are poor in lead, tin and platinum group metals (PGMs). Secondary anode slimes from recycling scrap like copper alloys or printed circuit boards (e-scrap) on the other hand, are rich in lead (up to ~ 10 % [1]), tin and sometimes palladium, while gold and selenium are generally only present in small amounts. The composition of secondary slimes varies much more compared to primary slimes, while it is a function of highly variable scrap feed compositions. Treatment of such considerably different streams requires specialized processes to capture the contained metal value and to deal with impurities.

Also from a residue management perspective treatment is necessary. For example CRU estimated the 2003 production of copper anode slimes to be about 43,000 t [2]. Lastly processing of anode slimes and other by-products is important from a resource perspective. Non-ferrous by-products are an important source of minor (special) and precious metals, which are used in high-tech and clean technology applications. For example most of the Se and Te used for thin film photovoltaics among others, is produced from anode slimes. The transition to a ‘sustainable’ clean technology society will increase the demand for these metals.

The effectiveness of in-house treatment can be questioned as the costs and disadvantages are rarely fully recognized. Furthermore these change over time, making an assessment of the choice to treat a material internally or externally something that should be done on a regular basis.
