#### 2 In-house treatment 

When discussing in-house treatment of by-products or sidestreams a distinction should be made between 1) internal recycling and 2) sidestream processing. The former entails the (direct) reintroduction of the impurity stream into the main flow sheet, while the latter represents a dedicated process for the impurity stream. Each choice has a fundamentally different set of considerations and costs. 

##### 2.1 Internal recycling 

Reintroduction of impurity-containing sidestreams or by-products more upstream in the flow sheet is at first sight an easy way of dealing with them, as it does not require capital investments. This is often done for slags, residues and flue dusts for example. To make the material suitable for reentry into the flow sheet additional handling might be necessary and sometimes even treatment such as drying, filter pressing or other preparatory treatment. 

The impurities in the returned material go several times through the internal recycling loop, accumulating until (finally) removed in a by-product. In the returned sidestream or by-product also a high amount of recoverable elements is present, which is also carried back into an earlier stage of the process. As a result it takes longer for the recoverable metals and valuable impurity elements to leave the flow sheet and be valorized; longer retention times are then leading to considerable capital hold-up; an effect that is often underestimated. 

Besides capital hold up, internal recycling also puts constraints on the flow sheet. Internal recycling streams occupy capacity on the smelting step, that otherwise would be available for fresh feed, and take capacity in the refining stage. In the refining stage the feed has composition limits for Cu, As, Sb, Sn, Bi, Se and Te and these can be reached earlier when internal recycling is practiced, as the recycling stream increases the impurity level in the feed stream. This can even have impact on the composition of new feed taken in at the smelter, reducing operational flexibility. As a result the freedom of movement in sourcing feed materials for the commercial department is affected. Materials with higher impurity content can be lost for the company and competitiveness is reduced. Furthermore, the higher level or tonnage of impurities requires more reagents for treatment leading to higher reagent expenses. 

Lastly, internal recycling can lead to increases of the material to be internally recycled when in

termediate or end-products do not meet the quality specifications and are repeatedly reintroduced in the flow sheet. Also internal recycling can demand additional environmental measures or solutions to mitigate the effect of internal recycling on the composition of off gas or effluents for example. This leads to increased costs per ton refined metal produced. 

Internal recycling can thus limit the freedom on intake of fresh feed with regard to tonnage and certainly with regard to composition. Consequently, technical and metallurgical constraints lead to

commercial limitations. Loss of freedom represents a disadvantage that is often forgotten in the evaluation, besides the underestimated effect of capital hold-up. 

##### 2.2 Sidestream processing 

Installation of separate processes is another way to deal with sidestreams or by-products. Sometimes it is perceived as a solution to overcome the difficulties associated with internal recycling, although one set of problems might be replaced with a different one instead. Outsourcing could be a breakthrough solution. 

Behind the concept of sidestream processing is a range of considerations. Firstly it has to be decided which sidestream processes will be used as it is a process for a very limited tonnage of materials, hence economies of scale are lacking. 

For example copper anode slimes treatment generally involves oxidizing leaching of Cu, followed by recovery of Se and Te, removal of detrimental elements and production of dorй bullion and last separation of the precious metals and PGMs [1]. Installing the entire process for a limited tonnage does not make sense from a cost and investment perspective, while partial installation could lead to new sidestreams or by-products that need to go for external treatment or for which no outlet exists and so reduces the feasibility of the process. External treatment of the original sidestream then becomes a more attractive alternative. 

Furthermore sidestream processing often entails moving into non-core activity operations so economies of scope and scale are small or missing. Additional expertise is needed to operate the process, to achieve sufficiently high yields and to ensure all Environment Health and Safety (EHS) measures are taken. Sometimes the processes are operated in a batchwise manner, causing unprofitable startup and shutdown issues and higher capital employed among others. 

Often the smaller scale involves more manual labour, which might not be optimal for ergonomics. Besides an additional operation to manage for which operational costs are made for personnel and maintenance, it also requires additional EHS measures. As this is all for a very limited tonnage the expenditure per ton will be higher. 

Sidestream processing also requires a different management philosophy. Instead of the focus on high throughput and low costs as done in

the main flow sheet, it has to be on removing as much of the valuable elements from the sidestreams as possible and concentrating the impurities in the final residues. 

Evaluation of the pros and cons of sidestream processing and internal recycling is relevant for all operations. Also for operations that have established sidestream treatment it can be worthwhile to (re)evaluate the processing of every by-product, even if they are deemed useful and taken care of. By-products generated within the sidestream treatment can be outsourced, for example the dorй slags produced in a precious metals flow sheet (Figure 1).

#### 3 External treatment of sidestreams 

##### 3.1 Benefits 

Outsourcing or external treatment of sidestreams removes many of the disadvantages associated with internal recycling or in-house sidestream processing. Benefits are generated in the technical, economical and environmental areas. 

In the technical domain constraints on fresh feed composition and tonnage associated with internal recycling practices are removed, allowing optimization of the flow sheet for core business activities as well as for impurity management. Furthermore extensive expertise and technology for state of the art processing of sidestreams does not have to be available in-house anymore. Instead external experts can be consulted. 

Using state of the art technology also leads to environmental benefits, as these processes meet stringent environmental performance requirements, which can be uneconomic when small-scale processes are used. The large scale processes also make the implementation of health and safety measures on the work floor easier. Outsourcing can also reduce the amount of waste streams and can avoid the generation of products for which there is no final outlet.

Economic benefits can be achieved through cost and efficiency savings as costs will be predominantly made for core business related activities and not anymore for internal recycling of materials or sidestream processing. For sidestream processes the fixed costs and investments do not have to be born anymore, as costs are only made for the tonnages that are actually outsourced. External treatment can allow for a decrease in retention time of payable metals and will allow for an increase in flexibility with regard to fluctuations in both fresh smelter feed and smelter by-product tonnages or composition. Although these benefits are more difficult to express in financial terms, they play also an important role. Also staff that used to work on sidestream processing or other resources tied up in sidestream processing can now be employed to expand the core business activities. 

Evidently the technology, environment

and economic factors are linked as changes in one also affect the others. As the boundary conditions change over time a regular re-evaluation of the benefits can be worthwhile. Re-evaluation might lead to the conclusion that although it was not favourable to use external treatment in the past, it could be interesting to start outsourcing. 

##### 3.2 Concerns 

The decision to outsource the treatment of by-products or sidestreams is not made overnight. It is a process during which many considerations pass in review and concerns are raised. Questions relating to for example loss of managerial control over the details of sidestream processing, performance of external treatment and impurity limits, and dependence on a third party are encountered when outsourcing is discussed. Solutions such as long term contracts, a good track record and transparency on terms and conditions among others are a prerequisite. 

The social aspects related to external treatment are a concern as well as it can be interpreted as a bad sign by the work force. Still external treatment can lead to improved working conditions as workers have to do less manual handling and the exposure to specific chemicals might be reduced. Also the external treatment frees resources and space that can be used for expanding the core business leading to employment. 

Careful selection of a reliable counterpart for by-product treatment is therefore another important aspect of the outsourcing process.

##### 4.3 Metal valorisation 

As discussed earlier in the paper by-products often contain a) an extensive range of different metals or b) metals in less easy-recoverable combinations and amounts. This poses high demands on the processes used for their efficient and environmentally sound recovery, as these have to deal with the valuable elements as well as with the other elements. 

A limited number of valuable elements provide the economic incentive for by-product treatment. In the case of by-products from the copper industry this is the copper and the precious metals and for some cases also lead and selenium. However, the other elements (Bi, Sn, etc.) can be recovered with suitable technologies, as done in the Umicore process. They are either converted to marketable products or converted into compounds for safe disposal, e.g. for cadmium. The value-carrying or ‘paying’ metals offset the expenses made for the recovery of less valuable metals or metals present in very low concentration, ensuring their recovery and availability for the metals market. 

In the contracts for by-product treatment this reality is reflected. Only a selected number of metals is credited for, the others are treated in an environmental and sustainable way. If the cost of recovery of a metal is higher than the value of the saleable product this can lead to a penalty if a threshold concentration of the particular metal is exceeded.

#### Abstract 

This paper estimates a cost function for the Chilean copper industry, which identifies the involvement of various inputs in the cost structure of domestic firms. This is important because in an environment where price behavior is uncertain, some guidelines are given to mining companies that tell them where they could eventually put the emphasis to reduce costs. This process of reorganization can gain in efficiency if also information about economies of scale, cost elasticities and impact of head grade on total costs is known. This document provides this information.

Finally, to know if there are economies or diseconomies of scale and what range of level of output, it is important for decision-making process. In particular, the correct identification and analysis of economies of scale is a key determinant in investment policies particularly in growth industries. 

Usually the concept of scale economies is defined as the relative increase in output resulting from a proportional increase in all inputs. In other words, shows the response of the output to proportional changes in the employment of all inputs by a common factor _k_ . A natural way of representing the economies of scale is as the proportional increase in costs resulting from a very small proportional increase in the level of output. Then scale economies (SCE) can be defined as unity minus this elasticity: 







Thus, if SCE is greater than zero, there are economies of scale, if less, diseconomies. This means that if SCE > 0, the increased cost is proportionately less than output growth, while if SCE < 0, the increased cost is higher. Now if SCE = 0, there are constant returns to scale, i.e., the increase in costs is proportional to the increase in the output level. 

Unlike other specifications such as the Cobb-Douglas form or Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES), the translog functional form has the advantage of being quite flexible due to it does not restrict the production structure to be homothetic, nor imposes restrictions on the elasticities of substitution. However, these restrictions can be tested statistically. Thus, if any of the restrictions is valid, it is preferable to adopt the simplified form. If not, it is of economic interest to measure the impact of these restrictions on the shape of the cost curve.

The analysis of results shows that, on average, the participation of different inputs on total costs could be decomposes in approximately 25 % in direct labor, 10 % in indirect labor, 20 % in costs related to energy consumption, 30 % goes to spending on other inputs needed for the production process. The remaining 15 % is explained by production costs via depreciation on capital invested in the operation (in other words, cost of capital via depreciation). Also, it follows that the impact of the head grade is negative and significant, as expected. The coefficient of -0.36 suggests that for every 10 % points increase the head grade, average production costs decrease by 4 %. That is, a higher head grade contributes to lower production costs. Thus, the present scenario indicates that the lower oil prices and the sharp fall in prices of electricity generation, should contribute to an easing of the cost for this item, something similar should happen with the other inputs (steel, spare parts , tires, sulfuric acid, lubricants and other chemicals products in general). As for labor, its impact on total costs is about 35 % (decomposes into 25 % direct and 10 % indirect), it follows then that this is a key factor in the cost structure of firms mining, thus reducing their amounts is critical for realizing the urgent low cost that the Chilean industry requires. In this context, it could be very useful actions such as the renegotiation of supply contracts for indirect labor and implementation of incentive systems (awards for efficiency) for the workers themselves. In regard to capital, it should not face large fluctuations, as the amounts currently impacting on the costs are investments in the past.

reater involvement of firms to devote resources to such actions. Also, it verifies the existence of economies of scale, occurring at a level of production of 400 thousand tons, although for the first 200 thousand tons, average costs fall quickly. In the range from 400 thousand to 900 thousand tons, average costs continue to fall but at a far lower rate, while for levels above 1 million tons, it appears that average costs tend to remain relatively constant. As for the elasticities, results reveal that there is a low responsiveness of costs to changes in energy prices and capital. This is not surprising, since energy is a critical and specific input in mining, something similar is observed with capital. The opposite is observed with the direct

labor; in fact, the direct labor is highly sensitive, largely due to the real possibility of replacing it by indirect labor. The results also indicate that all inputs are substitutes for each other. 

So, if what national firms want is to continue along the same path of development and growth that has kept the national copper industry in recent years, contributing to the development and welfare of Chileans is urgent to intensify efforts to reduce costs. In this paper some guidelines are given to focus into this point. But it is clear that the consolidation of a competitive mining industry also requires a different set of initiatives: a fair but flexible labor market with skilled manpower, good training programs, related business development and alliances with universities and institutes, among other measures. Of course, public policies aimed to encourage innovation and research and development are also very important and will certainly help to reduce costs.

The

first drivers of the copper market discussed in this paper are in first place the demand for copper and copper alloy manufactured products and the second place the supply restrictions of refined cathodes from copper mines and recycled scrap. The copper content in the scrap directly melted by copper and alloy semis fabricators is a third factor, followed by changes in the global trade flow of new and old copper scrap, and by changes in its copper content. Both variables will set limits to the copper available for semis fabricators and secondary smelters if copper coming from mines and refined by SX-EW or primary smelters and refineries faces short supply. The expansion of the Chinese industrial base in recent years and the contraction of the industrial base in developed nations, highlight the importance to understand the copper market balance in China as other key driver of 2010-2015 global copper market: domestic copper availability, exchange and of exchange warehouse reserves, semis industry balance, downstream manufactured market balance, changing trade policy, same as domestic recycling and investment plans in domestic and foreign mines and plants, are the main factors to be included in an outlook of the role of China as a driver of the global copper market in the next five years. As important as the Chinese demand are the global changes in investment plans in new mines and expansions of operating mines: decisions to start or delay a copper mine related project will play a central role in the future mine supply available for domestic and for international trade. The operational, economic and even social and environmental factors affecting future copper mine supply also need to be considered to avoid the recurrent over estimation of copper supply in recent years and the recurrent underestimation in the 1998-2003 surplus world copper production, after supply sources moved from industrial economies to developing countries creating a supply that exceeded the global demand for an extended period. In this paper we discuss briefly how the financial crisis that was perceived only in 2008 and evolved to an economic crisis in 2009, affected the plans

#### 1 World Copper Use from Mining and from Scrap 

The most recent data of total global first use of copper from the ICSG, including refined copper and copper scrap used by the manufacturing industry worldwide are pre-crisis (2007) and reached nearly 23.7 million tons of copper (Mt-cu) of which more than 8.2 Mt-cu came from recycled copper and 15.45 Mt-Cu came from copper mines. Consequently, over one third of the copper used in the world is coming from recycling, and this usage varies with changes in the price of refined copper: in times of high prices we see much more use of copper scrap, mainly by fabricators, as in the case of secondary smelters the balance with concentrates available plays a role on scrap usage. Although the cathode production from scrap has been growing rapidly between 2001 and 2007 the world total still remains close to 2.7 Mt-cu without significant expansions observed. The rest of recycled copper, more than 5.5 Mt-cu annually, is used directly by the semis manufacturers of copper, and consists of copper scrap with relatively higher copper content than the scrap going to the smelters. These industries smelt directly different qualities of scrap depending on the requirements of downstream manufacturers needs. This is how more than one third of the copper used in the world comes not from mining but from recycling copper from different sources: high copper content scrap from the manufacturing industry (new scrap), and old scrap from building demolition, from recycling obsolete industrial equipment, from recycling electric and electronic equipment, and in a more reduced proportion from used vehicles and municipal solid waste treatment. Our forecast for global first use of copper in 2008 is close to 8.1 million tonnes with 2.7 million tonnes from secondary cathodes and 5.4 million tonnes from copper in direct melt. This estimation will be crossed against our annual recyclables survey in April 2010. 

#### 2 Semis Copper First Use, End Use and the Scrap Trade 

Copper semis production critically depends from the fine tuning of a global network of copper mines, SX-EW plants, smelters and refineries. In the past 60 years old scrap transformed in cathodes by secondary smelters and semis directly melted copper scrap has proved unable to increase global copper supply to the increasing rhythm of copper semis demand and has been growing at the same

As global trade never played an important role in the global copper semis industry with exports only 10 % of global production, and mainly from countries around China, the global semis production has been historically concentrated in a few industrial economies, with China leading the new capacity expansion in recent years. When we compare current global copper first use with estimates of end use of copper in various economic activities, we ob

serve that almost half of the 23.7-cu MT used in 2007 in the world (48 %) is concentrated in only four pure copper products without alloys: wire for construction, high voltage electrical cables, cable for magnets and copper tubes. If we add almost 2 million tonnes of copper bars used in alloys of other metals (RBS) we can observe that close to 57 % of the end use of copper worldwide is concentrated in 5 copper semifabricated products. The remaining 43 % is distributed between low-voltage cables, plates, sheets and strips (PSS), castings, cables for cars, electronics and telecommunications, alloy tubes and other minor use as plates, mechanical cables and copper powders. The copper scrap generation observed in the developed economies, driven mainly by domestic consumption instead of investment and exports is well over the declining copper scrap use of their industrial base: in the United States for example the four secondary smelters and two electrolytic refineries disappeared in 1996-2001 and a similar situation happened in Europe. In consequence, the increasing old scrap was not recovered or is recovered mainly for exports to industrializing economies, willing to pay higher for the scrap: in the United States 60 % of old scrap is not recovered and close to 75 % of the old scrap recovered is exported (USGS 2009). This increasing global imbalance between first use in Asia and end use in the West, explains most of the increasing scrap trade flows to China observed in recent years.

If we measure the copper content of the reported dollar value of world trade of scrap copper, exporters consistently report copper content of less than 3 Mt-cu annually, while importers reported more than 4.2 Mt in his import statements to customs. #### 4 Copper Scrap Trade Value 

The international trade of copper scrap in gross weight is a business with annual sales close to 17,000 millions of dollars in 2007, and many participating countries. Imports from China, Germany and South Korea accounts for over 60 % of the payments, well over imports from Belgium, Italy and Japan (18 % remaining payments), and followed by the United States, India and Hong Kong (China) with less than 3% paid by each country. Payments for imports reported by China and Hong Kong reached nearly 7 billion dollars in 2007. This money goes mainly to the U.S., Germany, Britain and France that accounted for 55 % of all export earnings. Chile, after Japan, Holland and over Mexico is one of the countries reporting important revenues from exports (nearly 700 million reported in 2007 by exporting copper scrap, according to UN COMTRADE) despite the low volume of exports (> 100 Kt-cu in 2007), which makes Chile the country with largest copper content in its exports with 95 % in 2007. We also note that exporters of scrap metal from Hong Kong reported significantly less commercial value than the value reported by importers in mainland China. Finally, the copper content of imports reported by China's official trade flows reveals some very high value relative to the volume imported, particularly from Romania, Turkey, Venezuela, Lebanon, Morocco, Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic , Saudi Arabia and Kyrgistan that merits a more disaggregated analysis. 

#### 5 Investing in Copper Semis Capacity Expansion 

Global investment processes and good credit conditions for semis plants capacity expansion in the period 2004-2007 experienced a freeze in late 2008 in some countries. Most of the new global capacity started recently was to wire rod plants (1.7 million tonnes in 2008). More than 400,000 tonnes of new brass mill capacity was joined by marginal but dynamic and valuable growth of new copper foil mills. Capacity utilization was estimated around 61 % for 2006-2008 for the group of countries with the highest production capacity. China presented the largest overcapacity before the current infrastructure plan and large overcapacity was also observed in Japan and United States since 2006, unfortunately fiscal infrastructure plans had not been launched in those countries so the capacity utilization rate must be reducing even more in 2008 and 2009. A part of the global semis capacity potential growth, estimated in 7.7 M tonnes for 2008-2013, was realized in 2008 as wire rod capacity expansion was growing fast: new operational capacity of all fabricators expanded +2.1 million tonnes in 2008, with operational capacity of wire rod plants growing + 8.3 % and other copper first uses, mainly brass mill product expanding more than +9 % in 2008, even when the new brass mill capacity was less than 25 % of new wire rod capacity. #### 6 Crisis and Fiscal Rescue of the Copper Semis Industry 

The credit crisis of 2008 froze global semis industry growth to 2007 production levels, with wire rod production very dynamic as is one of the main inputs for the fiscal infrastructure expenditure expansion in China. But global trade has been freezing for manufactured exports in 2009 particularly to the developed world most indebted economies, as the indebted private sector starts an effort to rebalance its finances and the monetary policy try to revive private sector interest by more indebtedness, increasing the public debt in the debt economies or reducing reserves in the creditor economies. As public debt taken from risk adverse savers in the West is channelled to fiscal infrastructure packs in the East by effect of a fixed exchange rate policy in China, domestic demand for wire rod is growing strongly. Brass mills demand, hit by the collapse of manufactured exports, is refocused in the domestic market and receiving fiscal incentives to renew home appliances and subsidies (mainly in China) and to keep the car manufacturing and auto parts industry alive, both in the west and east economies. Some developing countries governments as China are supporting the non ferrous metal industry after the collapse in 2008 export revenues. The Chinese State Owned copper sector strategy is domestic integration and to go multinational, this is a new role for some State owned Chinese semis producers. We observe an on the march redesign to increase domestic demand for copper semis intensive manufactured product in China. China also increased export tax rebates to 2 digits in value added semis products to increase its competitiveness. The unknown sector of small/medium enterprises (SME) producing copper semis in China is not strongly supported by the Chinese plan, strongly focused in large public plants. By contrast the developed economies allocated funds to support copper related SMEs. Increasing manufactured productio

n for local use may keep brass mills busy in the countries with fiscal expansions and local fabricators. But few economies are planning the development of the copper semis industry beyond 2010-11 public debt driven recovery.

Copper semis production for exporters of manufactured products has been affected too. #### 8 Copper Use and Recycling: China in 2008 

The accelerated industrialization of the Chinese economy has increased the use of copper cathodes from mining and from scrap metal to more than 4.9 Mt-cu in 2008 from just over 3 Mt-cu in 2003. If we add more than 1.1 Mt-cu copper content of scrap used by Chinese manufacturing and we add the net imports of manu

factures of copper, we can conclude that China copper use was close to 6.4 Mt-cu in 2008. Preliminary estimates indicate that not less than 1.9 Mt-cu are leaving China every year in exports of household items, in copper cable and in electrical equipment, and also as exported machinery, office equipment, vehicles, computers and other products. Part of this copper will be recycled in the importer country and probably will be re-exported to China or other manufacturing region as copper scrap in the future. In 2008 not less than 2.1 Mt-Cu recovered from copper scrap was used by the industry and by the smelters and refineries producing secondary cathodes in China. Between 1.2 and 1.5 Mt-cu came from almost 6 Mt of gross weight imported scrap and less than 1 Mt-cu came mainly from the domestic recovery of scrap metal in electric, building demolitions, electric equipment and a lesser amount from copper recovered within the industry manufacturing as new scrap. Most of old scrap was used by secondary copper smelters (993 Kt in 2008) and the scrap with a higher content of copper was going to the Chinese copper manufacturers as direct melt. #### 9 China Copper Semis Industry in 2009 

The collapse of copper scrap imports observed in late 2008 and early 2009 as a result of falling refined copper prices was offset by rapidly increasing imports of refined copper and scrap at very convenient prices in the first half of the year. However the scrap drought revealed how dependent to the global supply of copper scrap is a good part of the Chinese manufacturing industry and even more dependent are the secondary copper smelters relying on imported old scrap. The global supply of old copper scrap proved to be much more sensitive to price changes versus the global supply of new copper scrap. Although the largest exporters of scrap (United States, Germany, Britain and France) reacted to low prices by raising the gross exports to China and elsewhere, the world reacted to the lower prices as expected, reducing their gross exports of copper scrap in about 18 % in 2008. This was the cause of an 11 % drop in world exports, dramatically affecting the availability of copper scrap in China in the first half of 2009, and risking production of manufacturing copper semis and smelters producing cathodes from old scrap. This suggests that the regulatory environment is less important than other factors such as the potential benefits and geology in determining investment decisions in the copper mining industry, and the Chinese investment program is a good example of the criteria described for investing in copper mining. A summary of the main decision 2225 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Risopatron_ factors to invest in mining are discussed below. Michener (1969) provided a classification of mining investment across countries balancing the concept of political and geological risk allocation. Johnson (1990) surveyed managers of major mining exploration, which gave first priority to the country's geological potential, followed by political stability and thirdly to the infrastructure, location and experience in mining. As Johnson, Otto (1992) confirmed that the geological potential is the most important factor when investing in a sample of countries and companies in the Asia Pacific region. The World Bank (1999) surveyed 35 governments and mining companies in operation, obtaining similar outcomes on the central role of the geological potential of the metals and minerals over other factors. Behre Dolbear, a consulting firm in the mining sector, published rankings based on survey investment analysts who gave priority to investments in Australia, Canada, Chile and the US. #### 14 Exploration Expenditures in 2009 Otto (2009) in a recent study for the ICSG found that a nation with copper resources is the determining factor for investment in copper mining between different countries, not the potential of its mining policy: investments go to countries with good prospects for copper production even if the mining law and tax policy are poor. Factors such as the size of the deposit, grade of ore and extraction metho

d (surface or underground) are particularly important for investments in copper. The study of Otto also found that the effective tax rate paid throughout the life of a project, over the total value of the project flow should be between 40 % and 50 % for a typical copper mine. Jara, Lakes and Tilton (2008) found that the investment climate of a country is well measured by expenditures in exploration, but this factor is largely limited by the minerals that the country produces. Large investments in exploration in minerals other than copper in other countries, as for example diamonds, explains the declining rate of mineral exploration expenditures in relation to the global expenditures observed in Chile in recent years. As exploration costs are widely recommended as an adequate guide to anticipate investments in mining, the ICSG reviewed the cost estimate of 2009 for exploration of the mining group Votorantim presented in the Latin American Mining Conference in June 2009. This estimate indicates a decline of 37 % from 13.9 billion to 9.2 billion in 2009 compared to 2008: the reduced availability of credit and liquidity problems observed in the TSE and ASX mining stock exchanges explains lower levels in exploration budgets planned for the next three years, although copper and gold could be best scenarios for exploration 2010-2013 versus other metals, due to reduced industrial demand for metals, the decline in mining production and the portfolio of projects deferred. The shortage of capital has affected many junior explorers and some exploration companies are close to insolvency in 2009, which could allow some larger mining to improve the quality of its portfolios. However, the exploration will return to pre crisis only when the industrial production will be recovered, because there is an important amount of lost production and new projects postponed in the mining portfolio. Also because is not easy to retrieve the qualified personnel fired in the economic crisis.

stment in new copper mines and expansions could remain low in real terms for some time. It is possible that new investment projects in copper mines should choose less capital-intensive technologies if the shortage of credit to finance mining projects subsists. #### 18 Impact of the Credit Crisis on Plant Capacity 

The capacity of the SX-EW plants reached 4.1 Mt-cu in 2008 and was expected to grow to 6.2 Mt-cu in 2012 before the crisis: the new target for 2012 is 5.2 Mt-cu. This is one Mt of capacity less, due to the lack of funds to build the hydrometallurgy plants related to the crisis of the financial institutions, which also reduced the production plans of SX-EW to about 1.3 Mt-cu. However, recent field surveys show that some of SX-EW plants in operation are rapidly expanding their production c

apacity in 2009, after the cathode production by SX-EW almost touched 3.1 Mt-cu in 2008. Electrolytic refineries capacity was reaching 17.7 Mt-cu in 2008 and their plan was to reach 18.7 in 2012. The refineries do not seem affected by the crisis: new plans to reach 19.1 Mt-cu of capacity in 2012 and about 19.6 Mt-cu in 2013 had been announced recently in 2009. A situation similar is observed by smelters, whose capacity of 17.6 Mt-cu in 2008 could rise to almost 19.4 Mt in 2012-cu and to 19.6 Mt in 2013. The main projects for new smelters and refineries are located in China and are sensitive to changes in investment decisions of the Chinese Government, now in a process of vertical integration and holding creation. Copper concentrate production capacity should not fall much more than 200 Kt-cu with respect to the investment plans of 2008, reaching 17.4 Mt-cu in 2012 and growing to 17.4 Mt-cu in 2013. World production of concentrates failed to take off from the annual ceiling below 12.5 Mt-cu in recent years: given the low rates of capacity utilization of smelters in recent years would not be expected bottlenecks in the balance of concentrates if not major technical problems or maintenances in smelters are considered. The proposed implementation of a proposed global ban in mercury emissions by the United Nations Environmental program (UNEP) supported now by a US legislation under discussion (Mercury Market Minimization Act) may put some additional pressure to copper smelters costs in 2010-2015.

#### 19 Peace and Security Constraints in Emerging Copper Economies 

The status of future copper exploration projects in Pakistan and Afghanistan is likely to raise security challenges not unlike those observed today in countries like Congo, Indonesia and Mindanao in the Philippines. In Indonesia the safety factor is not only an additional production cost, despite the determined efforts of the authorities, bombings have injured copper mining executives, and vandalism have been followed by shootings and human losses in 2009. In the case of Congo, the DRC is the country with the lowest income per capita in the world (FMI 2009) after experiencing a devastating war with the participation of armies from 7 African nations between 1998 and 2003, in the eastern region of the country where major mineral resources are located. A massive and growing intervention of UN peacekeepers since 2000 has reduced the conflict, with more than 22,000 UN troops on the ground in 2009 and an annual budget of 1350 millions of dollars. These security costs are not counted in the cost of copper production from the current and future mining projects in the Congo. According to the Security Council of the UN in June 2009, military operations against foreign armed groups from Rwanda, other countries in the region of lakes and

southern African countries (UN 2003-2009) as well as Congolese armed ethnic groups, continues in 2009, with large movements of refugees, and attacks to the civilian population, although much of the military situation is stabilized and Congo moves on to local elections. Nevertheless, the UN suggests that progress in reducing corruption and the humanitarian crisis is limited, while the economic crisis hampers efforts to build a civil order based in the security that the government receives taxes from the exploitation of minerals in the neighbour countries in the great lakes in the eastern DRC. Eastern Congo is rich in natural resources including copper, tin, cassiterite, columbite-tantalite or coltan (tantalum), wolframite (tungsten) and gold among others. Metals derived from these minerals are used in electronic products including mobile phones, laptops and digital cameras. In 2009 the U.S. Congress debate a proposed law (Senators Brownback, Durbin and Feingold) asking the U.S. State Department to monitor the financing of armed groups in the mineral-rich areas of eastern Congo and proposing that American firms selling columbite-tantalite, cassiterite, wolframite (tungsten) or derivatives of these minerals would be required to disclose annually to the Securities and Exchange Commission the country of origin of the minerals. If the mineral is coming from the Democratic Republic of Congo and surrounding countries, the company should disclose the mine of origin. 

#### 20 Operational Constraints on Copper Mines: Water Supply and Falling Ore Grades 

There are some operational limitations of high concern in the copper industry: one is the limited availability of water for copper mining processes in arid zones as is the case in northern Chile, Peru and Australia. #### 21 Skilled Workers, Shipping and Sulphuric Acid Constraint 

While neither sulfuric acid or shipping costs appear to be a major constraint to copper mine production and trade in 2009, is important to remember 2007 and part of 2008 when fast credit expansion accelerated quickly the demand for fertilizers, absorbing the oversupply of sulphuric acid from the copper smelters and increasing sulphuric acid prices and costs of SX-EW plants. The availability of skilled workers for exploration, mine design and operations do not seem so critical in the midst of a recession. Also the globalized labour market, facilities for obtaining visas and remuneration commensurate to the risk and distance from population centers ,plus the attractive remuneration should mobilize qualified personnel to jobs in mines and copper plants. Although in Canada is expected a shortfall of 92,000 workers over the next decade, many young graduates are going to Australia, where it is common for a graduate engineering to start with a basic salary of $100,000 plus benefits with very little experience. In South Africa the mining industry consider re-employment of retired engineers, metallurgists and geologists, because of the shortage of workers, while Namibia changed its immigration laws to be more competitive. In Chile and the U.S. with labour markets more competitive, workers benefits are more closely related to changes in copper prices. #### Abstract 

During the design of a copper concentrator (or indeed any processing plant) it is not uncommon that there is uncertainty about the most appropriate design criteria to apply to processing circuits or equipment. So-called ‘safe’ approaches to oversizing conflicts with the interest in capital efficiency (and also may not be an appropriate solution) while undersizing can be of serious detriment to the project result. The uncertainty can be compounded by the expected run times of the specific system and/or the upstream and downstream systems. One approach is to replicate from other projects. However that is not always easy or appropriate and can incur unnecessary higher capital costs. A preferred alternative is to develop a dynamic model that incorporates maintenance conditions (availability and equipment down time) as well as operating conditions (run time). 

This paper shows how some models have been used to provide optimized sizing for a processing circuit or equipment. It also pres

ents possibilities for doing sensibility analysis in order to optimize a circuit or equipment. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Modeling of industrial processes and development of dynamic simulations have evolved noticeably in recent years. This is attributable to the availability of increased computational power and the concomitant development of sophisticated commercial software that has made programming of these models easier. 

One area that has taken more advantage of the dynamic simulation tools is the one related to the process automatic control, using non-linear advanced multi-variable processes, fuzzy controllers and neural networks, among others. 

2235 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_

By comparison, for the development of engineering projects, it is not common to apply modeling and dynamic simulation techniques for the design and further verification of the treatment capacities of each of the pieces of equipment separately, and of the systems they constitute; more specifically, the inventory capacities of hoppers and ore stockpiling yards involved in the operation of the pant being designed. 

A primary advantage from use of dynamic simulation in the design of production plants is the early and clear identification of potential bottlenecks that could impede the intended production performance. The modeling can also detect inappropriate sizing, and related capital costs, of hoppers, stockpiles and requirements of ancillary equipment. 

Trend results obtained from the dynamic simulations are a demonstrable information base of the designed plant operation, which can be integrated into engineering documents such as for operating philosophy and process control. They describe how the interactions between the different process stages can be in the real operation, according to the expected operation (Run Time and maintenance times) and selected equipment sizing. 

#### 2 Methodology 

The methodology comprises the formulation of numeric and differential equations for the mass and energy balances associated with the modeled process steps. These are based on representation of the cause-effect interactions, selected in each case with the appropriate degree of complexity or detail to comply with the purpose of the dynamic simulation study. The dynamic models generated during various stages may be very complex in some cases or simpler in others. 

For this purpose, a series of phenomenological and/or empirical equations are developed, as also taking account of minimum and maximum operating conditions stated in the catalogues of main equipment and empirical rules describing aspects of the operation itself. One of the most important aspects with impact on the plant design is the correct modeling of the operation time (Run Time) of plant and equipment. The Run Time is a direct consequence of the execution of scheduled maintenance as well as non-scheduled shutdowns of the plant. Examples are equipment and/or system problems due to electric power ou

tages or part failures with operating equipment. The group of equations and rules representing the desired operation of the plant are coded in proprietary software, which performs the simulations and provides results from selected inputs or criteria. The results are analyzed and validated to establish if they comply with the conditions established by the process design criteria or project operation philosophy. This process usually becomes an iterative process that in some way tries to optimize the operation, design and investment cost of the project. For the development of this paper, validation of the proper sizing of hoppers and stockpiling yards has taken into account certain conditions of a typical copper concentrator plant. 2236 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Capital Savings Through the Use of Dynamic Modeling_ In many projects, sizing of the hopper volumes and stockpiling capacity of intermediate or final product are usually based on basic estimate methods but not on detailed system analysis of all potential inter-related effects such as is possible with computational dynamic simulation. #### 3 Results The following items and Figures present results of simulations of example facilities of a typical mineral concentrator but they do not represent a specific project. ##### 3.1 Mine and Primary Crusher Facilities This example considers a design where two mine trucks can unload simultaneously to the hopper feeding the primary crusher. In the field of mining and industry, Serbia is undergoing a transitional restructuring and a process of researching its long-term prospects and development options. This process has ownership, functional, institutional, organizational, market and other dimensions, with an aim of increasing competitiveness. In the future strategic options of the Bor copper complex, there are still many open questions and dilemmas regarding the best solutions. Thus, the factors of risk and uncertainty are introduced, as categories that should be considered in the choice of development plans for the region of the mining-smelting basin of Bor. General business risks and uncertainties in the development of the Bor basin and the company for the production and processing of copper MSB „Bor“ is

Risks are characteristic of every strategic development and business decision-making, so their successful management should be a part of the development strategy of the corporation, especially long-term. With the increase of uncertainty in the general socio-economic environment, there is mounting talk of „management risks“, risk control, risk culture, risk assessment, risk optimization. Management of strategy risks requires defining maps of activity management, policies, measures on a corporate and a local and national level, in order to eliminate or alleviate the potential negative effects. Among the key risks at a corporate level are the financial risks and risks of the regulative framework, especially in the field of environment and land use. In both cases, it is a question

of external risks, which the companies need to relativize and successfully manage. Some companies pay more attention to production risks and search for better solutions in that domain, which, however, is not enough. 

The analysis has included the identification and „assessment of the risk and uncertainty impact“ on the future development of the copper complex in the mining-smelting basin Bor. The research has included the general market trend and market positioning of the production and copper processing complex in the world and in Bor; the impact of the requirements and strategic goals of the EU on the institutional and other adjustments in the period of transition important for business in this sector; the influence of the new EU industrial policy; the impact assessment of the regulations important for business in the mining and metals sector (Kyoto Protocol, Directive IPPC, Directive CCS, Directive ETS, et al.). It is expected that the spatial-ecological aspects will have a great role in achieving future development of copper complex in the Bor area, in accordance with _the Lisbon agenda_ . [1, 2] 

In the following text, firstly the global factors of business risks have been analyzed, then the risks in the mining and metals sector. Finally, the main risks have been identified together with their possible effect on the strategic development of MSB Bor. 

#### 2 Global business risks 

According to data [3], the key global risks in business are strategic, financial, regulative and operative. _Strategic risks_ imply the weakening of alliances, a drop in transactions, radically “going green”, non-traditional new participants in the company purchases. According to available data [4], in the mining and metals sector, there has been a decrease in M&A activity and transactions for 60 % and purchases for roughly 80 % due to the impact of the global economic and financial crisis. The copper sector is one of the carbon-intensive sectors in which adjustments to the „green“ regulations are necessary (Kyoto Protocol, Directive on carbon emissions, Directive on CCS, and Directive on ETS). _Financial risks_ are the key flywheel in the birth and deepening of the recession in the copper sector as well, because of the 2008 credit crunch. Many countries in the world have verified the stimulus package of 1.760 billion $ for economic recovery, of which roughly 10 % is meant for the sector of energy and heavy infrastructure. [4] In Serbia, a „stimulus package“ was been present during all these years of transitional recession and during the restructuring of the copper complex.

Because of the operation difficulties of MSB Bor and the workers' strikes, the government has been co-funding part of the operation costs (writing off and taking on debts – approximately 550 million US dollars, investing in maintenance, buying part of the equipment, paying sever

ance for redundant workers, often, even salaries to the employed) [5]. 

Business risks due to the implementation of strict _environmental and other regulations_ , and because of the need for _obtaining permits_ are one of the main factors in the implementation of low-carbon development options in the copper sector. _Operational risks_ imply the reduction of costs, maintaining a reputation, management, etc. Other business risks are: the shifting of consumer demands, market change, new technologies, management of intellectual capital, energy supply shocks, innovation incompetence, infrastructural risks, new owners (private ordinary shares, rich foreign funds – public and hedge), supply channels, and management of new business models. 

#### 3 Strategic risks in the sector of mining and metals 

The mining and metals sector is known for the risks that, at the same time, present a challenge and a possibility for development. The principle risks and uncertainties for the development of MSB Bor are presented within several groups. 

##### 3.1 New EU industrial policy 

Frameworks of new industrial/economic EU policies were created in Lisbon, in 2000. [1, 2] The most important development goal in the following period is competition, meaning the capacity of the economy to provide a high and growing standard of living, as well as a high employment rate. Achieving industrial competitiveness based on knowledge, innovations and entrepreneurship presents a pillar of EU sustainable development strategies. One of the primary goals of industrial policy is the creation of a basis, of assumptions and conditions for the development of an innovative and market competitive industrial sector, which will provide „ecological sustainability“ of production in the development of the so-called „low-carbon economy“. In the field of mining, the application of basic principles of sustainability is more complex, considering the massive volume of material input. That requires a longer time for adjustment and the preparation of this sector for the application of the principles and policies of sustainable development, which should be applied by the government and corporations. 

##### 3.2 Market positioning of copper complex – collapse or recovery? 

Dynamic changes in the increase of copper demand, over longer periods, have triggered development changes up to the period of the global economic and financial crisis. The annual rate of copper consumption growth in the period 1980-2007 was 3 % [6], while it dropped to 2.2 % in 2008. The basic assessments on the growth of copper demand on the market (on average 3.9 % annually, with exception of China where the growth was 10 % till 2007) and the existing and planned deficits in

. The following aspects in the planning of sustainable developement are emphasised [7]: (1) Policies and regulations in the mining and metallurgy sector (copper complex) in relation to social, economic, environmental issues, local environment; (2) social issues and early involvement of local management /environment in the corporation’s development strategies; (3) risk assessment, shelf-life of a product, and implications concerning sustainability; (4) new development (copper/mining/metallurgy complex) on the grounds of better management of mining gangue, waste etc. (5) water and energy management (conserving energy and reducing the greenhouse gases), etc. 

Around 15.7 million tons of copper are produced annually in the world (2008), and considering the materially-intensive character of input and output in mining, this activity, generally, has certain problems in the realization of competition growth, i.e., in relation to the environment et al. This sector should be more open to ecological requirements. Establishing the indicators of sustainable development in European mining is a step towards helping the companies to measure sustainability and to improve their ecological performance, as well as to have an approach to sustainable development based on strict, scientific assessment of ecological and health risks, assessment of socioeconomic impacts of regulatory instruments, on the issue of competitiveness [8]. 

In the period between 1994-1997, the conditions for copper were extremely good, while in the period between 1998-2002 the copper market went into a recession. After this, there came a rapid growth in copper prices on the market (till the end 2008 > 8000 $/t, at the Q1 2009 were 3100 $/t, in August 2009 it sells > 6260 $/t). This recovered trend of growth is a stimulus for copper manufacturers. Before the production of copper in Bor amounted to 170,000 t per year, and the company RTB Bor was the greatest exporter in Serbia, in net foreign currency, with an export of around 300 million $. The reason for a drastically lower than planned physical scope of copper production and an average realization in the recent years, lies in the industrial conditions that were made difficult because of the war, the rise of inflation, non-solvency, lack of effective money, a fall in the prices of copper until 2003, etc., and due to NATO bombing of the RTB Bor complex. The greatest influence on the competitiveness of the copper manufacturers have production costs, the amount of copper in an ore, the method of mining, the productivity level and economy, the scope of gangue, equipment, traces of assistant metals (gold, silver, titanium…). The structure of costs of the mining industry depends mainly on local factors, while the prices of metals are determined on the market. The main components of the structure of costs in the copper complex are energy products, ecological taxation and employment costs, and they are closely linked to regulatory policies. Due to th

e EU regulatory decisions, which entail an increase in penalties and other ecological costs, the process of relocating companies that produce metals has begun followed by the expansion and transfer of know-how and direct foreign investments into the East. Available reserves of metal ores are harder to find and their exploitation is more and more expensive. This unbalance is expected to continue in the future. An increasing number of business risks require research in order to find options for influencing those trends, so they can be managed. For companies, what is important are identification and management of strategic business risks in order to determine the lowest possible prices of planned and applied measures, especially environmental measures. According to the document, „Territorial Agenda”, 2007, [9], among the main European challenges are „promoting a Trans-European management of risks, including the risks and impact of climate change”. 

After a period in which the price of copper was rising, there was a sudden fall in the prices on the global copper market in 2008, as well as in the volume of circulation of transactions and in the prices of shares of the mining companies (around 60 %). The global financial crisis caused the drop in prices of all commodity goods (including copper). The high price of copper on LME from 8000 $/t has been maintained since 2005 until the end of 2008, when it started drastically falling and reached its lowest level of 3100 $/t in January 2009. Since spring 2009, the prices of copper have slowly been recovering and in August 2009 have reached the level of 6260 $/t. According to stock-market data [10], a steady rise of the price and demand for copper is expected until 2012. 

The market for all metals, including copper, is in deep recession on a global scale. Given the general estimates, it seems that this market will remain in a depressed state for a long time. Owing to market trends and business risks, the development in copper complexes will continue with various changes, because the implied increase in production costs, especially those costs regarding the introduction of regulations regarding climate change (the reduction of CO2 emissions, CCS concept and others) will force some of the producers to reduce the production programs, even to close the mines or the processing capacities. According to estimations, the whole mining and metals sector is in trouble, [6] especially because of the decrease and nearly complete lack of investment in R&D, which has brought firms on the verge of collapse and extinction. Wider consequences o

f a potential collapse scenario are very unfavourable, because they mean further unemployment, political instability, riots, closing of firms, collapse in a greater part of the sector et al. The scenario for the recovery of the copper sector seems to be more realistic, because it is reasonable to expect that after the plunge of the price of copper and decrease in production for several years, the demand and production of this metal will grow. The slow rise of the price of copper in Q2and Q3 2009 (in August 2009 was 6260 $/t) indicates possible signals of recovery in its demand. Many developed countries have possibly stimulated increase in demand, as part of the massive fiscal stimulus package, especially because of the important packages for infrastructural projects that demand new quantities of metal. The drop in value of mining and metals companies at the stock-market has led to the fact that buying an existing mine is cheaper than building new ones, but the assumption is that in several years it will be cheaper to build than to buy capacities.

#### 4 General analysis of the risks in the development of the Bor basin 

The mining-smelting basin Bor is located in Eastern Serbia. The development of mining and copper metallurgy in town Bor started in 1903. Town Bor has a population of 40,000 and 12,090 employees in 2009, of which 4720 are employed in MSB Bor. The company’s total capital and commitments in 2007 were 413 million €, annual production in 2008 was 31,068 t, the average salary in June 2009 was 320 €/monthly/per employee (which corresponds to the average salary in Serbia). The mining-metallurgy capacities for processing copper are located inside the basin – the Copper Mine, The Smelter and Refinery and many industrial enterprises that were, earlier, parts of the MSB Bor. The ins

talled capacities are: copper production from native ores at 100,000 t/per year (mines and flotation plants); metallurgical capacities around 100,000 t/year of cathode copper; sulfuric acid plant 300,000 t/year, and copper wire plant of 30,000 t/year. 

Ten principle risks have been identified for the development of the mining basin and MSB Bor, as well as several others that could increase in importance in the years to come. The principle business risks for the development of the Bor copper basin are: 

1. _Shortage of qualifications, knowledge and skills –_ The growth and development of the sector imply qualified human resources, employees with skills and knowledge. Shortage of such human resources, especially managers, engineers and others is the main strategic business risk for the company MSB Bor. Because of the shortage of highly qualified human resources, the average age of the employees has increased in the company. The rise in unemployment, economic problems in the business activity of RTB Bor, a fall in the standard of living and a rise in poverty, with a slow dynamic in the establishing of new enterprises in the private sector, has started the immigration of the local population, in particular, the young, educated workforce. Due to the difficult economic situation in the period after 2002, around 10,000 inhabitants have moved out of the Bor municipality, i.e., around 20 % of the total population [12]. The structure of the population that has immigrated consists of mainly people who were technologically redundant, pensioners and young personnel (and unemployed young people). This process is very unfavourable for the development of MSB Bor, because this territory has become a significantly depressive area in Serbia due to drastic deindustrialization. The copper complex in Bor employed 24,000 workers in 1990, but 4877 workers in 2008.

2. _Industrial consolidation-restructuring and privatization of the company MSB Bor_ – For greater market power, increase of production and diversification of strategic business risk, mergers and acquisitions generally are taking place more often in this sector. Access risk and the increase of costs of capital can also be included in this due to the global economic crisis. China, Russia, Brazil and India's market share in the production of metal has increased several times in the period 2000-2007. Market consolidation has enabled the making of greater market power and leading new producers, which has led to a decrease of fragmentation in acquisition. This trend has mounted the pressure on companies to increase competition with the motto »everybody is flocking around the prey – make your way to food or you will become food for others«. Ernst & Young predict that 4-5 leading firms will emerge in the end and they will be geographically positioned in Russia and China [6]. 

The basic orientations of

program and development policies, for the following period, are determined by the development and modernization of the Mining and Metallurgical Complex of Bor, according to the results of the restructuring and privatisation. The government of Serbia has adopted an Action plan for the restructuring and privatisation of RTB Bor [13], and Strategy of privatisation and restructuring of RTB Bor [14]. The plan implies two groups of companies: 1) core activities (copper mines, smelter, refinery, and holding of RTB Bor) for which a financial consultant for the process of restructuring and privatisation of RTB Bor was appointed in October 2005, and financed by the World Bank; 2) dependent companies (Factory of equipment and spare parts, Factory of lacquer wire and “Jugotehna export-import” from Belgrade) for which consultants had been previously chosen. The Government of the Republic of Serbia has prepared a study with the World Bank about restructuring and privatisation of RTB Bor and the potential assessment of the Bor River. The restructuring program includes a social program (2500 workers redundant) and the Program for environmental protection adopted by the relevant organ in RTB Bor. The policy of the government’s Action plan, with the support of the World Bank, is to solve redundancy by providing loans for SME, as well. 

Resolving the question of debts towards the creditors of RTB Bor is vital for attracting future partners and a successful privatisation. According to available data [15], 78 % of debt is towards government creditors. The government has decided to write off around 550 million $ of RTB Bor debt. Apart from the question of debt settlement throughout the period of revitalisation of RTB Bor until 2010, the problem of business activities remains as well. The key problem of RTB Bor is the protection of the environment, especially the issue of the Smelter which has outdated technology. Planning of the rehabilitation and future development of RTB Bor is the subject of two-three studies and reports of the World Bank [16]. 3. _Access to infrastructure_ – The expansion of production in the mining and metals sector is being faced with increasing obstacles regarding access to infrastructure. Owners of the infrastructure do not follow adequately the needs of the mining complex, because they do not have clear signals from the market to invest in new infrastructural facilities (e.g., ports, ships, railways etc.) in order to maximize the production capacities in mining. Therefore, the mining and metals firms are greatly tempted to own their proper infrastructure, which is a paradox. By combining the high risks of production with the low risks in the infrastructural sector, this could reduce the value of the enterprise. 

The transportation and geographical position of the Eastern Serbian region, in which MSB Bor is located, is relatively favorable. From the viewpoint of regional transportation communications, this region is located approximately 75 km from Corridor X and approximately 40 km from Corridor VII Danube. Among the above-mentioned corridors PEN, network TINA, Corridor IV (BerlinIstanbul) through Romania and Bulgaria is the greatest competitor to Corridor X in this part of Europe. MSB Bor uses for transporting ores and finished products port Prahovo on the Danube, which is located near the Romanian-Bulgarian border, from where they are transferred to Bor by rail some 45 km. The lack of government funds for the quality maintenance of the rail infrastructure is a consequence o

f the overall situation in Serbia in the 90’s.

5. _Harmonisation and the Kyoto Protocol, which Serbia has ratified in 2007_ [22] – The effects of climate change are very important, because they imply changes in regulations, costs of changes and harmonization, limitations of infrastructure, political instability, a sudden change in consumer behavior and strategic business risks in accordance with the new development mode of mining and industry towards a mandatory introduction of a low-carbon economy. 

Emissions trading is an important policy measure to reduce environmentally harmful emissions. Mining, industrial sectors and/or individual companies are allocated a fixed number of emissions allowances by government for a specified period for a specific pollutant such as CO2, or SO2. If a particular participant’s actual emissions exceed these allowances, another participant’s surplus allowances may be purchased to ensure a balance of emissions and allowances. This gives participants the choice of reducing emissions in actuality (e.g. by investing in equipment, or by changing operations) or by purchasing an appropriate number of allowances to match actual emissions. Because the total number of allowances is capped, emissions reductions will be made, but for global

This measure allows emissions reductions to be made at a lower cost than if individual participants each had absolute caps. Undoubtedly the effect of CO2 emissions trading will mean an increase in copper prices and electricity prices as the generators pass on their costs to consumers. 

In the future, it can be expected that carbon will be labeled on products and traded globally, and that there will be strict regulations and significant taxes on carbon itself. Mining companies will have to adjust their business to the requirements of ecological regulations towards a low-carbon economy. Most companies will accept minimal responsibility and will radically lower their carbon intensity. Low-carbon companies will have a competitive advantage on the copper market. 

The EU Climate Package was adopted in December 2008, and includes the EU ETS Directive, Directive on renewable sources and Directive CCS. The industrial capacities that use fossil fuels independent of their type will have to use the CCS (Carbon Capture System), which is becoming the general requirement for the industries of Europe. The industry will have to pay for the collecting, transportation and storage of carbon, which should be implemented by 2020. The focal point of storing carbon lies on its collection in accordance with the IPPC Directive, while the transport is regulated in accordance with the regulation on transporting natural gas (by using EIA instruments on country level). 

In January 2009, the EC has adopted the Recovery Package with the proposal of 1.250 billion € for five b

ig CCS projects. According to the Directive CCS, the member-countries decide if and where to build CCS, i.e., the companies decide if they will use CCS based on the conditions in the carbon market. The main goals and principles of this directive are to provide the legal framework for managing environmental risks. According to the EU Directive of ETS, a public bid for the energy sector permits will start from 2013. The system of trading with CO2 emissions is simultaneously a catalyst for the support of the CCS concept. 

The EU has accepted to lower CO2 emissions by 8 % by 2012, which has certain implications for all sectors. In addition, the EU has committed to reduce the energy consumption by 20 % by 2020, so that renewable energy sources participate with 20 %. According to the data of Eurostat in 2007, equivalent emissions of CO2 in EU-27 were 5045.37 million t. The greatest contribution to this have Germany 956.1 million t, UK 636.68 million t, Italy 552.7 million t, Spain 442, Poland 398.8 million t etc. Total CO2 emission for Serbia in 2004 was 56.7 million t. or 242.5 kg CO2 per person. Serbia is not on the list of Annex B of the Kyoto Protocol and is not obligated to reduce a certain amount of greenhouse emissions, but was given the possibility to adopt this obligation. 

It is certain that the environmental protection costs will burden the business more in the future period. For the sanitation of environmental problems, great financial means are necessary. It is still unclear how the means for the sanitation of environmental problems of Bor will be provided i.e., priority sanitation for the environmental hot spots. 

Delaying with the application of the Kyoto Protocol would certainly postpone the writing of many new generations of development documents that are based on the principles and criteria of sustain-

6. _Increase of costs_ – The increase in demand influences the increase in the use of production capacities. While higher prices of commodity goods influence the increase of company revenue, the prices of capital and the increase of production costs make them marginal. The danger of an increase in costs is vital for company competitiveness. Costs of energy, materials and labor are subject to inflation. Inflation in the metals complex is usually calculated by 8-10 %. This impact on the mining and metals companies increases the pressure on the production limits resulting in the highrisk inv

estment profile of the company; increases the advantage of portfolio optimization, the consolidation and share of the risky arrangements. Due to a sudden rise in the prices of metals in the period 2003-2008, the production philosophy of the metal complex has „written off“ cost control as a regulator of business success and competitiveness and has applied the principle „production at all costs“. Mergers and acquisitions have enabled a drastic step towards cost control. 

In the era of the boom of commodity prices, the motto was „production at any costs”. During that period, there was no strict control of production costs. With the global financial crisis, this has changed and cost management at a corporate level is becoming an important business strategic risk. Uncertainties in the global markets and in international relations, climate change and other factors force the companies to be careful in creating a new development mode and managing costs. 

The greatest influence on the competitiveness of the copper manufacturers have production costs, the amount of copper in an ore, the method of mining, the productivity level and economy, the scope of gangue, equipment, traces of assistant metals (gold, silver, titanium…). The structure of costs of the mining industry depends mainly on local factors, while the prices of metals are determined on the market. The main components of the structure of costs in the copper complex are energy products, ecological taxation and employment costs, and they are closely linked to regulatory policies. Due to the EU regulatory decisions, which entail an increase in penalties and other ecological costs, the process of relocating companies that produce metals has begun followed by the expansion and transfer of know-how and direct foreign investments into the East. The implementation of the Lisbon strategy for competition growth has implications on the mining sector, especially on the growth of competition, GDP, productivity, together with mounting ecological and energy costs, and a possible further decline in profits in mining [8]. Excessive costs of basic activities, especially of energy products, production costs, as well as the absence of necessary investments and the opening of new deposits, could threaten competitive business activity of RTB Bor. It is still not clear how the necessary financial means for solving the ecological problems and their sanitation in Bor will be provided.

#### 5 Conclusion 

The main risks and uncertainties for the development of the Bor basin of copper are the following: 

1) Delay in the process of restructuring, consolidation and the completion of privatisation, as well as alternatives to a development that is not based on the principles of sustainability, could strenghten the current highly risky and socio-economically unacceptable trend of development. 

2) Very important risk for the RTB “Bor” are environmental requirements for the optimal utilization of resources and the protection of the environment; growth of costs because aplication of environmental regulative; overconsumption of energy products in the system of RTB Bor. 

- 3) The start of a new sustainable development cycle will be impeded, unless the problem with the lack of younger, highly-educated and highly-skilled population is not tackled. 

- 4) Without technological innovations and new tecnological knowledge, the Bor area has no perspective for starting a development cycle. 

5) The main risks for development of copper complex are: lack of capital for new investments; lack of working capital for the start of production; insufficient adjustment of production to a marketbased economy; the consolidation of RTB Bor. 

In the following period, it will be necessary to implement complementary measures of industrial policy, by which the mining-metallurgy-processing copper complex will gradually begin to eliminate its economic, social, and environmental-spatial problems. The following measures have priority: a) measures of economic policy for the consolidation and recovery of MSB Bor, especially by implementing structural-organizational and ownership changes in MSB Bor; b) rapid preparations of the plant MSB Bor for implementing measures of environmental protection, especially regarding the recovery from SO2, CO2, emissions, ashes, dust, heavy metals and other pollutants; c) improving the energy efficiency of MSB, investing into research and development of deposits, into ecologically sustainable and effective technologies; d) stimulating pattern changes in production and consumption of mining resources and energy, so that the market prices can reflect the real costs that a society has because of industrial activity, i.e., real soc

ial costs of resource exploitation and its impact on the environment; e) stimulating the development of regional clusters in the copper processing sector, et al; f) improving the informatics channels and other initiatives for supporting the mobilization and active participation of citizens in decision-making; g) improving the spatial-functional organization of the current zones of mining-metallurgy and energy supply activities.
