### Application of Ultrasonic Extinction for Simultaneous On-Line Particle Size Distribution and Solid Concentration Analysis of Mineral Slurries 

Dipl.-Ing. Christian Behrens, M.Sc. Andrew Smith, Dipl.-Ing. Axel Pankewitz Sympatec GmbH – System-Partikel-Technik Am Pulverhaus 1 37678 Clausthal-Zellerfeld, Germany 

**Keywords:** On-line particle size analysis, slurry analysis, ultrasonic extinction, OPUS 

#### Abstract 

After a first rough comminution of the ore body in a crusher, the following decisive process step is the fine milling of the ore in order to prepare the minerals for the subsequent separation steps. Here, the particle size distribution is of critical importance for the efficient operation of downstream processes such as flotation, cyclone separation, magnetic separation, settling, drying or others. In order to optimize the process an early control of the particle size leaving the milling stage is essential. 

Ultrasonic Extinction based particle size analysers are capable of performing on-line particle size distribution (PSD) and solid content measurement of mineral slurries such as iron ore, copper ore, fluorspar, quartz sand or others directly in a tough process environment. The method does not require any sample preparation or dilution, hence, instruments can be designed to be installed directly in the product flow without complicated peripherals. 

The

introduced instrument OPUS provides real time, on-line PSD of 31 size classes and can be applied for particles from nanometre range up to several millimetres with solid contents from only 1% up to thick pastes. The sensor is designed as a rugged in-line probe which is highly resistant to wear or contamination which plagues optical systems. The technique is independent of product flow, contamination, optical properties, vibrations, pressure or changes in solid concentration. Even air bubbles, known to evoke noise signal, are depressed by suitable algorithms. Various installations are presented.

#### 1 Introduction 

After mining, the first process step of ore handling is the mechanical size reduction of the ore body to small particles, which are subsequently provided to the following processing steps such as flotation, cyclone separation, magnetic separation, sedimentation, chemical pulping, dewatering etc. For all these process steps, the particle size distribution of the ore – typically presented suspended in water as slurry – is the decisive physical parameter. Hence, the particle size distribution needs to be controlled within tight specifications to ensure an efficient and economical operation of the pulping plant. 

The primary ore dressing step is the crushing of the ore rocks followed by grinding in autogenous mills. Oversized material leaving the mill immediately is cut off by hydrocyclones or screens and linked back to the mills again. Material passing the milling stage mostly passes another cutting step optimizing the slurry fraction even more with respect to the demands of the subsequent process step. 

As the composition of the ore body itself varies in from deposit to deposit, the physical properties of the ore such as e.g. density varies too, this exerts influence on the separation techniques. 

In order to optimize existing and new ore dressing plants, on-line control of the particle size distribution is of fundamental importance. 

With respect to the tough environment of these heavy duty applications, the applied analytical technology needs to meet stringent requirements such as mechanical and chemical robustness of the instrument and robust analytical methodology that must be independent from fluctuations in solid contents, temperature, pressure, pH-value or entrained air content. 

Optical systems typically fail on these applications for several reasons. Firstly optical components are extremely sensitive to scratches, wear and contamination, even minor contamination renders the data unreliable as any adhered particles are analysed with each sample. In order to determine the level of contamination frequent background measurements are required which demand a particle free liquid flow through the analyser. Secondly, instruments based on optical principles require either the use of a very thin monolayer of particles which is unrepresentative or need a strong d

ilution of the ore slurries in the order of magnitude of 1:100 to 1:10,000. #### 2 Technology – Ultrasonic Extinction The application of sound waves overcomes the limitations of optical principles and allows the design of robust instruments without moving parts able to operate in highly concentrated slurries without sample preparation. 2268 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Ultrasonic Extinction for On-Line Particle Size Distribution Analysis on Mineral Slurries_ ##### 2.1 Principle The design of an instrument for the determination of frequency dependent Ultrasonic Extinction (USE) is schematically presented in Figure 1. An electrical high frequency generator is connected to a piezoelectric ultrasonic transducer. The generated ultrasonic waves are coupled into the suspension and interact with the suspended particles, in simple terms particles which are very much smaller than the wavelength of the ultrasonic wave are entrained and do not attenuate the signal whereas particles larger than the wavelength scatter and attenuate the signal. After passing the measuring zone the ultrasonic waves are received by an ultrasonic detector and converted into an electrical signal. The extinction of the ultrasonic waves is calculated from the ratio of the signal amplitudes on the generator and detector side. The Ultrasonic Extinction of a suspension of mono-disperse particles can be described by the Lambert-Beer law according to Riebel [1]. The Extinction _–ln (I/I0)_ at a given frequency _fi_ is linearly dependent on the thickness of the suspension layer ∆l , the projection area-concentration _cPF_ and the extinction coefficient _K_ . The instrument is designed as probe and can be adapted to nearly all kind of process pipes (> DN200) or vessels using a DN 100 flange or process adapters for smaller pipe diameters (DN10 – DN50). OPUS is designed for fully automatic real-time particle size analysis in process environment. The system protection class is IP65 or ATEX rated and complies with the regulations of the CE label regarding electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) and electrical security to the applicable ISO standards. Parts in contact with the slurry are constructed from massive stainless steel (DIN/ISO 1.4571, SS316) and SIGRADUR® (high density carbon) to withstand mechanical and chemical attacks without exhibiting significant wear even after more than one year of operation. The OPUS system is designed to have product contact parts easily replaced in the field. Since no sample treatment is required and the analytical principle does not require any moving parts inside the sensor, the entire probe operates without any movement as static probe. Nevertheless, the gap distance inside the measuring zone can be opened and closed automatically if needed e.g. to assist cleaning if water flushing cycles are demanded (Figure 5). ##### 2.3 Bubble handling Ultrasound is known to be absorbed by gas phases in a much higher order of magnitude than in solids or liquids. Hence, entrained air causes a much higher sound attenuation than entrained solids showing a comparable volume concentration. The additional sound attenuation by entrained air is easily identified as a noise signal. Studies have been performed by Meyer [2] and Nishi [3] to demonstrate this effect. In contrast to optical principles which usually considers entrained air as particles and hence leads to incorrect results, ultrasonic extinction clearly discriminates between solid or liquid phases and gas phases. Physically this is due to the fact that signals from entrained air occur mainly at low frequencies while solid and liquid dispersed phases create their major effects at high frequencies. Figure 6 shows this effect. Consequently, whenever entrained air in the ore

slurry is recorded, the applied evaluation algorithm can distinguish between these signals and deduct the air bubble signal from the particle signal. Finally, a corrected attenuation spectrum is available for the evaluation of the particle size distribution [4]. Field experience from recent years indicates that no air bubble noise is normally recorded in the milling stages whereas in the flotation stages bubbles are present (Figure 6) and the bubble correction algorithm works reliably (ref. In order to judge this influence, different kinds of materials have been analysed using a uniform extinction _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2273 _Behrens, Smith, Pankewitz_ function. The resulting PSD from this USE measurement were compared to results obtained by laser diffraction. Deciding to use laser diffraction as reference method excludes possible mistakes which would occur on sieve analysis whenever significant variations of the material raw density of the tested minerals emerge. Laser diffraction also provides data of a similar interval to the USE output which is ideal for comparison of the complete distribution. Figure 8 shows six PSD – three USE analyses and three analyses performed with laser diffraction (HELOS) on a sample of platinum ore which has been separated using s

ieves The three samples clearly can be identified a being “Fine”, “Coarse” and “Mixed” quality. While the fine sample consists mainly of sand (SiO2), the coarse sample mainly consists of chrome oxide. The mean size sample is an inhomogeneous mixture of both minerals. Even though a single extinction function for both materials was applied, an excellent agreement to the reference method could be obtained. Blending both fractions, the quality of agreement between USE and laser diffraction is not degraded. More than 10 years of experience indicates that for most coarse minerals above 1 µm, a single model of extinction function is very reliable and robust without any significant dependency to the mineralogical habit of the ore. ##### 2.5 Comparability One of the most frequently asked questions concerns the comparability of USE results to other methods such as laser diffraction or sieving analysis. Also for applications on Alumina suspensions e.g. as present in the digester of the Bayer process, OPUS provides the necessary PSD information. Meanwhile, OPUS had been installed successfully in a number of ore dressing plants using various setups. Each setup provides specific benefits as discussed in the following sections. ##### 3.1 Copper Dressing – Multiplex Installation The integration of the sensor to the production stream is enabled by various process adapters which connect the measuring gap of the instrument to the product line. As no sampling and sample dilution is required by principle, the sensor can be mounted directly in the main product line, however in most cases it is preferable to install the sensor into a bypass line and provide a partial flow through the system. This approach allows multiplexing the sensor to several lines and at the same _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2276 _Ultrasonic Extinction for On-Line Particle Size Distribution Analysis on Mineral Slurries_ time it avoids possible wear on the system as the slurry speed in the bypass line is reduced and permits maintenance without disrupting production. Figure 11 and 12 show a typical OPUS installation. Here the sensor is installed in copper dressing plant and connected to 3 milling lines. It receives the product through 50 mm pipes directly behind the first cyclone stage after the mill. The product is taken from the main product lines (horizontal, Ш = 400 mm) on the second floor via an electrical valve and linked to the OPUS sensor located in a cabin in the basement. After passing the instrument for 2-3 minutes the slurry is pumped back to the process. Closing the main valves and activating a tap water flushing sequence, the instrument and pipes are cleaned and cross contamination is prevented. By alternately switching from one line to the other, each of the three lines is analysed approx. every 10 minutes. Control of all valves in the sampling system is facilitated by the sensor software via PLC. Results in terms of graphical, numerical PSD and trend diagrams of customer specific values are presented on the system PC as well as forwarded to the process control system via PROFIBUS. Figure 13 shows a trend chart of the R3(75µm) and solid content of several weeks of operation. #### 4 Conclusion 

Ultrasonic extinction overcomes the limitations of optical principles with respect to on-line particle size analysis in highly concentrated ore slurries and provides the opportunity to analyse particle size distribution and solid concentration simultaneously without sample preparation or dilution. Studies and applications show that USE is applicable to various types of ore and even changes in the composition of the ore do not reduce the analysis quality. Installation experience has shown that the amount of entrained air normally present in the process does not restrict the application of USE. 

Several field installations e.g. for copper ore, iron ore, fluorspar or phosphate dressing underline the instrument performance with respect to the physical principle and reliable operation.

Coppex S. A. development Granujet water granulation system for copper white metal and copper slag. ### Managing Refinery Constraints within an Automated Production Environment

**Keywords:** Refinery, automated production, permanent cathodes, simulation, planning 

#### Abstract 

In copper refineries the use of Permanent Cathodes is more and more implemented in installations. If implemented in a fully automated way, this methodology results in efficient handling of the installation. To enable this automated functioning of the copper refinery, Siemens developed the Intelligent Simulation and Control Platform – ISCP. The target of ISCP is to maximize the production rate with the available assets by reducing their non-productive time. 

The new platform generates a sequence of tasks for cranes and carriers within the copper refinery. Those tasks are planned and managed based on the production calendar of a copper refinery and the actual situation on the shop floor to reduce the non productive time of the in-plant logistic assets to a minimum. 

ISCP Plans-

Models-Manages internal transport flows. It generates a Master Plan to maximize production and to optimize workload for operators; schedules transport and product operations to affect correct resources to each task; integrates modeling and simulation of transport flows within the final production platform. 

ISCP monitors and tracks production units and product flows. It updates the detailed transportation plan in real-time; highlights executing conflicts; generates information for performance analysis. 

ISCP simulates operations off-line. It assists in the analysis and optimization of the in-plant logistics and the weight of constraints; helps validating consequences of equipment breakdown or modification of mechanical layouts; assists in adapting operations based on new products. 

This new software platform was successfully implemented in 2 copper refineries during the planning phase (correction with regard to mechanical specifications, performance evaluation) and during

operations (production targets reached even with partially unavailable equipment). The ISCP solution (Siemens NV, Belgium) brought added value to the in-plant logistics of these copper refineries. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Production automation requires a more and more aligned flow of materials within and between production units. A typical environment where those aligned flows are required is the automotive industry. Over the years we have acquired a large experience in production flow control for different production environments. Out of this experience we developed a solution named ‘ISCP’ – Intelligent Simulation and Control Platform. This platform has as main target to reduce the waiting time (=non production time) of intermediate goods between two production units to a minimum. Based on our contacts with three companies specialized in the engineering of copper refineries (UME, Paul Wurth and Femont) the requirements for our solution shifted towards a real time planning and scheduling support and the ability to adapt the scheduling of resources directly in response to the changing status of the environment. Hereby we report on the basic concepts that were necessary to cope with all requirements of the customers. 

#### 2 Environment 

Our contact with the three aforementioned companies introduced us into the world of copper refineries and more specifically with the technology of permanent cathodes. This technology enables the copper refinery’s to run in a highly automated environment with fully automated crane movements, intermediate blank storages, machine handling and copper stripping. This automated environment requires the continuous coordination of independent mechanical units (multiple transfer carriers on one track, automatic guided carriers that move between multiple transfer cranes and bay cranes, meeting points between bay cranes and transfer carriers, synchronisat

ion of movement with stripping machines and so on). 

Within a straightforward production environment this ‘coordination’ could be handled based on standard automation procedures and fixed sequencing that are handled by basic automation environment but within a more complex and larger environment (multiple bays, multiple carriers on one track, minimal stripping machines, …) a more intelligent coordination of all those elements is needed. This is where we evolved our ISCP solution together with our partners by adding the necessary elements to enable the real time control of a copper refinery.

#### 3 Definitions 

The main zones to be considered within the copper refinery are: 

- Machine zone (ZM) with the exchange zone (ZI). 

- Transfer zone (ZT) where the Automatic Guided Carriers are exchanged between bay carriers and transfer carriers. 

- Refining zone (ZR) with the bays containing the electrolytic cells. 





Figure 1: Main zones of a Permanent Cathode Copper Refinery 

Within the machine zone following machines are typically used for the permanent cathode process: 

- **MPA** machine that prepares lots of Anodes to insert in the system. 

- **MIB** machine that introduces the new Blanks into the system. 

- **MLS** machine that washes the Scraps after electrolysis. 

- **MDC** machine that strips the copper from the Cathodes and prepares the blanks to re-insert them in the system. 

The carriers transport the electrodes between the machine zone and the refining zone. There are three different types of carriers: 

- **AGC** carrier that can load or unload lots of electrodes. 

- **TC** carrier that can load, unload and transport an AGC from the machine zone to the refinery zone. 

- **BC** carrier that can load, unload and transport an AGC over the electrolysis cells and between the refinery zone and the transfer zone.

Electrolytic cells are emptied/filled following defined steps. These steps are part of what we call a “renovation”. A renovation treats a section of cells. 

The two classic renovations are: 

- **RT** Total renovation: scraps and cathodes are emptied from the cells and transported to the machines while blanks and anodes are transported from the machines to the cells. 

- **RP** Partial renovation: cathodes are emptied from the cells and transported to the machines (scraps remain in the cells, these are not yet completely used) while blanks are transported from the machines to the cells. 

The exchange zone (ZI) can be present to reduce the distance a transfer carrier has to run and thus speed up the sequence of movements between the refinery and the machine zone. 

Depending on the available space, the needed equipment and often, as we are typically in a revamping environment, the actual layout of the plant

can be more or less complex. From the layout and the different components, it is obvious that many components need to work together and need an optimal use of their time. Furthermore, if one of the components breaks down, even momentary, the whole sequence is disrupted and the efficiency of the refinery plant can drop drastically. Lost production time has to be minimal. #### 4 Concept To be able to handle the automated environment of the permanent cathode refinery, a clear automation concept must be in place. This concept must on the one hand support the necessary communication channels with the central control functions and on the other hand support the real time operation environment of the shop floor. Therefore we introduced a three tier concept: - Tier 1: automation level, individual automation systems for all production means (carriers and machines). Within those systems a standard communication function is installed to enable the deterministic and structured communication with the coordination level. - Tier 2: real time coordination level - PCO, one basic automation system that is in control of all individual production means and that communicates with the central controlling system. This is part of the total concept of ISCP and translates the instructions of the coordinator towards individual tasks for the carriers. It is also responsible for a back-up image of the actual status of the installation and coordinates the security functions between the cariers. - Tier 3: system coordinator and traceability engine - GCO, a GensymG2 based application server that controls all interactions between the production means and serves as a decision engine for the operators. This G2-based environment controls, tracks and traces discrete production flows. It handles the functionalities from the planning of the renovations to the task management, including traceability of the production goods and user interface functions. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2298 _Managing Refinery Constraints within an Automated Production Environment_ Figure 2: Automation concept of ISCP All systems communicate through industrial Ethernet communications. It is calculated within the GCO according to: - Process constraints (e.g. age of electrodes obtained from the traceability database), - Availability constraints (generated and validated by the supervisor prior to calculation), - Fixed constraints (inherent to the work organization and the production layout). _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2300 _Managing Refinery Constraints within an Automated Production Environment_ The tasks for the carriers are the result of one of the three following supervisor’s decisions (also called ‘Order’): - Activation of the calculated production planning: the sequence of task will correspond to RT’s and RP’s (normal working modes) - Move a lot and/or a carrier under special circumstances (DRAG & DROPS, individual orders on cell level) - Activation of a complementary working mode dedicated to a specific situation (empty a cell) The scheduler generates, based on the activated production planning, the sequence of tasks corresponding to the selected electrode handling activities. This scheduling engine is the real hart of the system that will control and coordinate all tasks. It combines the following elements: - Production planning, - Production layout, - (Detailed) timing of each individual machine and carrier, - Actual situation of the shop floor, into a detailed schedule for each carrier. This schedule is stored in a timeslot-list and monitored in detail. Each individual deviation of this time-schedule can trigger the re-evaluation of the scheduling or, in case of major impact on the execution of the schedule, can require the interaction of an operator to re-evaluate the planning or to authorize a change of planning. ##### 5.3 Monitoring The task-engine follows up the execution of tasks from their creation to their completion. Therefore the GCO holds continuously an updated image of the production floor, the ‘floor image’, based on information received asynchronously from the PCO. The floor image within the GCO will be a visualization of the real floor due to up-to-date component state information. By keeping the floor image up to date, the GCO will be able to follow each lot of electrodes from the time of delivery in the ZT by the machine till the return of the lot to the stripping machine: some events change the attributes of the lots and will be stored by the GCO to a tracking database. The GCO establishes the link between a cathode lot and its original anode lot. This is what we call ‘traceability’. ##### 5.4 Simulation When the GCO is set into the simulation mode, the simulator calculates the movement of the individual equipmen

This real behaviour is modelled based on the mechanical parameters of the system received from the engineers but can also be updated based on historical data once the installation is running in a steady state mode. #### 6 Planner 

Based on a number of rules, determined together with the plant operations, the planner offers the user a pre-calculation of the production planning for a pre-defined period of time. After validation by the supervisor the planning can be transferred to the scheduler. 

The planner is an individual module, which permits to establish a prevision on the partial and total renovations to be executed. Apart from the specific production rules it will take into account: 

1. The age of the electrodes. 

This data is read from the traceability database. The refresh of the age of the sections is done every hour. It is always possible to enter manually, at the planner level, the age of the anodes and the age of the cathodes to overrule the information from the database. 

2. The actual availability of resources (teams, carriers, bays, sections). These data are to be introduced semi-automatically: starting from default values, a calendar assists the supervisor to modify the parameters on range of shifts. 

3. The localization of the simultaneous “total renovations” or “partial renovations”. 

4. Other fixed absolute rules like the number of “total renovations” and “partial renovations” in the same shift, rules to take other operators activities in the tank house into account, … 

5. Other parameters like calculation period, … 

The planning is calculated on demand. If asked (by the supervisor), the scheduler sends a reminder to the supervisor before the end of a pre-defined number of planned shifts. 

The planning is calculated for a certain time period. After acceptance of the calculated renovation program, this program will automatically be passed on to the scheduler. 

The planner module will run with estimated execution times based on the theoretical values available to the system, as parameters. To evaluate those execution times the system uses the same set of parameters and rules as are used by the simulator module. 

The planner module runs also in evaluation mode. In this case it returns an evaluation of the proposed planning but doesn't compute a new one. This evaluation mode is used to check e.g. if a modification to a previously calculated planning is useful or is possible (complying with the production rules). The output of an evaluation is either an estimation of the quality of the planning or a refusal of the planning (with reason of refusal). 

#### 7 Scheduler 

The scheduler is the tool that converts the orders calculat

ed by the planner or introduced by the supervisor (RT, RP, Drag & Drop, …) in individual tasks for each carrier.

Orders may come from different sources: 

- The result of the calculated planning (RT’s and RP’s). 

- The manually triggered renovations on a section. 

- Drag & Drop orders. 

Those orders are scheduled in a list for execution. At the start of the execution the scheduler calculates all the individual tasks resulting from this order. A task may be for one of the carriers, the PCO or the GCO internal. As long as an order is not finished, it stays in the scheduler list and can be manipulated through the scheduler interface. The following actions are possible: 

- Start an order. 

- Suspend a running order. 

- Cancel a suspended order. 

- Delete an order. 

The scheduler also represents the state of an order based on the feed-back it receives of the task engine or simulator module. 

#### 8 Task engine 

The task engine handles the task related actions: 

- Creation of the tasks. 

- Conversion of the task in a communication telegram. 

- Follow up of the execution of the telegram. 

A real-time action on shop floor level is performed using the multi-layer approach. GCO forms the top layer, and sends tasks to the PCO layer in advance. The PCO stores these tasks in a buffer, and executes them on the fly, the moment they are required. The PCO foresees one buffer position pro carrier (so one task executing and one task waiting). 

To be able to exchange data on a consistent and deterministic way, this task engine has a standard counterpart in each resource it controls. This makes the communication transparent for the system. This communication is based on a telegram structured communication with a fixed sequence of data exchanges so that on each level the status of the execution of a task is checked and guaranteed. This status is then fed back to the scheduler to evaluate the actual proceedings of the orders.

#### 10 Results 

By introducing the ISCP solution we reduce drastically the lost production time due to break downs by assisting the operator in making the right decisions to keep the production level on target. The ISCP concept was successfully implemented in the copper refinery environment of 2 large copper refineries and the following results were obtained: 

##### 10.1 Planner 

The advantages of the planning module were that, due to its high level of integration, it evaluates the planning and the status of the plant at each moment and gives direct feed-back to the supervisors if the overall system is not behaving according to an optimal sequence defined by the plant design. In case of differences between this optimal sequence and the actual situation of the shop floor the planner will define an optimal way to realign the operations with the optimal sequence of the plant. We experienced an efficient return to normal operations after particular events in the installations. 

##### 10.2 Scheduler 

The scheduler runs in real-time operation and interacts directly with the task-engine. Thus it could adapt the time schedule of each individual engine according to the actual situation on the shop floor. Hereby we observed he took into account instant changes as e.g. the break-down of a bay carrier, a slow down of a stripping machine, and created new instructions for the remaining available resources as to stick as much as possible with the defined planning. In this manner, the non production time of the installation was reduced to a minimum even in the case of individual issues with specific resources. 

##### 10.3 Simulator 

The integrated simulator procured us, once the system was designed and the floor plan data was introduced into the ISCP-system, with a view of the actual operations of the factory so that it could be tested and trained to the operators. As this simulation is integrated on the lowest level of the overall system, it provided a realistic feed-back with regard to the final behaviour of the system. Furthermore it permitted us to evaluate the plant specific modifications to the software and to tune the planner and scheduler before operations effectively started. In one case the simulator module was used in an early design phase of a plant to determine the feasibility of the layout as, due to the situation of the factory, it required a specific crossing of carriers to keep the building cos

t under control. It turned out that, due to this crossing, the stable performance of the would-be factory was too low and an efficient operation could not be guaranteed. Hereby a limited investment in simulation prevented our customer from a high investment in a non efficient factory and other opportunities were evaluated.

### Prediction of Slag Coating Thickness on Mitsubishi Converting Furnace Jackets 

B. Desai, T. Bhatt, S. Thakre, B. Basu R. S. Chugh, R. S. Mishra Aditya Birla Science & Technology Company Limited Hindalco Industries Limited Process Engineering and Sciences Birla Copper Taloja, India Dahej, India 

**Keywords:** Slag coating thickness, heat loss, solidus, heat transfer, thermal conductivity, refractory, jacket, freezing line 

#### Abstract 

The increasing need for higher and consistent copper production with low and varying concentrate grades within a single furnace depends on robust and well-controlled pyrometallurgical furnace operation, leading to high online times. The key features of such high rate furnaces include a strong, thermally robust wall cooling system and a stable slag coating. This prevents the corrosive liquid slag from directly coming into contact with and penetrating into the sidewall refractory and eroding it. The formation and control of the slag coating is dependent on the quantity and direction of heat flow through the coating, slag chemistry, melt temperature and refractory properties. Less slag coating may lead to reduced lining life or even break out, which results into loss of production. Excessive slag coating, on other hand, can lead to operating difficulties with magnetite and loss of smelting efficiency. It was therefore important to develop a computer based system to predict, monitor and control the optimum slag coating thickness and also to predict the erosion profile of the refractory. 

The focus of the present work is to develop a mathematical thermal equilibrium model that takes into account the slag chemistry, bath temperature, heat loss, refractory properties in achieving a stable slag coating thickness for Mitsubishi converting furnace jackets. The model predicts the equilibrium slag coating thickness as well as the depth of refractory erosion based on the on-line temperat

ure data and jacket cooling water flow rate. The paper discusses about the offline testing of model with an exhaustive plant data and the work being carried out for the online implementation of the model. The online implementation would work as a soft sensor for the continuous prediction of slag coating thickness and provide continuous guidance to the plant operation. This would enhance the decision making ability of the operators, resulting in reduced process variations and an improved operation.

#### 1 Introduction 

The advances in pyrometallurgical technology have led to the development of larger furnaces operating under more intense process conditions. One such furnace is the Mitsubishi furnace operating at Birla Copper with design capacity of 250,000 MT/anno. In order to maintain the reliability of these furnaces, the design of the refractory, cooling systems and air gap free bindings has become more critical. There is general consensus among smelter operators that furnace vessel integrity, from the viewpoint of refractory maintenance, is improved by strategic placement of cooling elements  [1-7]. Uceda et al. [8] claimed that a water-cooled element in the furnace lining was very effective in constraining the refractory erosion. Lee et al. [9] reported that chemical wear (corrosion) and mechanical wear (erosion/abrasion) take place when liquid slag comes in contact with the refractory. The cooling element (copper plate, panel or finger) freezes a solid layer of slag which prevents the corrosive liquid slag from directly coming into contact with the side wall refractory and eroding it. The formation and control of the slag coating is dependent on the quantity and direction of heat flow through the coating, slag chemistry, melt temperature and refractory properties. Less slag coating may lead to reduced lining life or even break out as shown in Figure 1. Such break-out could lead to considerably loss of production. Excessive slag coating, on other hand, can lead to operating difficulties with magnetite and loss of converting efficiency. Thus, it is imperative that the optimum thickness of the frozen layer of slag be always maintained between liquid slag and the refractory. Presently, there is no tool available in the plant to predict the slag coating thickness for Mitsubishi converting furnaces. The health of the jacket and refractory is judged by operators’ decision making ability from jacket cooling water outlet temperature, which often causes process variations and increases the risk of break-out. Hence, there is a need to design and develop a tool to know the solidified slag coating thickness from available operating parameters and thereby improve the operation.

A common and cost-effective way of knowing the solidified slag layer thickness in advance is by means of mathematical modelling [10-12]. While comprehensive mathematical models which include the heat and fluid flow phenomena of the furnace exist [13, 14], it was found that a thermal conduction model could be sufficient to capture the essence of the heat transfer at the furnace wall. Supplemented with plant data, the thermal model can provide reasonable prediction of the frozen interface location. Schmitz [15], for example, provided some guidelines for furnace design in the primary aluminum smelters, which avoids the more complex convective flow equation. The focus of the present work is to develop a mathematical thermal equilibrium model that takes into account the slag chemistry, bath temperature, heat loss and refractory properties in achieving a stable slag coating thickness for Mitsubishi converting furnace jackets. The model predicts the equilibrium slag coating thickness as well as the depth of refractory erosion based on the on-line temperature jacket cooling water flow rate data. The paper also discusses about the offline testing of model and the work being carried out for the online implementation of the model. 

#### 2 Mathematical formulation 

##### 2.1 Physical system: The converting furnace 

Mitsubishi continuous converting furnace has been installed at Birla Copper, Dahej for converting copper matte into blister and is a well proven process by commercial scale operations. The schematic view of converting furnace is shown in Figure 2a. In the converting furnace (C-furnace), matte is continuously converted to blister copper with oxygen enriched air via vertical lances to produce blister copper. Slag produced from this process is essentially calcium ferrite in nature. Slag mainly floats over the blister and thus two distinct layers are formed in converting furnace. The exothermic heat generated from converting reactions is removed with the help of water cooled copper jackets located only at the slag level. The configuration of slag, matte, blister with refractory and cooling arrangement is shown in Figure 2b. The water cooled jacket at slag level consists of a single row of rectangular copper block inserted 250 mm into the refractory, as shown in Figure 3a.

The blister heat is contained within the furnace by the placement of refractory having low thermal conductivity. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2311 _Desai, Bhatt, Thakre, Basu, Chugh, Mishra_ ##### 2.2 Model description A comprehensive mathematical model will need to account for the heat generated by reaction species and heat loss due to the furnace walls and reaction products. The mathematical formulation of such models must incorporate the following major physical phenomena: fluid flow, heat transfer, chemical kinetics, turbulence, Marangoni forces and phase change. The complexity of the model and the scarcity of thermo physical and transport data, however, raise questions on the predictive accuracy and implementation of a comprehensive model. In fact, this is the modus operandi for most simulations of the type of metallurgical reactors where the key trends are important for delineating the furnace process window [2, 7]. The tri-diagonal matrix algorithm [19], also known as Thomas algorithm, was used to solve the set of discretized linear equations. It is computationally inexpensive and has the advantage that it requires a minimum amount of storage. Cartesian coordinates are used with uniform 520 by 130 cells at 10 mm cell size. Convergence is satisfied by the following criteria: (a) the sum of the residuals should continue to decrease with respect to the first iteration. (b) The input heat flux is equal to the exit heat flux – imbalance < 0.1 % (c) The spot temperature values at several critical locations are monitored to ensure that they have remained unchanged i.e. the percentage change in their value from the previous iteration is less than 0.001 %. Finally, the numerical code predictions were compared to the solution using MatlabTM PDE solver [20] to ensure accuracy, precision and compliance. ##### 2.4 Thermodynamic modeling A thermodynamic model was developed to determine the solidus for the convertier multicomponent slag system. A thermodynamic model consists of a set of model equations for the Gibbs energies of all phases in multi-component system as a function of temperature, composition and pressure. From these equations, all the thermodynamic properties and phase diagrams of simple _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2313 _Desai, Bhatt, Thakre, Basu, Chugh, Mishra_ systems can be reproduced and those of multi-component systems can be predicted. Technically, this is realized by storing the model parameters in solution databases, which are then used along with pure component databases by general Gibbs free energy minimization software that incorporates the model equations to calculate multi-component and multi-phase heterogeneous equilibria. Figure 3a wherein a water cooled pipe is extruded through copper block. Higher thermal conductivity of copper block ensures the efficient heat removal of heat at the slag level. Consequently, the temperature of slag in the vicinity of the jacket (copper block) tends to decrease. The slag becomes solidified (frozen) when the slag temperature attains its solidus. This can be clearly seen from Figure 4 wherein the liquidus and solidus lines are drawn schematically to show the precipitation of slag on cooling. Once the slag solidus is known, it is then used to determine the slag coating thickness. The slag coating thickness is measured as a distance from the refractory to the solidus. Figure5a shows the shaded area between the refractory outerface and the solidus (~1075 °C) as the solidified layer of slag. It is also observed that the solidified slag layer gradually shrinks towards blister side. Therefore, slag coating thickness at the gas-slag interface has been referred as the maximum slag coating thickness (SCTmax) and at the slag blister interface as the minimum slag coating thickness (SCTmin) in this paper. It should be ensured that SCTmin is positive in order to avoid the liquid slag coming in contact with the refractory. The process conditions such as slag chemistry, bath temperature and heat loss must be brought into the safe operating conditions which ensure SCTmin is positive. The negative value of SCTmin indicates that the slag solidus is inside the refractory and refractory tantamount to the depth of slag solidus has been eroded, as shown in Figure 5b. ### An Update on Praxair Coherent Jet Technology in Anode Refining at Kennecott Utah Copper 

Arsenio (Jun) Enriquez, Colin Nexhip, Gerald Poplar Adrian Deneys Rio Tinto - Kennecott Utah Copper LLC Praxair, Inc. 12000 West 2100 South 2430 Camino Ramon Magna, UT, USA San Ramon, CA, USA 

**Keywords:** CoJet process, scrap melting optimization, anode refining, hearth accretion 

#### Abstract 

Rio Tinto through its subsidiary Kennecott Utah Copper (KUC) installed Praxair’s Coherent Jet (CoJet<sup>®</sup> ) system in 2007 to increase scrap melting capability in the West anode refining furnace. During 2009 two new CoJet lances were installed and the system was adopted on both the West and East anode furnaces. This paper discusses the use of the CoJet process to remove a hearth accretion in the anode furnaces. Additional system improvements to the CoJet installation are underway at KUC. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Rio Tinto through its subsidiary Kennecott Utah Copper (KUC) implemented

Praxair’s Coherent Jet (CoJet<sup>®</sup> ) technology on the West anode furnace in late 2007 [1]. The system was designed to independently provide thermal energy to the process and to enable development of top-blown oxidation and reduction gas jets for fire refining. The KUC CoJet system concept, lance equipment, and gas control system have been described in detail elsewhere [1]. 

The general CoJet process provides both chemical energy and gas injection capabilities for metallurgical processes. The CoJet system fundamentals and concepts have been previously described elsewhere [2, 3]. Briefly, the coherent jet process creates a flame shroud around a high velocity gas jet. The flame shroud reduces ambient gas entrainment into the high velocity jet thereby maintaining the jet’s velocity profile over longer distances, compared to an un-shrouded gas jet. 

During commissioning in late 2007 and 2008, efforts at KUC Smelter focused on increased scrap melting rates in the West Anode Furnace, to melt large pieces of internally generated copper scrap. Scrap melting rates of about 9 mt/h (10 st/h) were demonstrated [1] in the West anode furnace, with up to 203 mt (224 st) scrap melted during one melting period. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

2327 

_Enriquez, Nexhip, Poplar, Deneys_ 



The CoJet system also demonstrated an ability to rapidly heat the molten copper bath. This feature enables the operators to recover bath temperature quickly in the event of a cold blister tap or adverse condition with the end-wall burner. Cold blister occurs infrequently. However if blister is tapped below 1193 °C (2180 °F) the operator needs to run the end-wall burner at a higher firing rate to increase bath temperature. The end-wall burner is a low-NOx Praxair-patented J-L burner that typically fires at 158 to 342 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h natural gas with oxygen (6 to 13 MMBtu/h). In the KUC anode furnaces the burner heats liquid copper at around 6 °C (10 °F) per hour. However the temperature increase depends on factors like slag layer thickness, end-wall burner tip condition, and also impacts on freeboard refractory. By comparison, the CoJet system at 237 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h natural gas firing rate on each of two CoJet lances, (9 MMBtu/h per lance), heats the molten copper at 17 to 33 °C per hour (30 to 60 °F per hour). 

Several significant issues were identified during the initial installation regarding practices for copper scrap melting. These included: (a) opening the CoJet lance port (often required jack-hammering and mag-lancing); (b) connecting the hoses to the CoJet lance (requiring elevated work practices and controls); (c) plugging the CoJet lance port for subsequent re-use (temporary fiber-blanket plugs tended to leak molten copper, while refractory plugs required jack-hammering to remove); (d) mounting locations for the devices (required two persons to install and remove). 

Several additional process issues were also identified: (i) high NOx emission during scra

p charging (a solution was developed); (ii) low sulfur removal efficiency during low-concentration-sulfur removal during refining (under development); (iii) port plugging on the CoJet lance tips (required daily lance cleaning and therefore a lance removal and cleaning procedure compatible with the overall refining process). 

In late 2008, during a furnace rotation after CoJet system scrap melting, a plugged CoJet lance port leaked copper as a result of refractory thinning around the south CoJet lance port. Development work was suspended pending refractory work to enable a sound mechanical seal. 

In an effort to overcome some of the aforementioned problems, early 2009 engineering work was completed on two other mounting options for the CoJet process. An end-wall mount was designed as one option. A mounting window in the tuyere area was designed as a second option. The mounting concepts were adopted from existing refractory designs and practices, to enable mid-campaign hot-repairs as required, with minimal anode furnace downtime.

The problem was identified as a large hearth accretion (build-up) increasing in size in both the East and West anode furnaces. The build up increased to where measurements indicated it was up to 1.2 m thick in places. The East Furnace Capacity/Output is shown in Figure 1 for the period from September 2008 to May 2009.

In basic oxygen steelmaking furnaces hearth accretions (bottom build-up) are removed by charging ferrosilicon and burning the ferrosilicon with oxygen supplied through the main oxygen lance and this option was considered [5]. Up to one foot of hearth accretion can be removed during a blow [5]. KUC experimented with ferrosilicon and thermite (30 % aluminum + 70 % soda ash) addition. However the anode furnace geometry is not symmetrical with respect to the oxygen source. Concerns over temperature control and the potential for refractory damage by excess localized heat generation was a concern in using this particular approach. Another solution considered was the addition of significant oxy-fuel burner energy in the vicinity of the build-up to partially melt and loosen the accretion. Owing to concerns regarding burner and refractory integrity, and potential emissions, Praxair proposed a new CoJet lance capable of delivering up to 474 Nm3 /h natural gas (18 MMBtu/h) through a single device. #### 2 Results 

A few days after startup of the CoJet system a large quantity of molten accretion was tapped from the furnaces. Figure 7 shows an example of accretion material tapped after several hours of CoJet system operation during September 2009. The results are quantified in the East and West anode furnaces capacity plots shown in Figures 8 and 9. 

The rate of increase of the accretion is shown in Figures 8 and 9 by the slope of the negative portion of the curve. The apparent rate of growth is about 45 tonnes per month (50 tonnes per month). After the CoJet system was adopted for accretion removal, the rate of removal was about 90 tonnes per month (100 tonnes per month). The reason for the apparent rate of removal was the incremental firing rate approach taken for accretion removal. 

Initially the objective was to arrest accretion formation and prevent it from growing any larger. Furthermore, limited time was available for accretion melting owing to the affect that the accretion had on increasing the frequency of refining required to maintain copper production. After initial CoJet system use, as some of each accretion was removed, the dynamics within the Smelter created more time available for further accretion melting.

Hearth accretions in non-ferrous reactors have been documented in early Peirce-Smith converter operation [6] (termed high-bottom). Recent accretion examples in non-ferrous smelting are those found in flash furnaces. These include both hearth and wall (or duct) accretions [7, 8] as well as a waste heat boiler throat accretion [9] and hearth and uptake shaft accretions in the Inco and Outotec flash furnace [10-12]. Some accretions are needed for successful pyrometallurgical operations, for example Sirosmelt topsubmerged-lance accretions [8], freeze linings in some electric furnace processes, and slag splashing for refractory protection in top-blown oxygen steelmaking converters (greatly extends furnace life). Hearth accretions of the type in this paper could be classified as falling into one class of furnace accretions. Other examples include blast furnace hearth accretions (salamanders), chromite-spinel build up in platinum smelting electric furnaces (particularly problematic with high chromite c

oncentrates), and hearth accretions in Outotec flash smelters [7, 8]. The mechanism of hearth accretion formation is thought to be a complex phenomenon that includes factors like slag chemistry, oxygen potential, as well as heat and mass transfer mechanisms. The anode furnace accretion formation mechanism is outside the scope of this paper. However the accretion is partly related to extended campaign life and operational practices that includes slag skimming frequency, porous plug performance and occasional upstream upset conditions. 

An unusual accretion type recently identified is oxygen lance accretions. Oxygen lance accretions occur in the basic oxygen steel making process (tip skulls) and are managed by periodic lance cleaning. Oxygen lance accretions (horns) were problematic for the Inco MK Reactor (reduced oxygen efficiency and increased the maintenance requirement and downtime for lance cleaning) and were solved using Praxair’s coherent jet technology [13]. Since 2003 Praxair has conducted laboratory research (melting tests of furnace accretion samples) from copper converters, copper, and nickelcopper flash furnaces, and oxygen lances.

### Breaking through Existing Limits – Using a Realtime Material Flow Management Solution for the Optimisation of Copper Production 

Stephan Gernerth-Mautner Markhof 

Aurubis AG HovestraЯe 50 20539 Hamburg, Germany

4Production AG Carlo-Schmid-StraЯe 12 52446 Wьrselen, Germany 

**Keywords:** Production management system, material flow management, real time transparency 

#### Abstract 

At Aurubis AG, the copper production consists of many different production steps and processes using a variety of feedstock (primary and secondary). During these processes many intermediates as well as final products are manufactured. 

In order to optimise the utilisation ratio of the different production facilities as well as the yield of the desired metals it is essential that the correct knowledge about the current material flow and the current stock contents is available for the production planners and engineers at any time. The real time transparency of the material flow provides the basis to make the right decisions for optimal production ways and optimal charge mixes at the

right time. Furthermore, this is the initial point to tap previously unattainable potentials. 

A Production Management System (PMS) is the foundation for this real time approach. This article describes the worldwide first implementation of a real time material flow management solution for an all-over production network in copper industry. It gives an overview of the implementation steps from engineering to start of operation and the current use of the PMS in the daily production. The outlook shows how the achieved transparency can be used for further optimisation in order to allow a cost effective production of copper.

##### 2.1 Initial situation 

At its Hamburg site, the company had a wide variety of information sources. The production knowhow had developed over many years and in a haphazard manner. Information islands had grown up in the form of a large body of documents held in different formats and in different media. Among other things, there were more than 1000 different Excel spreadsheets containing all manner of formulae and data and used as the basis for reports, with these in turn serving as the basis for the medium- and short-term production decisions. Day-to-day production, likewise, was based on the knowledge from these documents, combined with empirical experience. Alongside the furnace logbook and various batch reports, both batch specifications and feedback reports were produced in some cases electronically, but in many cases also manually on ordinary slips of paper and with the aid of tally lists. Data transfer was then done exclusively by hand. 

The time-lagged specifications and subsequent feedback reports were also handled differently from plant to plant. Keeping track of the complex material flows, in particular for the mutually interdependent production equipment units, was therefore a major challenge, and indeed sometimes a completely impossible task. In the latter cases, the people in charge had no alternative but to base their decisions on assumptions, i.e. to adopt a heuristic approach. As well as the key product information, analysis results, too, could only be provided even in the fastest case by fax; this was a highly impractical state of affairs both from the point of view of decision-making and in terms of evaluation needs.

fluence each other. Thus, the goals of stock minimisation and maximum plant capacity utilisation run counter to one another, in two different ways. 

On the one side, high security stocks are desirable in order to ensure full utilisation of production capacities; on the other side, however, use of the available plant capacity can lead to sub-optimal processing. This therefore puts the goals of lower energy consumption, higher quality and lower rates of waste at risk. To surmount this obstacle, the tendency is to wait for optimum production conditions. This, in turn, results in a further increase in stocks. 

###### 3.1.2 Obstacles in terms of organisation 

In addition to the obstacles in terms of content, there are also a number of organisational obstacles that have to be overcome. The most important are the contrary interests of the plants in terms of

material supply and utilisation of external capacities (such as logistics). Both have to be reconciled at any one site with the inter-plant interests to achieve a reasonable equilibrium. The same effect also applies to the relationship between the individual sites and the group as a whole. MES creates transparency in this regard. First of all, the conflicts are rendered visible. This is the precondition for being able to resolve these conflicts on an inter-site basis through transparent arrangements. 

A second obstacle is change management with regard to the feedbacks. The need for prompt feedbacks leads to changes in work methods. The procedures and processes at the production equipments and in logistics have to be rescheduled, if necessary, and implemented in the plants. MES requires a certain degree of timing, without which unnecessary loss of resources can occur. 

##### 3.2 Clearly defined roles and responsibilities 

In view of the wide variety of tasks to be performed by MES, clear definition of roles and responsibilities is essential. MES provides the right platform for this. Thus, more than 275 users are currently registered in MES; these belong to approx. 30 groups whose spheres of responsibility are precisely defined extracts from around 300 available functions. 

These functions and the subordinate, more precisely defined individual authorisations (approx. 1000) decide who is allowed to see which dialogues and in what form and detail, and which functions he/she is thereby allowed to perform. In combination with the detailed execution status and the master status of the individual, batch and production orders, the authorisation concept represents a powerful workflow system within the overall process chain. 

Important user groups include, for instance: operating production planner, production equipment controller, transport planner, transport controller, material preparer, material input controller, batch feedback reporter, analysis officer and verifier.

With the aid of several fine-tuneable mechanisms, MES steers the entire process, from order placement to planning, execution, confirmation and verification. Orders can be placed by various bodies (plants, sampling, logistics), whereby each order is provided with a desired performance date. The material as well as the source and destination can be defined very precisely or indicated only roughly. The material can be defined by the product group, material type and collection heap. The source and destination can be defined by storage areas, railway stations or concrete storage positions. Using a knowledge chart, MES generates any required approval requests for the possible consignors and consignees. ### Analysis and Improvements of a Radiant Cooling Chamber in a Copper Smelter 

M.A.Sc. L. H. Gunnewiek Hatch Limited 2800 Speakman Drive Mississauga, Ontario, L5K 2R7, Canada 

Bsc. Maximo Leon Ganem, Bsc. G. Zamorano Hatch Ingenieros y Consultores El Bosque Norte 500, 12<sup>th</sup> floor Las Condes, Santiago, Chile 

**Keywords:** Radiant cooling chamber (RCC), CFD design, 3D model, off-gas 

#### Abstract 

Radiant cooling chambers (RCC) are commonly used in Chilean copper smelters for off-gas cooling from process reactors such as Teniente and Peirce-Smith converters. The use of the RCC has been practiced in Chilean smelters since 1987 as they are effective and economically attractive. The RCC encompasses a pre-chamber to decelerate the gas flow and allow dust to settle, followed by a series of vertical ducts through which the gas flows for cooling, prior to further treatment in an acid plant, for example. Radiation heat transfer from the ducts to the ambient surrounds provides the mechanism for cooling the gas. The main focus in the design and operation of the RCC is the optimization of the cooling areas. 

C

urrent practice for sizing and design of the RCC is based on correlations, simple heat transfer calculations, and the operational experience of other plants. With the objective of improving and optimizing the RCC, advanced analysis tools like computational fluid dynamics (CFD) have been used. Presented in this paper is a performance comparison of a standard design. Flow variables, such as velocity and temperature distributions are provided to illustrate how this equipment works.  In particular, the radiation cooling is a function of the size of the ducts, the flow distribution inside the receiving chamber, and the distribution of cooling panels inside the receiving chamber of the RCC. The results presented in this paper provide insights into how the currently used standard design can be improved with only small perturbations in the original geometry. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The Radiant Cooling Chamber (RCC) is based on the principle of radiation as the main heat transfer mechanisms to lower the temperature of the off-gas generated during the process of copper concentrate smelting, for example. This type of equipment is widely used in the Chilean copper industry, 

2357 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Gunnewiek, Leon, Zamorano_ 



and it has been implemented for over two decades, and thus it has become a design standard for several copper smelter plants. 

Although there is other equipment that serves the same function of the RCC, such as evaporative spray water cooling, the use of the RCC is popular among Chilean copper smelters because it does not use water. Most copper plants in Chile are located in dry areas in the northern regions of the country where the water is a very expensive resource. 

A RCC consists of a receiving chamber or, as called here, the pre-chamber, that contains a cooled baffle intended to drop out coarse particles from the flow, followed by chambers with vertical tubes where the flow is continuously cooled. On the upstream side, the RCC is connected to a cooled hood the collects the off-gas from the process reactor. On the downstream side the RCC is connected to gas cleaning and treatment equipment. 

A brief description of the process is as follows. The inlet off-gas flow coming from a reactor has a range of temperature between 1400 to 1500 °C. It enters the cooled collection hood together with dilution air, and the mixed gas is received at the inlet of the RCC with an average temperature range between 600 to 700 °C. Upon entering the pre-chamber of the RCC the flow is directed into a cooled baffle, deflecting out the large solid particles and slowing down the overall flow velocity. Following this, the gas is directed to the first chamber where it flows into the radiant ducts, decreasing its temperature. Upon exiting the RCC, the off-gas is typically sent through an electrostatic precipitator (ESP) where the gas flow is cleaned before sending to the acid plants. The driving suction is generated by induced draft fans loc

ated after the electrostatic precipitators. At the inlet of the ESP the gas temperature ranges between 350 and 450 °C. It is important to note that this temperature cannot be outside this range, because higher temperatures will damage the ESP, and lower temperatures could produce the formation of SO3. 

The RCC design is primarily defined by the gas flow to be cooled and the desired exit temperature. The detailed design, however, is not exempt from several problems, in terms of getting a suitable efficiency of the equipment. A common additional problem in RCC is to get a suitable dust handling for avoiding build-up mainly in the pre-chamber. The design of RCC is commonly a result of the use of simple correlations, and rules of thumb based on experience. 

The analysis and design methodology described in this paper can be useful to achieve an efficient RCC design by helping to understand the flow distribution inside the chambers. The ineffective design of the radiant duct often results in modifications being made on site after the construction in order to provide more cooling, and to avoid severe damage in hood and pre-chamber panels due to high temperature, high accretion rates, among many other typical difficulties. 

This work has the main objective of showing how the use of CFD modelling allows for the analyzes of a typical RCC design, providing a detailed description of the heat transfer mechanisms, and locating possible critical points that, for example, could present severe damage to the equipment.

Off-gas entering the hood mixes with infiltration air coming from the surrounding environment, creating a hot gas plume that extends throughout the hood’s length. The plume is generated by how the off-gas coming from the converter enters the off-gas hood. As soon as the off-gas enters the hood, it is deflected to the right panel of the hood and then forms a recirculation zone inside the hood, as shown by Figure 3-left. The recirculation zones created by the deflected flow are present across both the pre-chamber and the first cooling chamber, as seen in Figure 3-left. The important feature of this flow inside the first chamber is that it is present in throughout its volume. It can be seen at the intake of the first row of radiant ducts. ##### 3.3 Temperature distribution 

Figure 7 shows temperature contours of the flow inside the RCC. As mentioned before, the plumelike flow entering the hood is deflected to the right wall, as shown in Figure 5 on the left side. The plume is characterized by three zones, which can be appreciated in Figure 5 on the right side. The _core_ is the zone where temperatures are the highest, ranging between 1000 and 1200 °C. A thin intermediate zone formed where temperatures are in the range of 750 to 860 °C, and a third zone where temperatures are in the range between 460 and 750 °C. 

It is important to notice that as soon as the plume is formed, temperature begins to drop by the effect of the infiltration air. When the flow is in the pre-chamber, temperatures are in the range of 560 to 600 °C. Inside the first cooling chamber, the temperature drops to 500 to 600 °C. 

The flow past the baffle impinges into the upper wall of the first cooling chamber, where the first row of radiant ducts is located. This zone has temperatures of 580 to 600 °C and is present in the first 5 radiant ducts. Again, it can be inferred that heat transfer is not uniform because the first 5 ducts will transfer heat at a higher rate than the remaining ones because of the higher flow rates. 

The temperature drop between the successive cooling chambers is approximately 150 °C, where the radiant ducts are responsible of the temperature drop in the off-gas, as shown in Figure 5. Th

us, it is clearly illustrated that the role of the radiant ducts is crucial in the heat transfer provided by the RCC. A design where the heat transfer is uniform in the radiant tubes would lead to more efficient cooling performance. A direct impact in the design of the RCC can be achieved by choosing smaller radiant ducts that will encourage more uniform flow, and therefore higher and more uniform heat transfer rates.

In the second row of radiant ducts, the average Nusselt number is relatively uniform, with the exception of the third and fourth duct. This is explained by the flow profile at the outlet of the first row of radiant ducts. Since the mean flow velocity at the intake of the third duct in the second row is the highest, the Nusselt number is also the highest. Again, the presence of recirculation zones at the intake to the radiant ducts results in lower heat transfer rates. Therefore, the design of the RCC can be improved by changing the geometry of the baffle and the size of the radiant ducts to improve flow uniformity. The improved cooling capacity of an RCC with uniform flow conditions would provide the opportunity to reduce the cooling surface area of the radiant tubes, e.g., reduce their height. The simplest solution from a construction point of view is the change of the baffle geometry, while in terms of costs, the reduction of the radiant ducts height would lead to a reduction of the construction cost of the RCC. 2367 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Gunnewiek, Leon, Zamorano_ #### 4 Conclusions The off-gas cooling performance of a typical RCC has been evaluated using CFD techniques. In general, the overall objective of the equipment is fulfilled, since it provides enough cooling for the high temperature off-gas generated by a Teniente Converter. However, the analysis has shown several aspects of the design of the RCC that reduce the efficiency of cooling. Such aspects can be improved in order to obtain a better efficient cooling equipment. The flow inside the RCC results in high temperatures in the hood and pre-chamber. Inside the first cooling chamber, flow has two marked recirculation zones that are created due to the effect of the baffle located inside the pre-chamber. The effect of flow distribution leads to inefficiencies in the heat transfer rates of the radiant ducts, particularly in the first row. This is because of the presence of large recirculation zones with length scales between 20 and 25 % of the duct height. In spite of this general attribute of the flows, an exception has been observed where the flow at the intake of the radiant tubes has little or no recirculation, and the effect is, as expected, a more uniform cooling performance, and thus it is said that the radiant duct is used in an efficient manner. Thus, improvements in the RCC rely in the ability to obtain uniform heat transfer for the radiant ducts. The way to achieve this is to eliminate the recirculation zones inside the first cooling chamber. The simplest change in the geometry that could lead to a uniform

flow with small velocities is the redesign of the baffle inside the pre-chamber. 

An important problem in the existing RCC is the presence of cooled gas where the recirculation zones are present. This condition results in that a dewpoint temperature is reached and SO3 formation is possible. Avoiding recirculation ensures that this condition is eliminated. In addition, if there is no recirculation, the chance for the build-up solids inside the RCC should be minimized.

#### Abstract 

The overall methodology involved mineralogical analysis of more than sixty concentrate samples, creating a mineralogy database for different mines, development of model to predict mineralogy from elemental analysis, thermodynamic analysis for phase analysis and development of the process model in Metsim. An elaborate material and energy balance, smelting reactions and their conversion rates and modelling of the plant dynamics, formed the basis for the development of process advisor. 

The mineralogy and process models were validated with the experimental and plant data respectively. A good validation of the process model with an exhaustive plant data shows the capability of the model to predict the effect of concentrate feed and operating conditions on the product compositions. The model is regularly used as a guiding tool for the evaluation of blends, prior to its processing in plant. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The flash smelting process developed by Outokompu is widely being used in copper smelters around the world. The process has been studied by many researchers both on laboratory and industrial scale. In spite of the increasing industrial stature of the process, the design of a flash smelting furnace largely remains an art. This is mainly due to the difficulty in understanding the complex physics of the individual sub processes taking place in the flash smelting furnace. Further the operation also operates at a very high temperature and under turbulent conditions posing a major challenge for the precise measurements of the product compositions and temperatures. 

The present process advisor at Birla Copper predicts the process conditions for a given set of input parameters. It considers only the elemental composition of the feed and neglects the effect of the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

2381 

_Joshi, Thakre, Basu, Shah, Chauhan, Chugh, Khandelwal_ 



mineral species present in the feed. This would probably mean that the advisor might have been developed for a fixed mineralogy, especially for high chalcopyrite mineralogy. The applicability of such a process advisor is challenging, since Birla Copper being a custom smelter, often has to process ores from various mines. The changing mineralogy within and from ore to ore pose a major challenge for blending and setting up of process parameters.

The continuous tuning of the process is needed by the plant operation to manage temperatures and product compositions. Various studies have been done on the mass and energy balances of FSF. Kosikinen has developed mass and energy balance model based on superposition principle assuming matte grade as an input parameter to predict the process conditions for the characteristic parameters of the feed materials [1]. The previous studies on development of mass and energy balance model (Goto’s model) have regarded the concentrate mineral components but neglected the combustion heat [2]. From the energy balance point of view, the challenge in Flash Furnace operation is to balance the heat production and heat losses such that the temperatures are within specs in the reaction shaft. The most stringent contribution to the heat production is the Cu, Fe & S contents of the feed. The increasing S content and decreasing Cu content of the feed pose a limit on the smelting capacity of the FSF. Constant control is required on the exothermicity of the concentrate mixture feed, based on the mineralogy of the feed and also its S/Cu ratio. Detailed study on raw material quality, process conditions and data analysis was carried out to understand the FSF operation i.e. predicting the process conditions and at the same time managing productivity. The above study and analysis formed the basis of the development of a process advisor incorporating the varying concentrate mineralogy. The overall goal was to develop a tool that predicts the furnace behaviour for all major variations in the input parameters and to operate the furnace in an optimal way. The various aspects for developing a new process advisor included development of process model for the material and energy balance, reaction mechanism and reaction heats, predicting the mineral components of the feed for different ores, studying the effect of varying input conditions on the product compositions. The modelling framework involved, (i) development of model to predict mineralogy from elements, and (ii) using this mineralogy as an input to the process model developed in METSIM. The development of FSF process advisor in the present work is limited to Reaction Shaft-Settler-Uptake Shaft only; its further extension to WHB and downstream process is future development and out of present scope. #### 2 Development of process advisor for FSF 2.1 Process description The reaction shaft, the settler and the uptake shaft together constitute for the Flash Smelting Furnace (FSF). Copper concentrate, silica flux and fuel are fed from the burners at the top of the shaft with enriched air containing oxygen in varying concentrations from 60 to 80 %. The copper concentrate particles are oxidized and melted by the heat of oxidation during the descent in the shaft. The phenomena of Reaction Shaft essentially consists of dispersing and oxidizing a dry concentrate in oxygen enriched air stream. Both flows enter the concentrate burner which disperses the gas-solid mixture [3-4]. As the gas-solid suspension leaves the burner and flows downwards through the reaction shaft, the solid particles are heated by convection and radiation reaching a temperature at which the oxidation reaction of the particles generates more heat than can be dissipated. This temperature is called the ignition temperature and varies between 400 to 550<sup>o</sup> C for copper concentrates. Once the ignition is reached, the temperature of the reacting particles can rise up to nearly 2000<sup>o</sup> C [5-6]. The reacted melt product flowing downwards is led to the settler zone. In the settler, the molten material separates into matte, slag and off-gas. Matte and slag are intermittently tapped from the respective tap holes. The slag is led to the Slag Cleaning Furnace (SCF) and the matte to the Pierce Smith Converters (PSC). The furnace off gas passes through the uptake shaft where the sulphidic dust is oxidised. This is followed by Waste Heat Boiler (WHB), where the gas is cooled and oxidised dust gets sulphatized before passing to the Electrostatic Precipitator (ESP). The majority of the dust is removed in WHB & ESP before the gas is led to the sulphuric acid plant.

##### 2.4 Development of the METSIM model 

The development of a process model was done in METSIM. Metsim is a dedicated flowsheet package for metal industry. It allows for pre-programmed unit operations to be linked together to form a flowsheet with the support of an extensive metal compounds database. Since most of the available unit operation modules are customized for the copper specific metallurgical operation, the flowsheet can be built be relative ease. Metsim uses the Sequential Modular Simulation approach for solving the set of equations. One of the greatest benefits of Sequential Modular Simulation is that the process is straightforward, it is easy to visualize and can be easily linked with common tools such an Excel spreadsheet, etc. The Metsim model was developed for Reaction shaft-Settler and Uptake shaft.

A detailed thermodynamic analysis of FSF process w.r.t. input parameters and oxygen potential was carried out to understand the formation of various phases. A thermodynamic software FACTSAGE was used for this purpose. Based on the plant process manuals, process & lab data, thermodynamic analysis and literature [12, 14], following reaction mechanism was modelled in METSIM.

The settler has been modelled as a unit operation for separating slag-matte off-gas, under the assumption of thermodynamic equilibrium and the completion of majority of the reactions in the reaction shaft as explained above.
