ween the phases is an important consideration for the temperature distribution and is governed by the heat transfer coefficients. The heat transfer coefficients built in METSIM, obtained from their experience from several FSF smelter, was used. The dust is modelled on the basis of carryover of molten droplets of the reaction shaft products and the entrainment of mainly the slag and the matte phase. The dust and the off gas further pass through the Uptake Shaft which has also been modelled in METSIM. Besides furnace chemistry and settler equilibrium, areas of importance for the FSF modeling are the feed mineralogy, water flow rate, fuel requirement and the requirement of enriched air and sulfatization air flow rate.

#### Abstract 

This paper considers the optimization of a plant with a numerical flow simulation, using a copperrefining furnace as an example. The goal of this optimization is to improve the conversion rate of the reducing agent. To achieve this, the way the reducing agent is added and the mixing of the melt must be improved. Both measures will lead to a reduction in reducing agent use. 

A smaller input of reducing agent also lowers the combustible content in the off-gas behind the refining furnaces. In turn this means a smaller afterburning system. 

The improved input/mixing causes the temperature of the melt to be more uniform which leads to less caking in the furnace itself and therefore less wear of the fireproof material. 

The starting point for the optimization is a copper refining furnace with an injecting nozzle for heavy oil. The existing furnace geometry and the present operating mode make up the actual condition. This actual condition is investigated in the first stage using the numerical flow simulation. This actual flow analysis is followed by flow optimization. The major parameters involved are the number of nozzles, the injection speed of the reducing agent into the melt, the number of nitrogen purging plugs, and the nitrogen purging quantity. In addition, the significance of the refining medium on the reduction process will be considered. 

It will be shown that optimization of the process parameters improves mixing, and the retention time of the reducing agent can be increased significantly, causing an increase in the reducing agent conversion rate.

The process begins with delivery of copper concentrate containing 30 wt. % Cu. The concentrates and the silica, used to form slag, are transported to the loading preparation centre. From there they undergo a drying process where the water content is reduced. The dried copper concentrate is loaded into a furnace together with silica and oxygen-enriched-air. Here sulphur and iron in the ore mix are reacting to generate heat that smelts the material. The products of this fusion are a metallic product called matte with 60 wt. % Cu, a slag and gas emissions. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2400 _CFD-Simulation as a Tool for System Optimization_ The gas released by the furnace and the converters is treated in a sulphuric acid plant. The smelting process includes two processes for cleaning the slag produced in the furnace and the converters. In the slag cleaning furnace the matte, contained in the slag, is recovered and then returned to the conversion process. The cleaned slag is deposited in the slag heap. After cooling, the slag is transported to a flotation plant, where the copper is recovered as concentrate and the tailings left over are deposited in a tailing dam. During conversion, air/oxygen is blown in the molten metal and thereby the copper content in the matte is separated from the sulphur and the iron. The iron oxide combines with the silica, producing slag. The metal phase is called now blister with 99 wt. % copper content. The blister copper is removed from the converter and undergoes an oxidation and reduction process in a so called anode furn

ace to remove the remaining traces of sulphur and excess oxygen. In the period of reduction a relatively high quantity of carbon emissions are polluted. The high carbon emissions are mainly caused by low refining media efficiency and ineffective afterburning of the furnace off-gas. After the anode furnace process and settlement of target quality the copper is then poured into moulds, producing anodes with 99.6 wt. % copper content.

##### 3.2 The anode furnace 

The anode furnace is one of the last steps in the process chain for gaining and producing pure, metallic copper. In the anode furnace oxidation and reduction reactions increase the purity, and therefore the quality, of the copper melt, thereby refining the copper. 

To do this the melt must have been as evenly mixed as possible so the reactants meet. 

The refining system consists of a number of oxidation and reduction nozzles each with a control system for compressed air, and oil or gas. 

The gas porous plugs are porous stones through which inert gases enter the melt. Normally they are distributed evenly across the floor of the furnace and use the mammoth pump effect to mix the melt. 

In the neutral position of the furnace the refining nozzles have been screwed out of the bath and positioned opposite the taphole, to the side of and below the slag door. 

The refinement is divided into four process steps: 

###### Level 1: Charging or maintaining temperature 

In the charging or heat-maintenance phase the furnace is in the neutral position so that the nozzles are above the surface of the molten material. If required, the supporting or holding burner is used during this phase. To minimize wear of the nozzles, cold air is blown through them during these phases. 

###### Level 2: Oxidation 

In the second refinement phase air, that is oxygen, is injected through nozzles, which have now been lowered below the surface, into the melt so that its impurities are oxidized and dispatched to the slag or off-gas. This slag is scummed to avoid a reverse reaction in the bath. The intensity of the oxidation and its duration depend on the quality of the blister copper coming from the converters in the anode furnace. Pre-oxidation is already carried out during the charging phase. 

While the slag is scummed, the refining nozzles can be above or in the melt to support movement in the bath. 

###### Level 3: Reduction 

In the reduction phase the released oxygen and resulting copper oxide are again reduced in the bath due to the injection of the reducing medium, e.g. diesel fuel or natural gas. The reducing medium is injected through the same nozzles. The oil/gas is atomized using compressed air to distribute the oil/gas better and to create larger reaction surfaces.

#### 4 System optimization 

##### 4.1 Opportunities for variation 

In order to reach the stated goals-improvement of the conversion rate of the reducing agent by inputting and mixing the reducing agent better and improved mixing of the melt – the flow conditions and the reaction and material transport equations are worked out using a numerical flow simulation. 

The current furnace geometry with one reduction nozzle (see Figure 4 only with nozzle 1) and the present mode of operation represents the actual situation. This actual condition is investigated in the first stage using the numerical flow simulation. 

Following the actual-situation analysis of the furnace is the flow optimization. The major parameters here are the number of nozzles, the injection speed of the reducing agent into the melt, and the number and quantity of nitrogen porous plugs. 

The simulation shows the altered flow with the same mass flow rate brought about by the increase in number of nozzles, and its direct effect on the mix of the reducing medium. 

The alteration of the injection speed of the reducing agent into the melt also alters the flow, allowing derivations to be made on the mixing process and the retention time. 

An additional consideration is the influence of nitrogen porous plugs which serves the same purpose. In addition, the best use of the porous plugs can be derived. 

As well as the flow conditions in the melt, the simulations show the conversion of the reducing agent and its input and mixing. 

##### 4.2 Flow optimization 

For the numerical analysis of the drum furnace, a three-dimensional scale model of the furnace is produced on the computer. A suitable calculatory mesh is added to this geometrical 3D model. The calculatory mesh is sufficiently thin to ensure a mesh-independent solution.

The numerical model takes into account the physical processes responsible for the circulation in the bath and the distribution of the reducing agent in the melt. Because the same simplified model is used for every geometrical set-up and all operating variations, a statement on the increase in energy can be made based on the kinetics of the bath and the reducing agent. For this it is assumed that the chemical kinetics, compared to the mixing kinetics, are of negligible speed. 

The momentum of the the reducing agent is essential for the mixing process in the bath. It is also expected that the inert gas flow introduced by the porous plugs will affect the bath kinetics. Due to the large difference

s in density and the impossibility of the reducing agent, inert gas, and copper melt mixing on the macroscopic level, it is expected that the gas phases will move relatively to the melt. For the numerical simulation this means that for each of the phases involved the momentum maintenance equation and the mass-balance equation have to be solved. To do this the Euler-Euler model used in the simulation is particularly suitable. For the modelling, the phases involved are considered as self-mixing, continual-like phases. Continual-like in that the reducing-agent- and the inert-gas-phase consist of small gas bubbles which interact with the copper melt. In the numerical model the gas phase is given a characteristic medium bubble diameter and the local gas phase ratio. The momentum exchange between the phases is calculated using the equation derived by SCHILLER and NAUMANN [3]. 

The turbulent flow conditions in the drum furnace are described with the `realizable k-epsilon model´. This model allows the turbulent rotational flows in the furnace to be described with sufficient accuracy. 

The complexity of the real-life process is further simplified in the following ways. During the entire reduction process the melt is entirely in liquid form. Therefore, any distribution of temperature in the melt does not influence the mixing behaviour. The focal point of the process analysis and opti-

The area calculated is reduced to the part of the furnace filled with molten copper and the surface of the bath is considered to be completely flat. This simplification rests on the assumption that the undulations on the surface of the bath can be disregarded due to their size in respect of the furnace. In the numerical model the flat surface of the molten copper is an inviscid wall; however, in the dispersed gas phase this wall is completely permeable and allows the gas to escape the melt into the surrounding area. 

All real-life system phases are reduced to two phases. The first phase is the molten copper melt; the second phase is the reducing agent and the required compressed air. The second phase is a pseudophase, whose average density is calculated using the reducing agent and air flows being injected.

#### 5 Estimation of productivity 

Taken from the above results and in comparison with the original state (actual situation), the following can be stated. 

Increasing the number of nozzles from one to four results in eighteen percent more of the furnace’s content being reached. 

Reduction of the diameter of the nozzles and the consequent increase in momentum of the reducing agent leads to the same level of tracer penetration during the refinement phase after just forty p

ercent of the time. In comparison to the actual situation, that is after the same amount of treatment time (e.g. thirty seconds), the reducing agent is completely dispersed throughout the melt rather than sixty percent dispersion. This corresponds to more than a sixty-percent improvement in the distribution of the reducing agent. From this is can be concluded that the conversion rates improve accordingly, thus reducing the quantity of reducing agent and the processing time. Well-positioned porous plugs that support the flow of the melt contribute fifteen percent to the situation described above. If the effects on the processing time and the reducing agent consumption are considered from a commercial point of view, the following savings would be made: - 30 % of the reducing agent per charge; and - 30 to 40 % of the processing time for reduction. At the same time the temperature in the melt would be homogenous, allowing about a 2 to 5 % reduction in energy consumption for the entire refinement process. The aforementioned flow improvement has a very positive effect on the oxidation phase of refinement – though this has not been assessed explicitly here – and this in turn is reflected in a shortened processing time for this stage. The simulation of the actual flow situation, where just one nozzle is operated, showed that the reducing agent can only reach a maximum of sixty percent of the content of the drum furnace. By just increasing the number of nozzles, mixing is improved so nearly eighty percent of the content of the bath is reached. If the input velocity of the reducing agent is also increased, the results show that almost one hundred percent of the molten material can be reached. To improve mixing, porous plugs will normally be added to the drum furnace too. Investigation of the flow with and without porous plugs showed th

e reducing agent mixed about fifteen percent better. 

Observations on adding the reducing agent to the content of the bath were the first part of the investigation. In the second part of the investigation, the time it took for mixing was looked at more closely. It was seen that the time for the oxidation and reduction processes can be reduced by around thirty percent with the bath content mixed to the same degree. 

Improved mixing and shorter mixing times lead to less consumption of refining agent. Older refining systems are often operated using double stoichiometry. Improved mixing allows another reduction of the stoichiometry, that is dynamic adjustment of the quantity of refining agent to the process sequence. As well as the reduced quantity of reducing agent, the associated CO2 will clearly also drop. 

Taking productivity into consideration, it could be seen that alone the annual savings of refining agent for the anode furnace looked at here, consisting of a combination of high-velocity lances and porous plugs, leads to the system being worth the investment after one or two years at most. 

Currently, an optimized refining system is being built. Once complete, the data from the simulation will be tested on the re-fitted plant. 

In addition, the result of better mixing in the bath is a uniform temperature throughout the drum furnace. This causes heat in the furnace to be transferred to the bath better. Consequently, the required burner capacity can be reduced by an estimated five percent. The uniform temperature also leads to less solidified slag, in particular on the sides of the drum furnace. This is good for the fireproof material. These additional points were not incorporated into the productivity considerations.

#### Abstract 

Minor element deportment for As, Pb, Bi, Cd and Mo in the Smelter flowsheet has been reviewed. The historical data trends will be compared to theoretical distribution coefficients derived using thermodynamic modeling, and comparisons also made with literature data pertaining to the Copper Industry. The implications of various impurity levels for control of product quality, industrial hygiene and environmental impacts will be dis

cussed. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The Kennecott Utah Copper Smelter utilizes Outokumpu Flash Smelting in conjunction with Kennecott-Outokumpu Flash Converting to process over 1.0 million tonnes of copper concentrate per year, while achieving the lowest emission rate of any copper smelter. The smelter commenced commercial operation in June of 1995 and is now operating above the original design rate. The copper concentrate feedstock originates entirely from the Kennecott Bingham Canyon Mine. 

Concentrate feed to the Smelter contains valuable metals such as Au, Ag, Mo and Re as well as deleterious impurities such as As, Pb, Bi, and Cd. The level of As in anode can influence in-plant hygiene at the Smelter, electrolyte chemistry and resulting cathode quality at the Refinery, and environmental impacts. Lead can influence ‘slimes’ mass flow within the Refinery, and also cathode quality. Bismuth primarily impacts cathode quality, whilst Cadmium mostly impacts in-plant hygiene. 

In order to attain optimum conditions during smelting for the elimination of impurity elements and recovery of valuable metal by-products, the distribution behavior of such elements in the slag, matte, blister and gas phases needs to be well understood. In the current study, the distribution be-

##### 3.2 Fractional distribution 

Fractional distribution is the fraction of element M in a given phase i based on the total input: 



Fractional distribution is affected by the composition of element M in phase i (matte, blister, slag, or gas), the mass of phase i, as well as the composition of element M in the feed and the mass of the feed. Therefore, fractional distribution can vary with changes in composition of element M and the changes in mass. On the contrary, there would be little impact on the distribution coefficient as it is not affected dramatically by changes in composition or mass. The minor element equilibrium would be thermodynamically re-shifted to maintain chemical equilibrium. 

In the current work, the distribution coefficient will be used to describe matte/slag and blister/slag distribution behavior whereas the fractional distribution will be used to quantify minor element

##### 4.1 Matte/slag distribution coefficient 

The matte/slag distribution coefficient for As, Pb, Bi, Cd and Mo in the KUC flash smelting furnace as a function of matte grade is illustrated in Figure 3. The FSF operates at a temperature of 1315 °C and pO2~10<sup>-8</sup> atm. The FSF slag is based on the iron silicate (FeOx-SiO2-CuOx) slag system. Where available, the matte/slag distribution ratios in the FSF are compared with literature data from other smelting operations as well as laboratory experimental data at similar operational conditions and slag system. As seen in Figure 1, _LmAs_ / _s_ tends to remain constant with an increase in matte grade from 60 % to 70 % Cu in matte. Above 70 % Cu in matte, the distribution coefficients increase. Inefficiencies in the Hydrometallurgical Plant resulted in a higher than design deportment of As to tailings and also compromised capability to segregate As to a RCRA waste stream. A planned Rectification project will improve the Hydrometallurgical Plants’ ability to optimize the sulfide circuits used for Cu and As segregation, and also improve control of ‘free’ acid which can adversely affect Cu/As and Cu/Bi separation. Construction work on the rectified Hydrometallurgical Plant will commence in early 2010. 2425 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Kaur, Nexhip, Wilson, George-Kennedy_ Figure A-2 shows that Pb is essentially deported through to the anode refining furnaces; Pb containing FCF slag is re-processed through the FSF. Figure A-3 shows that Bi mainly deports to the refining furnaces, but can also be removed from the circuit through use of the Hydrometallurgical Plant, whereby quantities of FSF process dust are leached to remove Bi from the re-circulating FSF dust load. Inefficiencies associated with separation of Bi will be addressed in the Rectification project. Figure A-4 shows the future capability of the KUC Smelter, post Hydrometallurgical Plant rectification, with the addition of a ‘Slag Concentrate Leach’ stage to further reduce the re-circulating load of As. #### 7 Conclusions 

The distribution ratios of As, Pb, Bi, Cd and Mo between matte/slag and blister/slag was found to be in good agreement with published data under similar operational conditions and slag systems. Whilst the KUCC FSF and FCF achieve high degree of elimination of impurity elements such as As, Bi, Pb and Cd, the loss of valuable metals such as Mo is also high. Various projects are underway at the KUC Smelter to improve overall copper product quality, in-plant hygiene, and environmental impact associated with As, Pb, Bi and Cd minor elements.

### Control of Copper Concentrator by LOI Measurement 

Hossein Nematollahi, Farajollah Kiani, Sedigheh Zeidabadi 

Kian Madan Pars.co No.64-Bahar Ave-Garmsar Gharbi Ave-south shiraz Ave-Mollasadra street Tehran, Iran 

**Keywords:** Copper, flotation, LOI measurement 

#### Abstract 

At SarCheshmeh Copper ore concentrator, the process is controlled by measuring Cu, CuO and Fe in the feed to mill. Sometimes, the adjustment of flotation parameters on the basis of the above measurement is unsatisfactory and the grade and recovery of copper in the concentrate decline to very low values. 

A research program is carried out to find a more confident parameter to control the process. A systematic sampling is carried out and microscopic studies, as well as XRD and chemical analysis and bench scale flotation test are done on the samples to characterize the minerals having the major effects on flotation. 

The most effective and outstanding parameter found, is the LOI of the samples at a precise temperature. On the basis of this parameter and its expansion for the whole ore body, a convenient feed could be prepared for the mill. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The SarCheshmeh copper mine is located at 60 km south of Rafsanjan, a city at 120 km west of Kerman, the major city of Kerman Province in Iran. 

The concentrator of SarCheshmeh has started up since 1981 with a capacity of 40,000 t/d. Since, 2004 a new concentrator has been installed and nearly doubled the capacity. 

The blending of ore from different zones of mine is controlled by the grade of Cu, CuO and Fe, measured during blast holes drilling. These parameters are also used for the adjustment of the concentrator.

Roughly in 40 % of one-year period, the preceding controls are not effective and the operation of concentrator is unsatisfactory. 

A research program is carried out to prepare an effective device to control the process. Many parameters as microscopic character, XRD, chemical composition of different characteristic elements, thermal properties, etc are studied and their relationships towards the process are inspected. 

In addition, the conditions of flotation are tested for different types of ore and some more effective conditions are proposed. 

#### 2 History 

The SarCheshmeh copper mine, which may rank third or fourth largest in the world, containing 1.2 bn t averaging 0.7 % copper and 0.03 % molybdenum, is located near the center of the Zagros Mountain range. 

The SarCheshmeh orebody is oval in shape, 2300 m long Ч 1200 m wide and is related to a late Tertiary granodiorite porphyry that intruded an earlier Tertiary sequence of fine-grained andesite lavas and tuffs. Ore occurs in the porphyry and the surrounding altered andesite. The SarCheshmeh porphyry is a member of complex series of magmatically related intr

usive emplaced in the Tertiary volcanics a short distance from the edge of an older batholithic granodiorite. More than half of the presently known copper ore at SarCheshmeh is contained in biotitized and sericitized andesite outside the contact of the granodiorite porphyry. 

The leach and oxidized capping of the orebody mainly carbonate, averaging 26 m thick was stocked during the opening period of the mine, since 1981. Actually, it is processed mainly in a heap leaching plant, and in a smaller scale, in a bacterial leaching plant. 

The cap overlies a blanket of supergenes sulphides averaging 37 m thick and giving way to a hypogene zone with a copper content about half that of the supergene zone. Hypogene grade rapidly drops off peripheral to the andesite ore halo. 

The principle supergene copper mineral is disseminated chalcocite; covellite occurs nearly at the bottom of the blanket of secondary enrichment dikes containing low-grade hypogene. 

The predominant hypogene sulphides are pyrite chalcopyrite, and molybdenite. Bornite occurrences are rare. Hypogene ore maintains grade consistency with depth. 

The highest-grade hypogene ore occurs as a ring in altered andesite around the periphery of the SarCheshmeh stock. 

The open pit was mined initially at the rate of 40,000 t/d of ore, doubled since 2004, after expansion of the concentrator.

The concentrator is equipped shortly, with three stages of crushing and two stages of grinding, following the concentration by flotation method. 

The capacity of the initial concentrator was production of 1480 t/d of 34 % copper, which approximately has doubled since the second plant is started up. 

Technical assistance for the main project was provided by Anaconda Co., through its subsidiary Anaconda-Iran. The expansion is carried out by the assistance of Svedala Co. 

#### 3 Processing control 

The combination of the ore carried to concentrator, from different blocks of the mine is actually controlled by chemical analysis on Cu, CuO and Fe of blast holes powder collected from every block. 

Despite the above adjustment of the feed, the function of the concentrator is not convenient. During a period of 296 days, the operation of the concentrator has been unsatisfactory for 112 days (nearly 38 % of above period). There is no correlation between the output of the concentrator and the chemical analysis results of Cu, CuO and Fe. 

A research program is carried out to determine a confident parameter, capable of adjusting the concentrator. 

A complete sampling is done from the actual quarries as well as drilling cores. On the basis of different lithology, valuable and gangue minerals, grades, and the type of mineralization the orebody is classified to fifty different types. In addition, sampling is done from the typical geological zones of the mine, as follow:

##### 3.1 Ore microscopic studies 

Upon the microscopic studies on different size fractions and different samples, the orebody could be classified to nine types as follows: 

- 1 hypogene or supergene ore of weak mineralization, accompanying fine pyrite as well as coating of copper minerals by pyrite, 

- 2 ore of convenient grade accompanying metamorphosed ore, 

- 3 ore of high pyrite, high metamorphosis, high coating and low grade, 

- 4 ore of low pyrite, low grade (peripheral ore), 

- 5 high pyrite, accompanying fine chalcopyrite intrusion, intergrown with sericite, chalcopyrite coating on pyrite, high metamorphosis, low grade, 

- 6 variable and complex mineralogy, coating, metamorphosis and high pyrite, 

- 7 hypogene type, low pyrite, convenient copper grade and grain size, 

- 8 supergene type, low grade, high pyrite and coating, 

- 9 hypogene type, simple mineralization and convenient molybdenum grade. 

##### 3.2 Semi-quantitative XRD 

Determination of quantitative analysis, using XRD, did not show any accuracy, especially for the samples containing high quantity of clay minerals and silica. 

##### 3.3 Chemical analysis 

The samples are analyzed for Al2O3, SiO2, K, Na, Fe, CuO and Cu. The categories obtained by these analyses confirm the geological categories, recognized in the region. 

##### 3.4 Differential thermal analysis (DTA) 

On the basis of microscopic and XRD studies, the thermal properties of main valuable and gangue minerals of different types, containing pyrite, chalcopyrite, kaolinite and halloysite are studied (Figure 1). Concerning the variations of the weights of the samples at different temperatures, the LOI (loss of ignition) is measured at 180 °C, 550 °C, 750 °C and 1100 °C for fifty different representative samples of determined ore types. ### Oxidation-Volatilization of Enargite and Stibnite at Roasting / Smelting Temperatures 

Dr. Rafael Padilla, Alvaro Aracena, Dr. Maria C. Ruiz 

University of Concepcion Department of Metallurgical Engineering Edmundo Larenas 285 Concepcion, Chile 

**Keywords** : Pyrometallurgy, oxidation, volatilization, As, Sb 

#### Abstract 

In the production of copper by smelting/converting technology, arsenic and antimony are detrimental minor elements in the concentrates that undergo vaporization side reactions. It is well known, that when these impurities are present in appreciable amounts in the concentrates, the risk of ambient contamination with arsenic and antimony increases dramatically and the quality of the final copper deteriorates. In the present work, the results of an investigation on the volatilization of arsenic from enargite (Cu3AsS4) and antimony from stibnite (Sb2S3) at the temperature range of 500 to 1100<sup>o</sup> C is discussed. The study was conducted in controlled atmospheres of nitrogen and air using pure minerals samples of enargite, pure Sb2S3 and prepared enargite – Sb2S3 mixed samples. The results indicated that in oxidizing atmosphere enargite undergoes complete volatilization of arsenic leaving a residue of CuO as the final copper compound. Stibnite vaporizes partially with the formation of cervantite (SbO2) and the extent of volatilization is greatly dependant on the temperature. At temperature of 800 and 1000<sup>o</sup> C, the vaporization of stibnite reached about 45 and 75 percent, respectively. On the other hand, in the case of oxidation–volatilization of the mixed enargite-stibnite samples, the volatilization of antimony was enhanced by the presence of enargite. The degree of enhancement depended also on the temperature. At 1000<sup>o</sup> C, about 99 percent of Sb2S3 was

volatilized very rapidly in less than 5 min. 

#### 1 Introduction 

At present, the majority of copper is produced from copper sulfide concentrates by smelting/converting technology; in this technology, arsenic and antimony present in the concentrates as impurities are detrimental minor elements that undergo vaporization side reactions in the various stages of the smelting/converting process. When these impurities are present in appreciable amounts 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

2443 

_Padilla, Aracena, Ruiz_ 



in the concentrates, the risk of ambient contamination with arsenic and antimony increases dramatically and the quality of the final copper deteriorates. 

The handling of the minor elements As, Sb, and others impurities is one of the crucial problems that face the Chilean copper smelting industry, because the copper concentrates are becoming increasingly richer in these elements. A pretreatment such as roasting could be used for processing such “dirty” copper concentrates to eliminate these deleterious elements previous to smelting. On this matter, it has been reported that in industrial roasting of copper-gold concentrates in an oxygen deficient environment (< 2 % O2) most of the arsenic in the feed volatilized but about half of the antimony content remained in the calcine [1]. However, to understand properly the elimination by volatilization of these minor elements in roasting or smelting processes, fundamental studies on the oxidation/volatilization of enargite (Cu3AsS4), the main mineral of arsenic in Chilean copper concentrates, and stibnite (Sb2S3) are necessary. In the present work, the results of an investigation on the volatilization of arsenic from enargite and antimony from stibnite at the temperature range of 500 to 1100<sup>o</sup> C are discussed. 

A literature survey on the behavior of enargite at high temperatures showed that the decomposition of enargite in nitrogen atmosphere is fairly well understood as reported by Padilla et al. [2] and Winkel et al. [3], who demonstrated that the decomposition of enargite in nitrogen occurs through the intermediate tenantite (Cu12As4S13). However, little is known on the oxidation/volatilization of arsenic from enargite mineral in an oxidizing atmosphere at the roasting and smelting temperatures. On this matter, Mihajlovic et al. [4] conducted an oxidative roasting of a copper-arsenic mineral with a significant concentration of enargite in a horizontal tube furnace at 400-800 °C. These investigators indicated that the maximum desulphurization was obtained at 800 °C after 30 min, and 81 % of arsenic was also removed at 750 °C after 30 min. 

Concerning Sb2S3, in 2002, Živkovic et al. [5] studied the oxidation kinetics of Sb2S3 in air in the range of 200 to 800 °C by a thermogravimetric method (TG), and concluded that the oxidation proceeds according to: 

Sb2S3 + 9 O2 = 2 Sb2O3 +6 SO2(g) 

Sb2O3 + ½ O2 = 2 SbO2 





By using the Osawa method, activation energies were calculated

and reported as 90 and 97 kJ/mol, for Reactions (1) and (2), respectively.

### New Technologies and Optimization of Reagents in Sulfide Flotation 

Mike Peart, D. R. Nagaraj, S. A. Ravishankar, Ricardo Capanema

**Keywords:** Froth flotation, flotation reagents optimization, base metals, copper ores, sulfide, sustainability 

#### Abstract 

The mining industry is facing the challenge of process optimizing while the availability of natural resources such as water and energy are declining and ore bodies are becoming more complex. In this scenario, new technologies need to be developed to enable truly sustainable solutions considering all social, environmental and economical aspects. To achieve this goal, mineral processing, especially the flotation processes, are evolving in all possible ways including mechanical, operational and chemical. Typically the mechanical and operational aspects are limited by physical constraints and subject to significant capital investment; however greater benefits can often be achieved with very little or no investment by optimizing the chemical components. Cytec has developed new chemistries such as the AERO XD-5002 promoter through the FLOTATION MATRIX 100<sup>TM</sup> process that can replace aged chemistries like xanthates. These new products can deliver better metallurgical performance in the flotation of precious and base metals, in addition to having a more environmentally friendly profile. An overview will be given using examples to highlight the industrial scale use of the FLOTATION MATRIX 100<sup>TM</sup> process and new reagents. 

#### 1 Introduction<sup>1</sup> 

The chronology of development of flotation reagents in industrial processes during the past 100 years is divided by Booth and Freyberger (1962) in two distinct periods (or phases): oil flotation (1860–1920) and chemical flotation (1921–present). A closer scrutiny would suggest three distinct periods (see Table 1), the first being still oil flotation. The second period might be characterized as discovery and expansion (1921–1950<sup>2</sup> ), and the third period is targeted design (1951–present).

- Frothers: Polypropylene glycols and ethers, triethoxybutane

In the early days of flotation, large quantities of fatty and oily materials were used in the range of 10 % to 20 % of the weight of the ore to separate the value components from gangue minerals in ore pulps. Later, various gases replaced these large quantities of oil as a buoyant and separating medium, decreasing oil requirements to less than 1 % of the weight of the ore. With this reduction in oil consumption, inherent differences in the frothing and collecting power of various oils were noted (Booth and Freyberger 1962). Several important modifiers were used to enhance separations, such as lime, sulfur dioxide (SO2), sodium carbonate, and copper sulfate (CuSO4). 

The year 1921 marked the beginning of a major revolution in flotation reagents that set the stage for the next 80 years or so. A trend was established toward reagents of small organic molecules and oils containing sulfur (either naturally or by direct sulfurization). This trend has moved the industry toward reagents of a defined chemical composition. Several major patents appeared (e.g., Perkins 1921; Vivian 1921) which taught that small, water-soluble molecules could be used as collectors instead of large amounts of oil. This trend continued by the later application of N- and S-containing

compounds such as naphthylamines, diamino benzene, toluidines, thiocarbanilide, and several other organic complexing (or chelating) agents for sulfide mineral flotation. Their consumption was low (0.1 to 0.5 lb/t). This was followed by differential flotation using sodium cyanide (NaCN) and the discovery of xanthates, dithiophosphates, dithiocarbamates, mercaptobenzothiazole, and amines (for nonsulfides). It is important to note that the majority of chemicals used for flotation in the period from 1921 to 1950 were developed in other industries (e.g., rubber, textile, tanning). During the third period, 1951–

present, the trend began for developing reagents specifically targeted for flotation application rather than merely evaluating chemicals developed for other industries (see Table 1 for examples). Modern chemical flotation is built on this foundation and thus the industry now accesses rational, scientific rigor from the more recent developments in organic, polymer, and coordination chemistry. The ideal goal is the development of mineral-targeted, high-performance reagents that not only provide improved value recoveries and selective separation, but also provide the platform to extend flotation technique to a much greater variety of mineral and nonmineral separations. 

#### 2 Critical Analysis of the status of flotation reagents<sup>3</sup> 

##### 2.1 Collectors 

It is well established that the main function of the collector is to impart sufficient hydrophobicity to the mineral surface so that the probability of bubble–mineral attachment is increased. It is also well established that a collector molecule accomplishes this function by adsorbing on the mineral surface. Collector adsorption and the consequent development of hydrophobicity on the mineral surface does not guarantee the desired flotation outcome, because flotation is a probabilistic (or rather, pseudo-probabilistic) process. 

A perusal of flotation literature on chemical aspects in the past 100 years would indicate that collectors have been accorded paramount importance and close attention at the expense of modifiers and frothers. From the perspective of the flotation plant’s overall goals of maximizing recovery, grade, and profitability, such an emphasis on collectors alone, limits performance enhancement. Collectors do play a critical role in providing a part of the solution and are necessary but not sufficient. 

Many of the classical problems in flotation that were recognized in the first half-century of flotation – for example, the effect of water chemistry, slime coatings, recovery of coarse and fine particles, difficult mineral separations – have yet to be solved and have received relatively little attention. Even in fundamental studies related to such problems, the tendency has been to focus on xanthates and fatty acids rather than to consider alternatives that posse inherently advantages.

##### 2.2 Modifiers 

Unlike collectors, discussion of modifiers is limited in the literature, although selective flotation is made possible by use of a large number of modifiers. Their importance is in direct relation to complexity of mineralogy. 

The chemistry of modifiers in flotation pulps is quite complex in comparison to that of collectors, and it is more complex in nonsulfide systems than it is in sulfide systems. Modifiers can affect multiple factors simultaneously in flotation pulps and, therefore, have multiple f

unctions. For example, addition of lime in a copper circuit can have the following effects: pH modification (and the resultant changes in interfacial chemistry, solubility of minerals, changes in water chemistry), depression of pyrite, formation of colloidal calcium sulfate precipitate and its adsorption on sulfide minerals, modification of froth characteristics and viscosity of pulp, modification of collector adsorption, precipitation of multivalent metal ions as hydroxides, removal of slime coatings from sulfides, dispersion and depression of certain gangue minerals, and reduction in grinding media wear. Thus, depending upon the type, modifiers can change pH, pulp potential (Ep), composition of the aqueous phase, and surface composition of the minerals and bubbles. They can affect properties of all three interfaces. They are also known to affect dispersion and rise-velocity of bubbles. The same modifier in different circuits could produce very different flotation outcomes, and different modifiers used for pH control in a circuit can have very different results at the same pH. 

Difficulties arise in the laboratory investigation of all aspects of the action of modifiers. Many of the complex effects of modifiers are evident only in real flotation pulps where the variability in mineralogy and operating conditions has a significant impact and is virtually impossible to simulate in the laboratory. Thus, effects observed in model systems used in laboratory investigation can be quite misleading. 

##### 2.3 Frother and Frothing 

The froth phase in flotation is probably the most neglected phase in flotation research, thus its importance, particularly in view of the disproportionate amount of research that has been conducted on collectors. This is not surprising given the complexity of the three-phase froths that comprise a variety of mineral species and aqueous phase species. 

Fundamental studies conducted over the decades to characterize and understand froths and frothing have tended to be mostly reductionistic; for example: study of froths and foams in the absence of solids or using unrepresentative model solids; studies that focus on equilibrium and dynamic surface tension at the liquid/gas interface; methods for evaluation and ranking of frothers, such as froth column tests and dynamic frothability in the absence of solids and other reagents (collectors, modifiers) and under idealized conditions; or studying collector–frother interactions, often in the absence of solids. Extensive studies have been conducted on the role of surface tension of frothers in two-phase foam/froth systems. In fact, some of the earliest surface tension measurements date back to the early period of flotation. Given that only two major classes of frothers: Alcohols and Polyclycols/Glycol

Although these studies have illuminated some fundamental concepts pertaining to froths and foams, they have had, unfortunately, little impact on control or manipulation of froth phase in a plant or on frother selection for a given application. As a result, frother selection and froth phase management are still dependent upon empirical testing, trial and error, visual observation in the plant, and reliance on qualitative descriptors: watery or dry; stability; persistence; and others; and not on surface tension, solubility, bubble size, and so forth. More recently, froth cameras have replaced the experienced eye of the traditional operator. A system much closer to the plant froth phase is a simulated three-phase system (solid/liquid/gas) in the laboratory. In these systems, it has been clearly demonstrated that a mere change in collector, either to a different class or to a different homologue in the same class, can have dramatic synergistic or antagonistic effects on froth characteristics. In extreme cases, the heavily mineralized froths can become very dry and flow with difficulty. Such effects can be linked to hydrophobicity of the solids in the froth phase, but literature is scarce in this aspect. The last extensive study was by Dippenaar, Harris, and Nicol (1978). Froth rheology in the three-phase system is recognized to be important, but again, literature is scarce. Much of the practical information pertaining to interactions between flotation reagents reside as proprietary information in the research and development (R&D) laboratories of reagent developers and are inaccessible. tion without reagents| #### 4 Reagent selection and optimization – Cytec´s Flotation Matrix 1004 ##### 4.1 Traditional reductionist process In the 1920s and 1930s, the number of commercially used flotation reagents was relatively small, and reagent selection for a given application was relatively straightforward. As the number and diversity of commercially available flotation reagents steadily increased to meet the ever-increasing technical and economic challenges, reagent selection became gradually more complicated. Four other factors have made the situation more acute: > 4 The material in this section is based on Nagaraj, D.R and S.A Ravishankar, 2007 and Nagaraj, D.R, 2005. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2458 _New Technologies and Optimization of Reagents in Sulfide Flotation_ - The obsessive research focus on “old” reagents (e.g., xanthate, fatty acid, cyanide) meant that the chemistry and applications knowledge for all other reagents remained woefully inadequate in the published literature. - Science did not keep pace with technology; the increasing emphasis on reductionistic research over the decades meant a widening gap between research and practice. - Application knowledge developed by in-house research in the chemical companies remained largely inaccessible in the public domain. - There has been a steady decline of expertise in flotation reagents in the industry over the decades. Consequently, at present, the process of reagent selection and optimization can be characterized as rather informal, reductionistic, and frequently based on extension of personal experience from one mineral system or plant to another, gut feeling, anecdotes, and myths (Nagaraj and Bruey 2003; Nagaraj 2005). There is no recognized “standard” practice, and the informal process is fraught with pitfalls. For a given separation, at first glance the pool of reagent classes – and homologues within each class – available for selection appears to be large and bewildering. This is partly the result of the evolutionary nature of reagent development over the decades. But more importantly, given the complexity of the flotation system, a particular reagent class or a specific homologue just happens to produce the optimum results for the separation and ore type in question. General guidelines are available for reagent selection in the form of an accumulated knowledge base in reagent developers’ handbooks and product literature (e.g., the Mining Chemicals Handbook [Cytec 2002]). This se

rves to narrow the selection for a given application; however, the metallurgist must still use additional filters to refine the selection to a manageable level in order to move to the laboratory testing phase. Historically, this stage of reagent selection has tended to be reductionistic and informal. Problems in complex systems invariably have multiple solutions, each with its degree of desirability. Even an arbitrary process of reagent selection will provide a solution to a plant’s problem. However, such a solution may not be sufficiently robust, that is, the selected reagent will have a narrow, unoptimized window of performance – and may only be a temporary fix – and its nonrobustness may not even be discovered for a long time, given the significant routine variability in plant performance. This approach is very costly in the long run and adds little to our knowledge base.

Typically the optimization of mechanical and operational factors is subjected to significant capital investments; however the chemicals can frequently have greater leverage in optimizing the process with little or no investment.

This chapter focuses on the sustainable aspects of the chemicals used in mineral processing and recovery, and will describe how mining operations can benefit from competitive advantages when using sustainable chemical solutions. Due to the diversity and complexity of this topic, equally relevant social-political aspects of sustainability will not be addressed. Albeit a recent trend, the key concepts of sustainability are not new to either the chemical or mining industries. The three foundational blocks of sustainability – social, environmental, and economic accountability – have been handled by the industry through actions such as focusing on worker’s safety, limiting the impact of mining on the surroundings, and increasing productivity. This concern for the overlap of the three basic fundamentals, shown in Figure 2, is the basis of the world’s demand for sustainable efforts. Figure 2: Sustainability as the confluence of the triple bottom line The importance of sustainable solutions has become more critical in the face of significant changes in the global balance. Population growth, urbanization, and industrialization have reached levels that have caused depletion of our natural resources. Energy and water have become limited and this represents a challenge both in availability and increasing cost. Likewise for mineral resources, we _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2461 _Nagaraj, Ravishankar, Peart, Capanema_ have already us

ed the easily treatable ores; the ones left are much more complex and demand more sophistication to be economically viable. 

Another aspect brought with industrialization is the implementation of more restrictive regulations. The advent of REACH in Europe is an example of regulations tightening the control of chemicals produced or imported into the region, and a much stricter evaluation of environmental impact of the new projects. 

Today every company including the chemical and mining industries is focusing on asset optimization, specifically through technical solutions. Most organizations are extremely lean, and need to make sure that the time and resources are being used in the right projects and the people with the right set of skills are in the right place. 

##### 5.1 Sustainable framework for the chemical and mining industries 

Both the chemical and mining industries are facing a similar challenge: the need to maximize production while minimizing the use of natural resources and waste generation. To achieve sustainable growth, mining and chemical industries have to earn the right to operate by making sound ethical and moral decisions in community affairs, civic responsibilities and environmental stewardship. 

Sustainability to Cytec is living our values in a changing world by: 

- Providing innovative and sustainable products that compete in a global economy, 

- Achieving the highest standards of safety, health and environmental stewardship, 

- Being responsible to our customers, employees, shareholders and other stakeholders. 

To do so, Cytec follows the twelve principles of green chemistry (Anastas, P. T., J. C. Warner 1998) with the objective to create new innovative reagents that can replace older chemistries, while enhancing (or at least maintaining) the technical performance of traditional chemistries. 

Since 2003, the CEO-led International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) has further defined the triple bottom line for the mining industry by developing industry specific areas of interest through their 10 Principles of Sustainable Development. Emphasis extends beyond the classic sustainable issues of protecting workers and the environment, and includes requiring ethical practices, contributing to improving the surrounding communities, and implementing transparent reporting to the public. 

Such efforts have allowed the mining industry to address public concerns and aid in winning community support when helping establish operational permits for new mines. Additionally, it has been argued that a focus on sustainable practice leads to lower labor costs, lower health care costs, lower production costs, lower regulatory burden, lower closure costs, lower cost of borrowing, lower insurance costs, and better investor relations. 

The mining industry cannot rest on its laurels. Limited resources and new environmental issues make it imperative that mines continue to challenge their processes. While mining has evolved from

##### 5.2 The chemical industry needs to assist the mining industry in developing sustainable solutions 

The chemical industry should strive to become an active partner with the mining industry to quickly develop more sustainable solutions. Future collaborative efforts will simplify logistics planning, increase both workers’ and the surrounding community’s safety, and also increase profitability. 

First, however, the chemical industry needs to become more aware of the impact it can make on the mining industry by understanding its needs. It will always be important to attain a high yield of desired metals or minerals, but it is also important to provide the highest value. Chemical companies need to provide value to the mining industry by considering other areas that impact the overall mining operations: raw materials consumption, processing labor, product handling and fine fees. Implementing sustainable solutions will automatically provide monetary savings around these areas. Collaboration between the industries will be required to understand the core issues and adjust reagents to address the critical areas of concern. 

Academia also needs to recognize and address the newer complexities of the industry; mining reagent research needs to expand beyond the classic fundamentals. Focusing on optimizing a single parameter of a single reagent (the ideal contact angle of a dialkyl dithiophosphate on chalcopyrite at a given size) with all other variables fixed does not bring value at the site level. New research needs to focus on understanding the interaction of combined collectors, frothers and modifiers with differing water quality to fully understand the synergies and conflicts that occur among the variables. Likewise the interaction with alternate water quality including recycled processing water and salt water needs to be further researched, due to decreasing freshwater worldwide. 

##### 5.3 Areas where the chemical industry can lead to a higher level of mining sustainability 

Collaboration between the mining and chemical industries can improve sustainability in multiple aspects; from gaining investor interest, to protecting wildlife, to increasing community support, just to name a few. Cytec focuses on three notable sustainable benefits which include: improving the safety of chemicals, increasing operational efficiency, and increasing mining resources. Cytec considers these areas to be some of the most time- critical issues and thus primary concerns for the mining industry.

#### Abstract 

In recent years, tellurium has been extensively used in the manufacture of semiconductor materials. For this type of application, high-purity tellurium is required. Selenium, lead and silicon are usually the main impurities in tellurium. 

In the precious metals plant of Mexicana de Cobre (MdC), a company subsidiary of GRUPO MEXICO, which is located in Nacozari, Sonora Mexico, a sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) based-slag is generated during the last stage of the dore refining in the precious metal refinery Kaldo furnace. 

In the original precious metals plant design, no process for tellurium recovery was considered. However, personnel of MdC were recently commissioned to study existing technologies for tellurium processing and eventually developed a selective new process for tellurium production in order to reduce the impurities content in the elemental tellurium product. 

In this new process, the formation of sodium tellurate (Na2TeO4) as an intermediate compound is proposed, instead of tellurium dioxide (TeO2) intermediate of the conventional process. Experimental tests under laboratory conditions indicate that the novel process yields higher precipitation selectivity for tellurium than the conventional process. A comparison of its efficiency regarding impurities co-precipitation with respect to the conventional process is discussed in this work. 

In addition to the idea to produce elemental tellurium of high purity by using the new chemical method and the known electrowinning technique, Mexicana de Cobre has started a preliminary study in order to identify and to propose an efficient process to recover the tellurium contained in all the

#### 1 Introduction 

In the metallurgical complex of Mexicana de Cobre S.A. de C.V., a company property of GRUPO MEXICO, there is a copper smelter, an electrolytic copper refinery, a rod plant, a precious metals plant and acid plants. The precious metals plant which has been operated since 1998 produces gold, silver and selenium. Although it is widely known [1, 2] that normally the anode slimes contain some important quantities of tellurium, this process recovery was not considered during the development of the project. This precious metals refinery uses a Kaldo furnace where the dore is purified and it is in the last stage of the refining process where tellurium is skimmed as sodium tellurite in a Na2CO3 based-slag after it has been oxidized with air. Together

with tellurium some other impurities and elemental silver are also carried out in the basic slag. Taking into consideration that independently of the high price of tellurium, the silver is a valued metal and it is necessary to separate it from the slag where both elements are contained. The conventional process for tellurium recovery consists of a first stage of water leaching where tellurium is dissolved as sodium tellurite (Na2TeO3) and the elemental silver remains in the leaching residue. After water leaching, the silver is recycled to the Kaldo furnace and the tellurium solution is neutralized to a pH value of 5.5 using sulfuric acid in order to precipitate the tellurium as tellurium dioxide (TeO2). During the precipitation of tellurium some impurities precipitate together with TeO2 and in order to remove most of impurities, normally it is necessary to dissolve the impure tellurium dioxide using NaOH and again tellurium is precipitated as TeO2 at pH of 5.5. This cycle is repeated until the tellurium dioxide has been reached an accepted chemical quality. Next TeO2 is dissolved in an acid (H2SO4-HCl) solution and then tellurium is reduced to element by mean of using SO2(g). This process is not very selective so the precipitated tellurium is not very pure. A more effective process is the dissolution of the tellurium dioxide in NaOH solution where tellurium is recovered by electro-winning. Mexicana de Cobre personnel have reviewed this method as an option to produce commercial tellurium but in addition following an alternative route they have found a new and better method for tellurium production which is based on the precipitation of the tellurium contained in the water leaching solution as sodium tellurate (Na2TeO4). The main characteristic of this compound is that it is non soluble in caustic solutions and also is precipitated more selectively than the corresponding TeO2 in the conventional process. In a previous paper [3], a comparison was done between the conventional process and the proposed process when tellurium is recovered using SO2(g) as a reduction agent. After doing this work, efforts were focused to test the new method for tellurium production by means of electro-winning in order to increase the tellurium selectivity. The test results showed that is possible to produce elemental tellurium of commercial grade (99.95 % Te). _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2474 _An Enhanced Process for Tellurium Production in Mexicana de Cobre_ Because of the excellent results, and that the price of this element has appreciated in the international market, our company decided to begin a global process for tellurium production and a study has been started in order to identify the main streams where tellurium could be recovered and finally determine the full production rate. #### 2 Process description and comparison Tellurium slag

### Penetration Behavior of an Annular Gas-Solid Jet Impinging on a Liquid Bath 

H. Y. Sohn, Nurzhan Dyussekenov Sung Sil Park University of Utah LS-Nikko Copper Inc. Department of Metallurgical Engineering 70 Daejeong-ri, Onsan-eup, Ulju-gun Salt Lake City, Utah 84112, USA Ulsan, 689 892, South Korea 

**Keywords:** Annular jet, lance, penetration depth, Mitsubishi smelting process, injection, gas-solid 

#### Abstract 

One of the problems associated with top-blow injection, as used in the Mitsubishi Continuous Smelting Process, is the severe erosion of the hearth refractory below the lances. A new configuration of the lance to form an annular gas-solid jet rather than the circular jet was designed in this laboratory. With this new configuration, solid particles fed through the center tube leave the lance at a much lower velocity than the gas and the penetration behavior of jet is significantly different than with the circular lance where the solid particles leave the lance at the same high velocity as the gas. 

The effects of solid feed

rate, gas flow rate, and lance height on the penetration behavior of an annular gas-solid jet were determined and compared with a circular jet. The results of cold model tests using an air-sand jet issuing into a water bath showed that the penetration of the annular jet is much less sensitive to the variations in particle feed rate and gas velocity than that of the circular jet. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The Mitsubishi process is a copper smelting and converting process capable of continuously producing blister copper from copper concentrates [1-4]. This process employs matte smelting, slag cleaning, and converting furnaces connected in series by a continuous gravity flow of molten materials through heated launders. In the smelting furnace, a jet that contains a much larger amount of solid particles than in the converting furnace penetrates deeply into the matte layer and strongly agitates the molten bath. The deep penetration and strong agitation provide a good contact between oxygen, liquid, and solid particles, resulting in rapid heat and mass transfer and high production efficiency [5, 6]. 

On the other hand, excessively deep penetration of the gas-solid jet causes serious wear of the refractory beneath the lances [1, 7-9]. In the late 1970s, Mitsubishi Materials Corporation [1, 8] studied the behavior of a gas-solid jet injected from a circular lance into a liquid bath to avoid sudden 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

2483 

_Sohn, Dyussekenov, Park_ 





melt leakages from the smelting furnace due to rapid erosion of the hearth brick that they had experienced. A series of cold model tests and subsequent hot model tests were performed to determine the penetration depth of the jet. The results of their study were applied to an improved design of the smelting furnace and lances to reduce the wear of the hearth bricks by setting a proper distance between the lance tip and the bath surface and to enlarge the diameter of the lances for a reduced jet velocity [8]. In spite of many improvements, the replacement of worn refractory on the hearth of the smelting furnace continues to cause costly shut-downs in the Mitsubishi process [7-9]. 

In addition, the existing lance system requires the solid charge to be under a pressurized gas to make a gas-solid jet at the intake of the lance pipe. Thus, it is necessary to transport the solid charge by high pressure pneumatic conveyors rather than simple drag or screw conveyors. The pneumatic conveying system causes frequent leakage in the conveying pipe due to erosion by abrasive solid particles and requires frequent and expensive repairs. The current lances are designed to form a gassolid mixture at the top end so that solid particles leave the lances at the same high velocity as the gas [1]. If the solid particles are separated from the gas stream inside the lance and exit the lance at a lower velocity than the gas, the penetration behavior of the jet in liquid would be significantly different. In the annula

r lance configuration, the inner pipe would be extended all the way down to the tip of the outer pipe, which would lead to the feeding of solid particles into the lance by gravity. In such a case, particles will exit the lance with a lower velocity than the gas. ##### 3.2 Experimental procedure 

The penetration depths for the air and air-sand jets were measured at various experimental conditions in terms of air mass flow rate, lance height, sand feed rate, and annulus cross-sectional area [20]. In the case of air jet injection, the annulus cross-sectional area was changed by varying both the inner and outer tube diameters. When the sand particles were laden on the air jet, only one inner pipe diameter was used because of the difficulty in controlling the feed rate with a smaller or larger diameter of tube. In this case, the annulus cross-sectional area was changed by varying the outer pipe diameter. The air flow rate was measured and controlled by the rotameter equipped with a throttle valve. The reading from the rotameter was calibrated with the operating pressure measured at the outlet. 

#### 4 Results and discussion 

##### 4.1 Comparison in the penetration behavior of circular and annular jets 

Air jets laden with sand particles were directed normally toward the water bath with varying sand feed rate, air flow rate, and lance height. The air-sand jets formed cavities of significantly different shapes. A cavity of a well-defined shape was formed only at relatively low mass rates of sand particles. In this case, the penetration depth was measured at the deepest point of a cavity. However, at the highest range o

f sand feed rate and with significant air flow rate, an emulsion of air bubbles mixed with sand particles penetrates deeply into the water bath without forming a well-defined cavi- 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

2489 

_Sohn, Dyussekenov, Park_ 



ty. In such a case, the penetration depth of an air-sand jet was recorded as the point where the sand particles separated from the air bubbles and fell down just by gravity. 

It was found that the penetration depth increased linearly with the mass flow rate of sand particles. Further, the slope of the line increased with air jet velocity and decreased with lance height. These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering the air-sand jet as a single phase jet changing in its density and velocity along the centerline of the jet axis [21]. When sand feed rate increased, the average density of the jet increased and the jet had a larger momentum to balance with a larger pressure force exerted by water at the bottom of a deeper cavity. When the lance height increased, the jet penetrated shallower because of the decrease in both the average density and velocity along the jet axis due to the expansion of the jet. #### 5 Conclusions 

A new configuration of lance was designed to form an annular gas-solid jet in which solid particles leave the lance at a substantially lower velocity than the gas. The penetration behavior of the annular gas-solid jet into a liquid bath was investigated by measuring the penetration depth and compared to the behavior of a circular jet. 

The experiments on the impingement of an air-sand jet into a liquid bath showed a linear increase in the penetration depth with the increase of sand feed rate for both the annular and circular jets. The rate of increase in the penetration depth with sand feed rate increased with increased air jet velocity and decreased lance height. The effect of sand feed rate and air jet velocity on the penetration depth of an annular air-sand jet was found to be much smaller than for the circular jet. 

The variation in penetration depth with the annulus cross-sectional area of a gas-solid jet depends mainly on the mass loading ratio of sand particles relative to gas mass. At a high mass flow rate of air and a low sand feed rate, the total momentum of air jet is dominant over the momentum rate of sand particles. Therefore, as the cross-sectional area of the air jet increased at the same issuing velocity, the momentum rate of the air increases, resulting in a deeper penetration depth. In the case when the volumetric flow rate of air is the same, the penetration depth decreases with increasing cross-sectional area because of the decrease in the jet velocity. However, when a substantial amount of solid particles is present in the jet, the variation of penetration depth with air jet cross-sectional area is quite different. The tendency of the penetration depth to increase with annulus crosssectional area at the same velocity of jet can be overshadowed by the contribution of the solid particles. When the annulus cross-sectional area is increased, the degree of spreading of particles increases, leading to a shallower penetration depth even with the increased mass flow rate of the gas. 

When the air jet issues at the same volumetric flow rate, the penetration depth can be shallower for a smaller cross-sectional area despite the higher gas velocity if the mass loading ratio is high. In this case, the effect of the increase in the spreading of sand particles at a higher gas velocity is much larger than the effects of the decreased cross-sectional area of the jet that confines the solid particles in a smaller area and increases the air jet velocity. 

It is also noted that the penetration depth decreases with increase

d lance tip height not only due to a decrease in the centerline velocity at the surface of water but also because of the increase in the particle spreading.

It is concluded that the penetration depth of an impinging annular gas-solid jet into a liquid is much less sensitive to the variations in gas velocity and solid feed rate than for a circular jet. The spreading of solid particles is one of the important parameters in gas-solid jetting that affect the penetration depth. The results of this study are expected to provide a basis for redesigning the lance to improve the service life of a furnace that uses a gas-solid lance.

#### Abstract 

Waste heat boiler (WHB), a standard unit operation used for energy recovery and dust removal in Flash smelting processes, often slow down the continuous operation of the smelter due to tube leakages, insufficient cooling, dust accretion build-ups, and surface fouling. Degrading concentrate mineralogy, frequent blend changes coupled with process variations adds to the severity, thereby affecting the consistent operation and performance of the Waste Heat boiler. 

The focus of the present work was to analyze the performance of Flash Smelting WHB design and to provide an optimal design for improvements within the operational and cost constraints. The scientific methodology involved regular mineralogical analysis of dust accretions and concentrates, process and data analysis, thermodynamic analysis and mainly CFD for design modification analysis. 

A complete three dimensional, non isothermal CFD model comprising the settler, uptake shaft and WHB was modeled in ANSYS-CFX 11. The radiative heat transfer was modeled using P1 thermal radiation model. The tube banks in the convection sections were modeled using porous loss model with momentum and energy loss coefficients obtained from the measured pressure drop and temperature measurements. A standard k-ε turbulence model was used for flow turbulence. 

The CFD model was validated with the plant temperature measurements for the radiation and convection sections. A number of design modification studies with boiler process and design parameters were carried out to arrive at the best possible solution with baffle. The overall improvement solution involved conceptualization & designing of the baffle and its implementation, followed with boiler revamping and improved operational practice.

#### 1 Introduction 

Waste Heat Boiler (WHB), an integrated part of the Outokumpu Flash Smelting process (FSF), plays an important role in the cooling of smelter off-gases, recovery of heat and flue dust and maintaining the continuous operation of the smelter [1]. Unfortunately, they often interrupt the smooth operation of the smelter due to many reasons viz., improper cooling, tube surface fouling, corrosion and erosion of tube surfaces, dust accretion/cornice build-up, tube leakages, etc. The SO2 rich off-gas from the FSF process carries a lot of heat energy and dust particles from smelter to waste heat boiler. Dust account for almost 4 to 10 % of the total feed materials that are being fed to the smelter by Outokumpu flash smelting process [2]. In the radiation section of the WHB, the temperature decreases leading to waste heat recovery, sulphates become thermodynamically stable and the sulphation of oxidic dust particles commences. Releasing heat may lead to an increase in particle temperatures, softening of the sulphated particles, a

nd formation of dust accretions on the heat transfer surfaces. Decreased heat transfer efficiency due to accretions and blockages of the gas flow paths may cause severe operational problems [3]. 

Previous works [4-6] have reported the importance of a proper hydrodynamic design of WHB, leading to minimum dust build-up and fouling, thereby enhancing the life of WHB. Initial efforts by Yang and Jokilaakso [4] were focussed on raising the ceiling of WHB in the first half of the radiation along with a cooling dam in the mid-way of the radiation section. Further, the work by Yang et al. [5] by using baffle shows the off gas leaving the radiation section gets cooled to about 750<sup>o</sup> C even at the rate of 60,000 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h leaving minimum volume of dead zones in the radiation section. Perhaps the most extensive review on the concept and implementation of baffles in the copper smelter worldwide has been given by Peippo et al. [6]. Processing higher gas volumes, higher cooling and managing the gas-dust chemistry at right temperatures, could be perhaps one of the most important features for the boiler modifications with baffles. Water tubes in the boiler are exposed directly to the corrosive environment by high temperature SO2 gas and also by flue dust. Therefore, it is very important to know the hydrodynamics inside the boiler [7]. Energy is recovered from the hot off-gas entering at ~1250<sup>o</sup> C to 1350<sup>o</sup> C through water circulation by which the temperature has to reduce to ~350<sup>o</sup> C before enterning the electrostatic precipitator (ESP). 

From the above studies, it is well understood that a proper gas-solid flow pattern, non-isothermal mixing, gas cooling and associated sulphation reactions are critical for the consistent performance of WHB and hence is the focus of the present work. The overall solution methodology involved regular analysis of dust accretions and boiler tube, thermodynamic study for phase analysis at boiler condition and design modification analysis using CFD. For the sake of brevity, only the major work component on design has been presented. Design modification studies with respect to the sulphation air velocity (effect of nozzle diameter) and baffle design (number, location, type & height) have been attempted. The boiler under consideration is from the FSF process, having problems pertaining to higher frequency of tube leakages, higher boiler temperature and convection section jamming.

The convection outlet should be near 350<sup>o</sup> C to fulfil the requirements of electrostatic precipitators. In case of the un-sulphated particles or partially sulphated particles enter the convection section, the sulphatation reaction will take place in the convection chamber and the softening of particles will sinter hard on the convection tube banks. 

All the above discussed critical aspects along with the process, design and operational constraints were taken into consideration for obtaining an optimal design modification of the WHB. The two important aspects viz., (a) Reduced impact on the roof and side wall (b) Cooling of gas in the range 700 to 750<sup>o</sup> C in radiation section to enhance sulphatation reaction, formed the basis for the design modifications. Another important consideration was minimal flow deviation from the original flow path and trend to avoid any complications with the original equipment’s process/design specifications. The convergence times and the solution efforts required for each simulation was considerably high due to the swirling effect created by the settler-uptake shaft-WHB design configuration, radiative and natural convection effects in radiation zone, forced convection effects in convection zone and number of design modifications attempted. 

#### 3 Results and discussion 

In the present work, only two main design modifications are described in the below discussion with respect to modification of sulphatation air nozzles and placement of internal wall (baffle). 

##### 3.1 Base case design analysis 

Radiation chamber gas flow of WHB is complex, irregular and recirculating nature. Almost 65-80 % of total heat transfer and 2/3 of total dust settling takes place in radiation section. On the other hand, convection zone chamber’s flow is relatively regular among the tube banks, irrespective of changes made in the radiation section. Hence, the understanding of flow pattern in the radiation section becomes extremely

important. The gas flow for the unmodified design is shown in Figure 2. The high velocity dust laden gas coming from the settler first takes a 90o bend in the uptake shaft and again turns 90o , resulting in highly swirling flow at the entry of the WHB. This leads to a biased flow towards the wall adjacent to reaction shaft, and severe short circuiting along the roof, leaving a larger lower portion of the radiation section unutilized for the off-gas cooling. Due to the higher impact of main gas flow mainly on the roof, this region is more prone for erosion/corrosion and dust accretion effects as seen from plant observations. A large flow recirculation, originating at radiation outlet, and mixing back into the main gas stream near the throat is also observed. Such a recirculating gas flow has the tendency of carrying the dust particles all the way back to the throat resulting in the throat jamming or cornice formation, a regular feature of almost all WHB. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2507 _Thakre, Kumaresan, Basu, Shah, Chauhan, Chugh, Khandelwal, Mathur_ The effect of flow pattern on sulphation air is observed in Figure 3.
